# Review: Bondarchuk, *Transfer of Training in Sports* Vol I, Chapters 1-2 (round 1, Opus)

Reviewer: independent round-1 reviewer (Opus), 2026-09-27. Scope: all 19 entries in
`staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/`.
Read-only on entries and source.

**Method.** Source: the Yessis text PDF (`Transfer of Trainng in Sports - Bondarchuk.pdf`, 236 pp.,
real text layer), not the Golden image scan. I extracted the text layer page by page with
PyMuPDF using the same 0-based index as the entries, checked every quote and number against it,
and opened load-bearing pages as images with the Read tool (viewer 38, 77, 164) to confirm the
text layer matches the printed page. **Locators below are written "PDF n (viewer n+1) / p. X"**,
where PDF n is the entries' 0-based index and printed p. = PDF - 17 in the body (PDF 18 = p. 1).
Front matter: PDF 2 = i, so PDF 12 = xi, PDF 14 = xiii.

**Confidence check.** No entry uses `proven`. Every `supported` / `untested` rating is within the
brief's cap for translated Soviet-era work. No confidence row is changed except where noted
(`contested` for a source contradiction).

**Duplicates.** No vault entry restates any of the 19 without a new angle. Closest overlap:
vault `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(secondary paraphrase of the four classes; the Bondarchuk entry is the primary source, so it
is a new angle). The Moyer `principle--sprint-transfer-motor-ability-vs-motor-skill.md` covers
Thorndike's identical elements; `framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer` adds the
generalist/holistic debate, so it is also new. Reciprocal links: Moyer four-categories entry
and Moyer `claim--exercise-selection-over-intensity-volume-sprint.md` (which quotes the PDF 24
"unnecessary muscle groups" passage second-hand) should point back here after promotion.

## Cross-cutting problems (apply to most rows; fix once, everywhere)

1. **Population is misstated as Soviet-only.** Nearly every entry says "Soviet" or "Soviet-era"
   athletes, and `_book.md` says the corpus is "entirely within the USSR system." The source
   says otherwise: "learning-training groups which included not only native, but foreign
   athletes" and "More than 7,000 athletes having different sports qualifications were
   examined" (PDF 8 (viewer 9) / p. vii); "The data used was received mainly through the use of
   questionnaires from native and foreign athletes having different sports qualifications.
   The questionnaires were carried out over the course of four Olympic cycles. Also analyzed
   were tests results of individual athletes as recorded in different literature sources"
   (PDF 76 (viewer 77) / p. 59). Table 8 lists L. Evans, T. Smith, M. Cox and Bulgarian athletes
   (PDF 48 / p. 31). **Correction for every "When NOT to apply":** "Population: native (USSR) and
   foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires
   over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF 8 / p. vii; PDF 76 / p. 59)."
   Keep "not football, not team sport."
2. **The significance threshold is never stated.** "A positive interrelationship between
   exercises begins at 0.349" (PDF 76 / p. 59); women's pole vault uses 0.423 (PDF 111 / p. 94).
   Every Chapter 2 claim entry quotes coefficients without it. Add one line to each claim entry
   (and to `heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect`).
3. **Non-steroid restriction.** The preface limits the data to "training systems without the use
   of steroids" and says steroid use raises results in all exercises, masking transfer
   (PDF 9 (viewer 10) / p. viii). This is a scope condition on every correlation; add it to the
   methodology heuristic at minimum.
4. **Unlabelled application examples.** The brief forbids invented examples without a label.
   Nine entries give an invented football or event example in plain text (listed per row).
   Correction in each case: prefix the Example with "Inference:".
5. **`_book.md` errors (outside the 19 but blocking for the next batch).** (a) "entirely within
   the USSR system" (see 1). (b) "PDF pages 52-65 ... pure normative tables, no narrative prose"
   is false: Tables 1-34 end at PDF 60; PDF 60-65 carry prose plus Tables 35-40 (implement
   weight difference norms), and PDF 64-67 carry the section's conclusions (PDF 61-65 / pp. 44-48).
   (c) The row "1.g Model Characteristics (Tables 1-34)" should read Tables 1-40.

## Entry table

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| `framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes.md` | FIX | (1) Voice. The entry treats the Glossary as "the book's" and argues it is probably Bondarchuk's. The Glossary contains translator voice: "In the U.S., these terms are most often used interchangeably" and "The physical education discipline is more highly developed and scientific in the Russian literature than in the U.S." (PDF 13 (viewer 14) / p. xii); "This is a unique term that has no analogy in the English language" (Motor Analyzer, same page). The task rule: a translator (Yessis) voice is not the author's. (2) Abbreviations. The entry labels "Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP", "SDE", "CE". The Glossary attaches "SPP" to a different term, "Specialized Exercises ... Also known as specialized physical preparation (SPP)" (PDF 14 / p. xiii); "SDE" and "CE" are not in the Glossary. (3) Example is unlabelled and conflicts with the author: "general preparatory = general conditioning running" for a shot putter, while Bondarchuk says short runs for throwers are specialized-preparatory and calls classifying middle/long-distance running as general "Even more surprising" (PDF 24 (viewer 25) / p. 7). (4) Population line (cross-cutting 1). Quotes checked: GPP at PDF 12 / p. xi, SPE and SDE at PDF 14 / p. xiii, CE at PDF 11-12 / pp. x-xi, local vs global at PDF 75 / p. 58: all correct. | Replace the voice note with: "The Glossary is unsigned and contains lines in the translator's voice (U.S. comparisons, PDF 13 / p. xii). Treat the definitions as the translated edition's, possibly Yessis's glosses; Bondarchuk's own usage is in Chapter 1-2 prose (e.g. PDF 24 / p. 7; PDF 62 / p. 45, 'we did not take exercises from the general developmental group')." Drop "SPP/SDE/CE" as Glossary labels or mark them "this entry's abbreviations"; note that the Glossary's "SPP" glosses "Specialized Exercises". Rewrite the Example as "Inference:" and use Bondarchuk's own placement: short sprints, barbell clean/snatch, half squat = specialized-preparatory for throwers (PDF 24 / p. 7); lighter/heavier implement throws = specialized-developmental (PDF 62 / p. 45; PDF 69 / p. 52); pick a general example the author does not reclassify, or say he gives none. |
| `framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer.md` | NO-GO | Reverses the author's conclusion. Entry: "Bondarchuk proposes that ... the achieved level from a previous stage can transfer to the following stage in one of three ways" (start / middle / end). Source: the three are "situations" one "can encounter" in "sports practice" (PDF 35 (viewer 36) / p. 18); his own conclusion is the opposite: "we came to the conclusion that the transfer ... takes place **not at the beginning, middle or end** of each of the following stages, blocks, **but over the duration of them**" (PDF 37 (viewer 38) / p. 20, opened as image). The entry quotes "we came to the conclusion that..." in Why it works as support for the three-situation model. It also omits his condition: transfer "can occur only in those situations in which ... a succession is observed in the methods of training used ... mainly specialized-developmental exercises. If a succession ... does not exist, then transfer is not observed" (PDF 37-38 / pp. 20-21). Secondary: current transfer is also "observed on stages of general preparation and in blocks of physical preparation when using the stage and block methods" (PDF 42 / p. 25), so "distant with the stricter stage/block methods" is incomplete. "multi-decade national training cycles" is invented. Discus Example is unlabelled. Eric's-baseline sentence ending "that is functionally the 'transfer in the middle' case" is the entry's reasoning, not Eric's. Keep current vs distant (PDF 41-42, 66 / pp. 24-25, 49), adding that current transfer also occurs inside stage/block general-preparation stages (PDF 42 / p. 25). Keep `untested` for the succession conclusion. Label the Example and the baseline mapping "Inference:". Fix population. |
| `framework--general-vs-specialized-tests-for-transfer.md` | FIX | (1) The entry defines "Specialized tests" as "most reliably results in specialized-developmental exercises". Source keeps these separate: "In specialized tests for each sport the exercises are very similar" and "Each event in this group has its own specific tests" (PDF 68 (viewer 69) / p. 51); the SDE point is a separate reliability statement ("Foremost in most of these are those tests that show the level of preparation in specialized-developmental exercises", PDF 68-69 / pp. 51-52). (2) Omits the author's first rule: the competitive exercise "in all track and field events, is the most important test" (PDF 68 / p. 51). (3) "less-confirmed reliability as *transfer* indicators" adds "as transfer indicators"; source says only reliability "still have not been fully confirmed" (PDF 69 / p. 52). (4) "the underlying logic ... is directly portable" is an unlabelled judgment. (5) Wide-receiver Example is invented and unlabelled. Checked correct: general-test list incl. Abalakov jump (PDF 68 / p. 51); "tightened up in the near future" (PDF 69 / p. 52); no reference number given. | Rewrite the two bullets as: general tests (shared across events) vs specialized tests (event-specific); then a separate sentence: "Of tests generally, the reliability of SDE tests (lighter/heavier implements, short-approach jumps, set segments at set speed and rest) 'has already been shown'; GP and SP test reliability 'not fully confirmed' (PDF 68-69 / pp. 51-52)." Add "The competitive exercise is the most important test (PDF 68 / p. 51)." Delete "as transfer indicators". Prefix "directly portable" sentence and the Example with "Inference:". Fix population. |
| `framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer.md` | FIX | (1) Block method misrepresented. Entry: Bondarchuk "credits the 'block method' ... as the holistics' practical answer to sequencing." Source: he names the block method (PDF 28 (viewer 29) / p. 11, ref [49]) and then says "there is a theoretical and practical error working at the base of the artificial division of form and content" (same page). The entry drops the criticism. (2) Omits the holistic deficiency he names: athletes peak first in non-specific exercises and "the level of trainedness decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized exercises" (PDF 28 / p. 11). (3) Specifist gloss "(muscle groups, coordination structure, biomechanics)" is not in the source, which says only "some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of elements" (PDF 20 / p. 3). (4) "dominant 1940-1960": source says views "were formed during the years from 1940-1960" (PDF 23 / p. 6). (5) "beyond two bracketed reference numbers ([34, 57, 182])" lists three. | `framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive.md` | NO-GO | Title and When-to-apply assert a rule the author contradicts.    those situations in which ... a succession is observed", mainly specialized-developmental
   exercises (PDF 37-38 / pp. 20-21); "without an increase in achievement with the exercises used,
   training transfer is not realized" (PDF 72 / p. 55); transfer is realized only within cycles of
   sports form development (PDF 7 / p. vi; PDF 73 / p. 56). Candidate principle entry.

   muscle groups.** Short runs for jumpers and throwers, the barbell clean and half squat are
   specialized-preparatory, not general; aerobic running is not "general" either; "extreme
   development of speed-strength abilities of the leg flexor muscles shows up negatively on the
   ... leg extensors", and excess arm strength in a hammer thrower reduces implement amplitude
   (PDF 24-25 / pp. 7-8). His study took no general-developmental exercises at all (PDF 62 / p. 45).

4. **Implement-weight dosing and the overdose warning.** Correlations peak when implements
   differ from competition weight by 10-20% (PDF 115 / p. 98); Tables 35-40 give expected
   distance differences per implement (PDF 62-64 / pp. 45-47); the "throwing boom" of 200-300
   (up to 500) standing throws a session produced negative after-effects, and imitation without
   resistance does not develop physical abilities (PDF 133 / p. 116); historically heavy
   implements in fall-winter, light before competition, in 4-6 week cycles, now 30-50% of
   training time (PDF 114 / p. 97).

   distance nears the competitive distance (PDF 160-161 / pp. 143-144); and "achieving a definite
   level of test results, even in the specialized-developmental exercises, does not guarantee an
   increase in sports achievement in the main event" (PDF 65 / p. 48). The first fits the

13	
14	# "Current" vs. "Distant" Transfer: When in a Training Block the Earlier Work Actually Pays Off
15	
16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk proposes that when a training cycle is built in successive
17	stages/blocks, the achieved level from a previous stage can transfer to the following
18	stage in one of three ways (PDF pp. 35-38, printed pp. 18-21):
19	1. **Transfer at the start** of the next stage/block — the previous stage's result can
20	   then be allowed to decrease, increase, or hold, because it already did its job of
21	   creating the "base."
22	2. **Transfer in the middle** of the next stage/block — the previous level must be
23	   actively maintained (not allowed to drop) while the next stage's exercises are
24	   developed, using reduced-volume maintenance work.
25	3. **Transfer at the end** of the next stage/block — the previous stage's level must be
26	   held all the way through.
27	
28	He then names two broader modes across an entire multi-stage cycle: **"distant" transfer**
29	(entering sports form in one exercise class first, other classes only later — harder to
30	manage because you must simultaneously maintain the earlier gains and build the later
31	ones) versus **"current" (flowing) transfer** (all exercise classes reach sports form
32	together, because a consistent, unbroken mix of general/specialized-preparatory/
33	specialized-developmental/competitive exercises runs throughout every stage rather than
34	being introduced and dropped stage by stage). Current transfer is associated with
35	variational, combinational, and complex methods of cycle construction; distant transfer
36	with the stricter stage/block methods. (PDF pp. 41-42, 66-67, printed pp. 24-25, 49-50.)
37	He also states that excluding specialized-developmental and competitive exercises for more
38	than 3-4 weeks under the variational method causes a real loss of the previously achieved
39	level. (PDF p. 38, printed p. 21.)
40	
41	**Why it works** — No physiological mechanism is offered; this is a purely descriptive,
42	practice-derived model the author says he arrived at by observing which cycle-construction
43	methods succeeded ("we came to the conclusion that..."), with no cited independent
44	verification or controlled comparison in the excerpted text. **Inference:** the "current
45	transfer" mode maps loosely onto what Western periodization literature calls concurrent or
46	conjugate training (train all qualities across the whole cycle, in varying proportions)
47	versus "distant transfer" mapping onto strict block/linear periodization (sequential
48	single-quality phases) — a connection this passage does not make itself.
49	
50	**When to apply** — Use as a lens for diagnosing a specific periodization complaint: if
51	an athlete's speed or strength level noticeably drops during a technical or in-season
52	phase, ask whether the program is using a "distant transfer" model (which requires
53	active, planned maintenance work for the earlier-built quality) without actually
54	including that maintenance work. **Eric's baseline:** in-season programming at Baylor
55	follows "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than continuing to build strength
56	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
57	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) — that is functionally the "transfer in
58	the middle" case above (actively holding a previously-built level while a new emphasis
59	develops), though the course material does not use Bondarchuk's terminology.
60	
61	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is presented in the text as the
62	author's own unverified conclusion from practical observation, not tested against a
63	control condition or independently replicated, and the book gives no citation trail for
64	it at all (unusual for this chapter, which otherwise cites bracketed references
65	throughout). Treat this as a plausible practitioner heuristic, not an established finding.
66	Population is elite Soviet track and field athletes on multi-decade national training
67	cycles; applying the three-situations timing model to a much shorter college football
68	in-season/off-season calendar is Inference.
69	
70	**Example** — A discus thrower doing a strength-emphasis GPP block followed by a
71	technical/competition block: under "current transfer," strength work continues at reduced
72	volume throughout the technical block so the strength level is still rising (or at least
73	held) when the athlete peaks technically; under "distant transfer" with poor execution,
74	strength work is dropped entirely once the technical block starts and the athlete arrives
75	at competition weaker than at the end of GPP.
76	
77	**Related** — [[heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]] —
78	the companion finding on how stage duration interacts with whether transfer can happen at
79	all.
80

13	
14	# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each
15	
16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk splits the tests used to study training transfer into two
17	families (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52):
18	- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
19	  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
20	  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
21	  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
22	  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
23	  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
24	  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
25	- **Specialized tests**: tests unique to each event's specific demands, most reliably
26	  results in **specialized-developmental exercises** — i.e., the competitive movement
27	  itself executed under lighter or more difficult conditions (lighter/heavier implements
28	  in throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
29	  events). He states specialized-developmental test reliability is the best-established
30	  of the test types; general-preparatory and specialized-preparatory test reliability is
31	  explicitly flagged as "not fully confirmed" and something to be "tightened up in the
32	  near future." (PDF p. 69, printed p. 52.)
33	
34	**Why it works** — The text itself gives no mechanism connecting these two ideas; it simply
35	asserts that specialized-developmental test reliability "has already been shown" without
36	citing why. **Inference:** connecting this to
37	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — specialized-developmental exercises
38	sit closest to the competitive event in that transfer chain, so tests built from those same
39	exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
40	from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.
41	
42	**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, prioritize tests that
43	are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the competitive skill under
44	altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power tests when the goal is
45	tracking competitive readiness specifically; reserve the generic tests (snatch, squat,
46	vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which the author himself
47	says have less-confirmed reliability as *transfer* indicators even though they are
48	common practice.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
51	methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented
52	without a formal reliability study of his own two test families in the excerpted pages
53	(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
54	no reference number here). Population is Soviet track and field testing practice of the
55	1970s-80s; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov jump, etc.) reflect
56	that era's tools, not necessarily current force-plate/GPS-based options. Applying the
57	general/specialized test distinction to Baylor's own battery design (`method-baseline.md`,
58	"Testing and assessment") is Inference in terms of which specific tests to pick, though
59	the underlying logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement for readiness
60	tracking) is directly portable.
61	
62	**Example** — For a football wide receiver, a "specialized" test in this framework would
63	be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route run against a
64	lighter or heavier resistance band, or a shortened-approach vertical jump), while a
65	"general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
66	position group.
67	
68	**Related** — [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer logic
69	this test-selection framework is built on.
70

  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
- **Specialized tests**: tests unique to each event's specific demands, most reliably
  results in **specialized-developmental exercises** — i.e., the competitive movement
  itself executed under lighter or more difficult conditions (lighter/heavier implements
  in throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
  events). He states specialized-developmental test reliability is the best-established
  of the test types; general-preparatory and specialized-preparatory test reliability is
  explicitly flagged as "not fully confirmed" and something to be "tightened up in the
  near future." (PDF p. 69, printed p. 52.)

**Why it works** — The text itself gives no mechanism connecting these two ideas; it simply
asserts that specialized-developmental test reliability "has already been shown" without
citing why. **Inference:** connecting this to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — specialized-developmental exercises
sit closest to the competitive event in that transfer chain, so tests built from those same
exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, prioritize tests that
are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the competitive skill under
altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power tests when the goal is

vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which the author himself
says have less-confirmed reliability as *transfer* indicators even though they are
common practice.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented

(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
no reference number here). Population is Soviet track and field testing practice of the
1970s-80s; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov jump, etc.) reflect

the underlying logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement for readiness
tracking) is directly portable.

**Example** — For a football wide receiver, a "specialized" test in this framework would
be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route run against a
lighter or heavier resistance band, or a shortened-approach vertical jump), while a
"general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
position group.

this test-selection framework is built on.

23	Menkhin's example, the best conjugation requires five things at once: (1) motor qualities
24	localized to the right muscle groups, (2) motor qualities matching the biodynamic demands
25	of the skill, (3) transfer into the most common forms of motor activity used for learning
26	technique, (4) enough work capacity to repeat the skill reliably across a long
27	competition, and (5) transfer into the competitive combination itself. (PDF p. 29,
28	printed p. 12.) Bondarchuk says he used this same conjugate principle to build his own
29	"principle of all-round specialized preparation" (ref [265]): mostly specialized-

14	# Three Competing Theories of Training Transfer: Specifist, Generalist, Holistic
15	
16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk frames the entire theory of training transfer as a debate
17	between three schools (PDF pp. 20-28, printed pp. 3-11):
18	- **Specifists** (traced to E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements," cited as
19	  ref [223]): transfer between two activities happens only to the degree the activities
20	  share identical elements (muscle groups, coordination structure, biomechanics). No
21	  shared elements, no transfer. (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3.)
22	- **Generalists** (dominant 1940-1960, per the text): argue for the "unity of general and
23	  specialized preparation" — build a broad general base first (a multi-year "base stage"
24	  of 4-6 years), then specialize. Bondarchuk reports this view was later revised once
25	  research showed general-preparation means only build a base for **low-level** athletes;
26	  for high-level athletes, transfer to the competitive event comes only through
27	  specialized-preparation means (citing refs [34, 57, 182]). (PDF pp. 22-24, printed pp.
28	  5-7.)
29	- **Holistics**: the body acts as one system, so any exercise affects the whole body's
30	  systems to some degree (non-specific reactions of the heart-circulatory/respiratory
31	  systems from any cyclical exercise, e.g. rowing or cycling helping a middle-distance
32	  runner's aerobic base). Bondarchuk explicitly rejects the holistics' full conclusion
33	  ("it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics") but keeps their
34	  narrower point about non-specific systemic reactions, and credits the "block method"
35	  (physical-preparation block before a technical-preparation block) as the holistics'
36	  practical answer to sequencing. (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp. 9-11.)
37	
38	**Why it works** — The author does not resolve these into a single mechanism in this
39	section; he uses the three-way split to set up why transfer is contested territory before
40	he presents his own correlational data in Chapter 2. **Inference:** the specifist view is
41	the closest ancestor of what this library already holds as
42	[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining, Verkhoshansky/Siff)
43	and of Verkhoshansky's Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
44	(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"); the generalist/holistic debate maps onto
45	the general-preparation-vs-specialization sequencing question this library already tracks
46	via Bompa's multilateral development model (vault, not yet cross-checked in this batch).
47	
48	**When to apply** — Use this three-way split as a diagnostic when reading any other
49	S&C source's claim about "general" vs "specific" training: ask which of the three
50	positions it is implicitly taking. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches exercise
51	selection on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation to
52	competitive exercises (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
53	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`) — that is functionally a generalist-then-
54	specifist sequencing, not a pure specifist position, and this entry gives Eric's course
55	material a named theoretical lineage (Thorndike/specifist vs. the generalist sequencing
56	debate) that the transcript itself does not cite.
57	
58	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
59	literature synthesis of a decades-old Soviet-era academic debate among track and field
60	scientists, not an independently replicated finding, and the book gives no citation for
61	exactly how "generalist" views were falsified beyond two bracketed reference numbers
62	([34, 57, 182]) this ingest did not chase down. The population behind all three positions
63	is elite Soviet track and field athletes; extending any of the three views to football
64	programming (e.g., "GPP only helps low-level players") is Inference, not something this
65	passage states.
66	
67	**Example** — A coach who says "just build a big general base before specializing" is
68	taking the classical generalist position Bondarchuk says was already revised by the
69	1970s-80s once high-level athlete data showed general work stops producing transfer past
70	a certain qualification level; see

72	revision.
73

75	staging) — the specifist position's closest modern-book relative in this library.
76	[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the exercise taxonomy this book actually
77	uses to operationalize the specifist/generalist tension.

14	# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration
15	
16	**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
17	preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
18	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
19	[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
20	improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
21	conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
22	specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
23	necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
24	well as for carrying out restorative measures." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He goes
25	further, speculating that specialized-preparatory exercises may function as
26	"'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the transfer to
27	the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves — a direct
28	echo of the "tie-in effect" idea from Chapter 1 (see
29	[[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]). (PDF p. 175, printed
30	p. 158.)
31	
32	**Why it works** — No new mechanism beyond the tie-in-effect hypothesis already flagged as
33	untested in Chapter 1; this is the author's own explicit hedge against a naive
34	misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data shows no further correlation,
35	therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns against).
36	
37	**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
38	any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
39	athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
40	keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance (residual strength
41	retention, consistent with the roughly-30-day residual training effect windows this
42	library already tracks — see `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power") and for its
43	restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.
44	
45	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
46	practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
47	separately tested finding in its own right — he flags his "stimulational factor" idea as
48	speculative ("it is very possible that... other methods... will be proposed"). Population
49	context is the same elite Soviet track and field throwers/sprinters/jumpers as the ceiling-
50	effect claims it responds to. Applying "keep it for maintenance, not for further gains" to
51	a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
52	directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
53	volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
54	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
55	training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
56	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
57	the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
58	different reasoning.
59	
60	**Example** — A discus thrower whose squat numbers have plateaued relative to further
61	distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
62	and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
63	weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
64	than dropping squats from the program entirely.
65	
66	**Related** — [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]] and
67	[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the data findings this heuristic is
68	a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —
69	the Chapter 1 idea (tie-in effect) this heuristic's "stimulational factor" speculation
70	echoes.

14	# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle
15	
16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
17	take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
18	though some individuals take 4-8 months. A general-preparation stage/block can only
19	function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the following specialized stage if it lasts
20	at least as long as that individual's own sports-form development timeline. He gives a
21	worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
22	15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
23	entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
24	needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
25	general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
26	(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
27	their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
28	endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
29	stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
30	transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
31	of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
32	(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
33	23-25.)
34	
35	**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
36	entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
37	duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
38	that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
39	training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
40	developmental phase in itself.
41	
42	**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
43	"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
44	phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
45	in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
46	it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
47	retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
48	days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
49	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
50	distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
51	developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.
52	
53	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month (up to 4-8 month)
54	sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
55	specific citation in the excerpted pages, and is drawn from elite Soviet track and field
56	athletes on year-round training cycles. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
57	calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
58	sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
59	a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
60	adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
61	is more portable than the specific duration numbers.
62	
63	**Example** — A 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very unlikely to
64	produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the Bondarchuk sense; it
65	functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training stress, and should
66	be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building a real strength or
67	conditioning "base."
68

70	model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
71	(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
72	duration question applies to.

14	# Aerobic-to-Anaerobic-Alactate Transfer Is Broad and One-Directional; Anaerobic-Alactate-to-Aerobic Transfer Is Almost Absent
15	
16	**What it is** — Tables 104-109 (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 149-154) report, for pairs
17	of energy-system training loads (aerobic, anaerobic-alactate, anaerobic-lactate), how many
18	of a set of physiological indices (heart rate, respiratory rate, lung ventilation, oxygen
19	reserve/debt, VO2max, blood lactate, energy expenditure/source, muscle fiber type, and
20	effect on time-to-sports-form) are "fully transferred," "frequently transferred," or
21	"non-transferred" from one training-load type to the other. The pattern is asymmetric, not
22	mutual, between each pair:
23	- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: mostly transferable — Bondarchuk states "6 of 7" of
24	  the cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices are "fully transferable" (Table 104,
25	  PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable factors are specifically blood-lactate
26	  level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with different
27	  fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers in
28	  anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
29	- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: broadly transferable both ways — "of the 16 tests
30	  looked at, only four were non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146); the
31	  anaerobic-lactate load actually *shortens* the time to enter sports form in aerobic
32	  training, while aerobic training does not shorten anaerobic-lactate's timeline (PDF pp.
33	  163-165, 171, printed pp. 146-148, 154).

# Aerobic-to-Anaerobic-Alactate Transfer Is Broad and One-Directional; Anaerobic-Alactate-to-Aerobic Transfer Is Almost Absent

**What it is** — Tables 104-109 (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 149-154) report, for pairs
of energy-system training loads (aerobic, anaerobic-alactate, anaerobic-lactate), how many
of a set of physiological indices (heart rate, respiratory rate, lung ventilation, oxygen
reserve/debt, VO2max, blood lactate, energy expenditure/source, muscle fiber type, and
effect on time-to-sports-form) are "fully transferred," "frequently transferred," or
"non-transferred" from one training-load type to the other. The pattern is asymmetric, not
mutual, between each pair:
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: mostly transferable — Bondarchuk states "6 of 7" of
  the cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices are "fully transferable" (Table 104,
  PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable factors are specifically blood-lactate
  level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with different
  fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers in
  anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: broadly transferable both ways — "of the 16 tests
  looked at, only four were non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146); the
  anaerobic-lactate load actually *shortens* the time to enter sports form in aerobic
  training, while aerobic training does not shorten anaerobic-lactate's timeline (PDF pp.
  163-165, 171, printed pp. 146-148, 154).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: almost no transfer — "non-transferable factors here
  are all the remaining factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147),
  attributed to the oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus
  the oxygen-dependent structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: also limited, though the reverse direction
  (anaerobic-lactate loads shorten anaerobic-alactate's time to sports form, but not vice
  versa) shows a similar one-way asymmetry to the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate pair (Tables
  106-107, PDF pp. 164, 169, printed pp. 147, 152).
Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of the practical upshot of well-combined
aerobic/anaerobic training: "S. Auita" (almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held
world records simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within
tenths of a second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional
career bests: 200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11.
(PDF p. 172, printed p. 155.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation is fiber-type recruitment: aerobic
training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers, while anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch) fibers, and he states plainly
for at least one asymmetry that "it is not known why" one direction shortens
time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed p. 147) — the author
himself flags this as an open question, not a resolved mechanism. Do not read a fuller
physiological explanation into this than the fiber-type note the text actually gives.

training transfers symmetrically: a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for
anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate capacity (per the "fully transferred" majority in
Tables 104-105), but a block of anaerobic-alactate (pure sprint/power) work should **not**
be expected to build aerobic capacity — per this data it does not, on all but 2 of 15
tracked physiological indices. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all
three energy systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target
the intended adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning
and energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`) — this
entry's asymmetry finding sharpens that general principle into a specific, one-directional
claim about which energy-system work can substitute for which.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported** for the aggregate Tables 104-109
findings (described as "collective data" in each table's own title, i.e. pooled across
Bondarchuk's tested athletes, sample size not stated in the excerpted pages).

offered as illustration, not independent evidence. The tested population is elite Soviet
and international middle/long-distance track athletes; the specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards. Applying this energy-system transfer asymmetry
directly to football conditioning (a repeated-sprint, intermittent-effort sport rather than
a continuous single-energy-system event) is Inference — no football or team-sport
population appears anywhere in this book.

14	# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier
15	
16	**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
17	jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
18	vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
19	running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
20	exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
21	consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
22	jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
23	women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
24	0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
25	for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). **High
26	jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
27	"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
28	0.400 level" for running exercises specifically. Instead, per his prose (PDF p. 105,
29	printed p. 88), "the most informative and transferable exercise appears to be the vertical
30	jump with a short run-up," at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women) — **note an
31	unresolved source discrepancy**: those exact figures match the "10-fold jump from place"
32	row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965), not the row literally labeled
33	"Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women 0.680-0.808, which
34	the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may be a
35	translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's row
36	label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian or
37	a second translation. Barbell snatch showed almost no
38	transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
39	with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
40	levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)
41	
42	**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
43	**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
44	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
45	event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
46	the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
47	closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
48	general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested, but this
49	connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation. High
50	jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
51	explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
52	takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
53	straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
54	"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.
55

57	supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
58	highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
59	with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach

61

67	stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
68	football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
69	data exists in this source.
70

72	reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
73	well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
74	short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
75	transfers the same way.
76

78	explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.

80	sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

14	# Training Transfer Comes in Four Flavors: Positive, Negative, Neutral, and Indifferent
15	
16	**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three standard types of training transfer plus a fourth
17	he flags as rarer and specific to high-level athletes (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15):
18	- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
19	- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
20	  another.
21	- **Neutral** (also "indifferent" in some literature he cites): no measurable effect
22	  either way.
23	- **Indifferent/double effect** (his own added category, "met more rarely," specifically
24	  in high-level athletes using a complex of different exercises): one exercise can help
25	  and hurt at the same time along different dimensions, e.g. heavier-implement throws
26	  positive for strength but negative for technique — "there is a noticeable worsening of
27	  technique in some throws with the use of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]). Bondarchuk
28	  gives a specific example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/anaerobic running in
29	  general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory function but worsened
30	  walking technique (ref [94]), a case of positive-physiological/negative-technical
31	  double effect. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)
32	
33	**Why it works** — Bondarchuk gives no mechanism for why transfer takes these particular
34	forms; he presents the three-way split as received terminology ("in the specialized
35	literature it is also possible to find 'indifferent' transfer," without naming a specific
36	source for that term) and adds the fourth (double-effect) category as his own observation.
37	**Note on scope:** Chapter 1's earlier discussion of E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical
38	elements" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3; see
39	[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]) is presented by Bondarchuk as the
40	basis for the *specifist* position on transfer generally, not explicitly linked by him to
41	this positive/negative/neutral/indifferent typology — this entry does not claim that link
42	was Bondarchuk's own. **Inference:** the double-effect category is a plausible, useful name
43	for a pattern coaches encounter often (an exercise that builds one quality while degrading
44	another), but this is this entry's own framing, not a claim from the text about how common
45	or well-recognized that pattern is elsewhere.
46	
47	**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new
48	exercise: is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect**
49	where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
50	technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
51	illustration — flag any high-volume general-conditioning block for a technical,
52	timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect risk, not
53	just a "general conditioning is fine" default.
54	
55	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The category examples given (heavier
56	implements degrading throw technique, aerobic-volume race walkers losing walking
57	technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed
58	reference number [18, 94, 152], not verified against the original sources in this ingest.
59	Population is elite track and field throwers and race walkers; extending "double effect"
60	reasoning to football (e.g., heavy sled work degrading sprint mechanics) is Inference,
61	plausible by analogy but not something this passage tests.
62	
63	**Example** — **Inference:** a college lineman doing high-volume heavy sled pushes for
64	GPP strength may show a positive effect on force production and a negative (double)
65	effect on start technique and shin angle if the sled load or volume is not periodically
66	reduced back toward the competitive movement pattern, echoing the walker's aerobic-volume
67	example here.
68

70	staging) — the mechanism this claim's negative-transfer cases plausibly run through
71	(mismatch on one of the ten specificity dimensions).

14	# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery
15	
16	**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
17	throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
18	0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
19	women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary: "there is
20	almost always a place for mutually correlated interrelationships... the amounts of these
21	interrelationships are sufficiently great," with only two exceptions found in the entire
22	dataset (javelin: no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and the 3-4kg standing
23	throw; no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements). (PDF p. 132, printed p.
24	115.) He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
25	(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
26	Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
27	implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
28	dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
29	his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (Tables 85-86, PDF pp. 130-131,
30	printed pp. 113-114). Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his
31	implement-weight throws increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances
32	(Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).
33	
34	**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
35	"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
36	and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
37	muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
38	**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
39	close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
40	movement, only the resistance changes), which under
41	[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
42	positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
43	stated by the author in these terms.
44	
45	**When to apply** — This is the strongest, most consistent transfer finding in the entire
46	book: for throwing events specifically, varying implement weight while keeping the
47	competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training method across nearly the
48	full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any strength, jump, or sprint
49	assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter. He does flag a real caveat: heavier
50	implements can degrade technique (release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect
51	he says clears up "in several weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the
52	double-effect pattern named in [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].
53	
54	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
55	finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa/Shulta individual case data (Tables
56	85-88) is **untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not
57	as independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
58	rather than proof. Population throughout is elite Soviet-bloc throwers (Olympic and world
59	champions/record holders for the case studies). This finding is specific to implements
60	that can be made lighter or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact
61	(shot, discus, javelin, hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight
62	manipulation in most football skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement
63	identical" as a general training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a
64	quarterback) is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.
65

67	implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight) targeting both speed and
68	strength qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw, but **only up to a specific result level for each
exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive improvement
disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m
(men) / 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended
furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three.
In shot put, snatch ended at 17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m
(men)/14-25m (women, likely an OCR artifact for a narrower band), squat at 19-20m
(men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). In javelin, snatch and power
clean both ended at 65-70m (men); at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for
either the squat or the bench press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat "showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135,
printed pp. 116-118.) Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the
close of this chapter: "specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an
increase in the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports
mastery. Further on, they do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.

**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
strength work maintained rather than chased.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — what to do with
strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.

ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.

+The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic sequencing rule follows directly from the
testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the

+# Active Flexibility, Not Passive, Is the One That Tracks Sporting Proficiency
+**What it is** — Citing a single Russian study of over 200 adult competitors (Iashvili,
+1982), the authors report that sporting achievement (rated by competition standards)
+correlates more strongly with active flexibility than with passive flexibility: R = 0.81
+versus R = 0.69. The same study found traditional static and passive stretching develop
+mainly passive flexibility, while combined strength-and-stretching exercises are
+considerably more effective at developing active flexibility, particularly when the
+strength conditioning is applied in the zone of active muscular inadequacy (i.e. the end
+of the joint's active range). (PDF p. 186, printed p. 175.)
+A later section (3.5.8) returns to the same Iashvili (1982) study across "several Olympic
+sports" with further detail: joint mobility level tracks sporting proficiency generally;
+static/passive stretching enhances passive flexibility but only moderately improves active
+mobility (described as "by far the most important flexibility quality needed in sport");
+the pattern and range of joint mobility is sport-specific (e.g. backstroke/butterfly
+swimmers show the greatest shoulder and ankle mobility, breast-strokers the least in those
+joints but the greatest hip/knee mobility; javelinists show the greatest shoulder
+mobility among throwers, hurdlers the greatest hip flexibility among track athletes); and
+the active-passive correlation itself depends on training method, running 0.61-0.73 with
+primarily static/passive stretching but rising to 0.91 when stretching is combined with
+strengthening. (PDF pp. 196-197, printed pp. 185-186.)
+A related measurement framework from the same section (Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980) defines
+three flexibility indices from a pulley-loaded limb: maximum passive flexibility (PFmax,
+at the pain threshold), active flexibility (AF, reached by non-ballistic muscular action),
+and loaded passive flexibility (PF, with a progressively increased sub-pain-threshold
+load), yielding a maximum active flexibility deficit (FDmax = PFmax - AF), a loaded active
+flexibility deficit (FD = PF - AF), and an interval of flexibility pain threshold (FPT =
+PFmax - PF). Using these indices, the same source reports: static/passive stretching
+increases passive flexibility while leaving the active-passive gap unchanged; full-range
+strength exercise increases passive flexibility and narrows that gap; and combined
+strength-plus-flexibility exercise increases both and narrows the gap most. A large
+active-passive gap ("flexibility deficit") is reported to correlate strongly with the
+incidence of soft-tissue injury. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)
+**Why it works** — The book gives no physiological mechanism for why active flexibility
+specifically tracks proficiency; it reports only the correlational and intervention
+results above.
+**When to apply** — Prefer testing and training active ROM (through the athlete's own
+muscular control) over passive ROM (examiner- or gravity-assisted) when the goal is a
+proxy for sporting flexibility demands, and prefer combined strength-and-stretch
+programming over stretching alone when the goal is to close a large active-passive gap.
+**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** These are single-source,
+Soviet-era correlational and intervention findings (Iashvili 1982; Tumanyan & Dzhanyan
+1980) not independently replicated in this corpus; the correlation coefficients describe
+association within that sample, not a causal mechanism, and "sporting proficiency" is the
+study's own competition-standard rating, not defined here. Do not treat the specific
+numbers (0.81, 0.69, 0.91, the sport-by-sport mobility patterns) as generalizable norms for
+a Baylor football roster without independent verification.
+**Example** — Two athletes with identical passive hip-flexion ROM on a table test may
+differ substantially in active hip flexion under their own muscular control during a
+sprint stride; per this claim, the active measure (and a program that narrows any gap
+between the two) is the one that tracks performance, not the passive number alone.
+**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
+[[heuristic--eccentric-quasi-isometrics-for-active-flexibility-and-starting-strength]].

+# The Book's Stretching-Benefits List Includes Items Modern Evidence Disputes
+**What it is** — Citing a literature and empirical-evidence review (Keith, 1977; Weiss,
+1976; Holland, 1968; de Vries, 1966, 1966), the authors list these benefits of stretching:
+increase in range of useful movement; reduction in the incidence of injury; decrease in
+the severity of injury; delay in the onset of muscular fatigue; prevention and alleviation
+of muscle soreness after exercise; increase in the level of skill and muscular efficiency;
+prolongation of sporting life. In the same section they also caution that inappropriate
+stretching can be detrimental: tendons and ligaments can be permanently deformed or
+damaged by over-zealous or prolonged stretching, impairing joint stability; unskilled
+ballistic stretching can cause muscle soreness and stiffness; and overstretching of the
+cervical or lumbar spine can damage nerves, discs and blood vessels, particularly in
+forceful yoga postures or amateur spinal manipulation. (PDF p. 187, printed p. 176.)
+**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for any item on the benefits list; it is
+presented as a summary of a 1960s-70s literature review, not derived from a stated
+physiological pathway in this text.
+**When to apply** — Treat "increase in range of useful movement" as the best-supported
+item on this list, consistent with the book's own later, more specific claim that ROM
+gains from routine stretching mainly reflect increased stretch tolerance (see
+[[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]]).
+**When NOT to apply** — **`contested`, named reason:** the muscle-soreness-prevention claim
+on this list is disputed by a later systematic review of randomized trials: Herbert RD, de
+Noronha M, Kamper SJ, "Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise,"
+Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2011, concluded that stretching (before, after, or
+both) produces little to no reduction in delayed-onset muscle soreness, whether performed
+pre- or post-exercise. The injury-incidence and injury-severity items are also not
+supported by a specific modern trial in this entry; do not cite this 1966-1977 review list
+as current evidence for injury prevention or soreness reduction without independent
+verification. Inference: several items (skill/efficiency increase, prolongation of
+sporting life) are broad, difficult-to-falsify claims not tied to a specific outcome
+measure in the cited sources, and should be treated as unverified assertions rather than
+established findings.
+**Example** — A staff member citing "stretching reduces soreness" to justify a mandatory
+post-lift static stretching block would be relying on the disputed half of this list; the
+Cochrane review found this benefit does not hold up under randomized-trial evidence.
+**Related** — [[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]].

+domain: strength-and-conditioning

+topic: methods of increasing range of movement
+category: [flexibility, programming, stretching]
+confidence: supported

+# Four Ways to Increase ROM, Ranked by Speed of Effect and Durability
+**What it is** — The authors give four practical means of enhancing joint ROM, in order
+of effectiveness, and note the first limitation on the list (skeletal structure) cannot be
+overcome by any form of exercise:
+1. Modifying the neuromuscular processes that control tension and length in the muscle
+complex. This increases ROM most rapidly and most effectively, but the change tends to be
+confined to short-term improvements unless the neuromuscular means are used as an ongoing
+part of all training.
+2. Increasing the length and strength of the soft tissues comprising the muscle complex,
+especially collagenous tissues such as fascia. These changes are slower to produce but
+long-term.
+3. Lengthening and strengthening other soft tissues, especially those of the joint capsule
+and ligaments. Also long-lasting, but if promoted to the point of joint laxity, joint
+stability can be severely compromised.
+4. Restructuring the articulating surfaces of the joints, a process mediated by many years
+of regular heavy loading in specific patterns; not a practical training target, more a
+by-product of loaded full-range sporting movement, and inappropriate/excessive loading can
+instead produce degenerative changes that reduce ROM.
+The authors add that stretching and flexibility training are not synonymous: some
+flexibility exercises increase ROM without being stretching exercises at all, because they
+work entirely by modifying neuromuscular processes (the stretch and tendon reflexes);
+conversely, many stretching exercises pay no deliberate attention to neuromuscular
+processes and instead aim at structural change in soft tissue, so static stretches may
+change muscle length without adequately affecting the dynamic ROM a given sport requires.
+(PDF pp. 185-186, printed pp. 174-175.)
+**Why it works** — The authors give no single unifying mechanism; the ordering reflects
+which physiological layer (nervous system, muscle/fascia, joint capsule/ligament, bone) is
+being changed and how quickly each layer adapts, from fastest-and-least-durable
+(neuromuscular) to slowest-and-most-durable (bone).
+**When to apply** — Use this ordering to set expectations for a flexibility intervention:
+a single session aimed at neuromuscular relaxation (e.g. PNF) can produce a same-day ROM
+gain that will not persist without repetition, while a multi-week soft-tissue-lengthening
+block is the one that produces a durable change. Match the method to the timeframe: a
+pre-competition warm-up should rely on method 1 (rapid, neuromuscular, session-specific);
+an off-season block targeting chronic ROM limits should emphasize methods 2-3.
+**When NOT to apply** — Do not expect a brief pre-event stretching routine to produce
+long-term flexibility change; the text is explicit that this is a category error common in
+"the average stretching programme." Do not pursue method 3 (ligament/capsule lengthening)
+without limit: the text names joint laxity and compromised stability as the direct cost of
+overdoing it. Method 4 should never be treated as a deliberate training target.
+**Example** — A pre-game mobility routine that relies on PNF contract-relax drills is
+working through method 1 and will not, by itself, change an athlete's baseline hip ROM
+measured a week later; that requires a sustained block emphasizing methods 2 and 3.
+**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
+[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

162	In dealing with construction of sports form development cycles, specialists are in

literature sources.  Results of the correlational analyses having a direct relationship to the 
studied factors is presented further on in tables 41-84 and 89-103.  A positive 
interrelationship between exercises begins at 0.349.

the pole vault with a short run up and long jumps from a full run up.  A positive transfer

the barbell on the shoulders.  In the bench press, the cumulative effect was not seen 
except at the 5.50-5.80m level.  There was no positive interrelationship with the two 
throwing exercises --- throwing the shot forward and throwing the shot backward.

vaulters are seen in table 68.  Here, a positive interrelationship begins with 0.423.  It 
shows the presence of a positive transfer in all the running and jumping exercises with
