The Mechanisms of Training Transfer 
 
In dealing with construction of sports form development cycles, specialists are in 
agreement that the level of physical, technical, psychological and other abilities, as well 
as definite functional results in each of the previous stages, the training block, should 
create the “base”, “foundation” for increasing sports achievements in the following 
exercises to be used.  However, none of the specialists make note of when and how the 
earlier achieved level is transferred.  In one case, transfer can take place at the beginning, 
middle or end of each following stage or block.  In the second case, there is no 
explanation of the essence of these changes.  It is known that transfer can influence the 
time of entering into the state of sports form as well as the beginning and ending level of 
results in the training used over the duration of the following stages, blocks.   
 
It is not necessary to be reminded of what takes place with the achieved level of results 
from the end of each previous stage, block, to the middle or end of each of the following 
stages.  Know that it can remain unchanged, be decreased or increased. 
 
Explaining these problems, which are organically tied in with one another, has major 
significance.  Without knowing the mechanisms of training transfer on the duration of 
each consecutive stage, block, our actions can be in error in selecting the system of 
exercises to be used in relation to the means of constructing the cycles of sports form 
development. 
 
In sports practice, one can encounter three different situations depending upon which, the 
use of an effective system of exercises for the duration of the following stages, blocks is 
based.   
 
The first situation—the transfer of the achieved level of results at the end of each 
previous stage, block, takes place at the beginning of each following stage, block.  In this 
case we are not interested in what takes place with the achieved level of sports results at 
the end of the previous stage, block.  It can decrease, increase or remain unchanged by 
18 


===== PDF page 36 (viewer 37) =====
fulfilling its role in creating the “base”, “foundation” for the means of training used over 
the duration of each of the following stages.  If this is so, then the earlier used exercises 
can be excluded from the training process. 
 
The second situation—is distinguished from the first by the fact that the transfer of 
training can take place in the middle of each following stage, block.  In this case, we are 
not indifferent to the level of results achieved.  Its decrease is not allowed or the effect of 
the transfer will be absent or it will not reach the maximum amounts possible.  
Consequently, for the duration of the following stages, blocks, we should use a system of 
exercises that allows us to maintain the earlier achieved level of sports results at the end 
of the previous stages, blocks, and to experience an increase in those exercises which are 
used during the following stages.   
 
The third situation—occurs if the process of training transfer takes place at the end of 
each of the following stages, blocks. In this case, it is necessary to maintain the achieved 
level of sports achievement at the end of each stage, block.   
 
Up to this time, only one method of maintaining the achieved levels of sports results is 
known.  It is a schematic in which the exercises are used for the duration of a specific 
segment of time. Thus, in using the complex stage method of constructing cycles of sports 
form development (Figure 1), we should not exclude general preparation means for the 
duration of the specialized preparation stages. Instead we should carry out the schematic 
at the beginning and in the middle using the exercises with significantly less volume. 
 
 
19 


===== PDF page 37 (viewer 38) =====
 
Figure 1 
Figure 1:  System of exercises that allows for maintaining the level of results in the 
general preparatory exercises toward the end of the development of the sports form cycle 
with use of the stage-complex method of construction.   
 
Figure 1 Key: ОЦ-General preparatory, CЦ-Specialized-preparatory, CP-Specialized-
developmental and C-Competitive exercise; ЄСЦ-stage of specialized preparation, 
ЄPСФ-Stage of development of sports form, Æ shows the time of change in the methods 
of training. 
 
 
In studying the mechanisms of training transfer when using stages, blocks, combinations, 
variants and complex methods of constructing sports form development cycles, we came 
to the conclusion that the transfer of the achieved level of physical and other capabilities 
at the end of each of the previous stage, block, takes place not at the beginning, middle or 
end of each of the following stages, blocks, but over the duration of them.  It serves to 
establish a new level of adaptation in the means of training used for the duration of the 
following stages, blocks. 
 
Here it becomes clear that the transfer of training can occur only in those situations in 
which, over the duration of the entire stages, blocks, a succession is observed in the 
20 


===== PDF page 38 (viewer 39) =====
methods of training used.  The exercises used appear to be those that over the duration of 
the previous stages, blocks, lengthen or shorten the time of entering into a state of sports 
form in the competitive exercise (event).  These are mainly specialized-developmental 
exercises.  If a succession in the use of the exercises does not exist, then transfer is not 
observed.  It can exist only in situations where these exercises are used simultaneously 
with specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.  Here general preparatory and 
specialized-preparatory exercises can have an indirect influence that accounts for the 
mechanisms of dispersing the activity onto the “neighbors”. 
  
It was also noted that excluding specialized-developmental and competitive exercises for 
the duration as for example, the third or fourth stage, block, lasting more than 3-4 weeks 
with use of the variational method of constructing the development of sports form cycles, 
it leads to a loss in the achieved level of physical and other abilities.

And still another example is related to the training of women.  Olympic champion in the 
shotput N. Lisovskaya, was the official world record holder in the throw of the 
competitive implement and unofficial in the throw of the 3, 7, 5 and 6kg shot.  Similar 
examples exist in other track and field throw events. 
 
There is almost always a place for mutually correlated interrelationships between special-
developmental exercises (throws and “shot putting” various implements having different 
weights from place) and exercises with lighter, heavier and competitive implements.  The 
amounts of these interrelationships are sufficiently great (see tables 69-84).  There is no 
relationship in only two places out of the many.  In javelin throwers, no positive 
interrelationship is observed between throws of a lighter implement weighing 0.6kg and 
throws of a heavier implement weighing 3 and 4 kg from place.  There is also no 
interrelationship between throws with a lighter implement weighing 0.7kg and heavier 
ones weighing 4kg. 
 
In the women, there is no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the 
competitive implement and in standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg.  Here once 
again as between the lighter, heavier and competitive weight exercises, there is a tight 
interrelationship between knowing the result in the throws from place, and making an 
early prognosis of sports achievement in the entire throw.  Also the opposite, at a definite 
level of sports achievement in the competitive exercise, there exists a definite level of 
results in the throw from place.   
 
In sports practice, in each track and field throw event, a specific number of specialized 
developmental exercises are used, mainly throws of the implement of various weights 
from place starting in various positions.  To a lesser degree, there are exercises that repeat 
other joint parts of the total competitive movement.  Discussion here is related mainly to 
the throwing steps taken by the javelin thrower, the turns by the hammer and discus 
thrower, and glides or skips by shotputters.  It appears to us that in the future, their 
portion of the total volume of training loads will increase somewhat.   
115 


===== PDF page 115 (viewer 116) =====
presence of a positive correlational interrelationship between lighter, heavier and 
competitive weight implements in the structure of the entire movement in all types of 
throws, on different levels of sports mastery.  The greatest amounts of correlational 
interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations between the 
lighter and heavier implement weights was insignificant in relation to the competitive---
from 10-20%.  The smallest correlation was fixed in the hammer throw when athletes had 
results in the at 60-65m range when throwing the 16kg weight (0.425).  A weak 
interrelationship (0.365) was observed between results in the shotput with weights of 5.0 
and 7.260 kg in athletes throwing the shot 20-21m. 
 
The compiled data once again substantiated the correctness of the position in the theory 
and practice of track and field, that throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to 
be the most transferable to the competitive exercise.  The reason for this is that they are 
identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical 
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the 
muscular groups in the execution, the muscle work regimes and so on.   
 
What is pertinent here is that those negative consequences, which always have a place 
here, are so insignificant that after ceasing use of one or another lighter or heavier 
implement, they can be eliminated in several weekly cycles.  The latter of these (heavier 
implements) relates to the deviations in technical mastery which has been noted by 
several authors [18, 152].  Foremost among these is the change in the release angle of the 
implement during the final effort, the deviation or lean of the trunk backward, the 
decreased amplitude of movement of the implement and so on.   
 
In practically all track and field disciplines, there are no identical actions, according to all 
parameters of the exercise, that repeat those in the competitive event.  Because of this, 
when using one or another exercise, it is necessary to a large measure, to think of its 
positive effects, not about its negatives.  The exercises should be selected so that the 
positive influence prevails.

===== PDF page 61 (viewer 62) =====
definite levels of results in the base exercises and in the means of specialized preparation.  
This to a great degree, is related to the specialized-developmental and competitive 
exercises.  The given task is resolved only in cases of their simultaneous entry into the 
state of sports form during one or another cycle of their development. 
 
Most model characteristics are very specific for each group of the track and field 
disciplines.  However, some of them can coincide.  This is noticed mainly in the speed-
strength events.  Here, we have in view several strength (snatch and power clean), jump 
(standing long jump, triple jump from place, vertical jump) and throw exercises 
(throwing the shot put forward and backward).  According to the level of achievement in 
these exercises it is possible to some degree, to judge the speed-strength abilities of each 
individual separately.  However, this does not to any degree determine the amount of 
increase in the competitive exercises (events).   
 
In working out model characteristics in all groups in the track and field disciplines, 
specialists used individually-selected and collective-average methods.  The first of them 
oversees selection of the individuals best test scores and the level achieved by one of the 
ten strongest athletes in the country or world in this or another track and field discipline.  
For example, one athlete shows the best result in the snatch and another in the standing 
long jump and a third in the squat with the barbell on the shoulders and so on.   
 
In using the second method, the test scores for each of the exercises are added up, as for 
example, the results of the ten best athletes in the world are summed up and then 
averaged.  The average result then serves as a base score for the athletes who want to 
achieve this sports result in the competitive exercise on the world standard level. 
 
The collective-average method is used most frequently in determining the test scores of 
athletes having different sports qualifications.  In the beginning, test scores are 
established for the means of general preparation, as this encompasses the stage method of 
constructing cycles of sports form development.

-# Case Study: Bondarchuk's Developmental/Competitive/Restorative Blocks and the 1988 Hammer Throw Podium
-**What it is** — Issurin credits Anatoly Bondarchuk, hammer-throw coach, with one of the
-precursor systems to Block Periodization (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21). Based on his own
-athletic career (1972 Olympic hammer-throw champion) and doctoral research on throwers'
-training programs (1988), Bondarchuk built a periodization chart using three types of
-specialized mesocycle-blocks: **developmental** (workload gradually increases to maximum),
-**competitive** (load stabilizes, athletes focus on competitive performance), and
-**restorative** (active recovery, preparing for the next developmental block). Stated
-durations: developmental and competitive blocks are "usually four weeks," restorative "can
-be shortened to two weeks." Sequencing depends on the competition schedule and individual
-athlete response. The book also gives what it calls Bondarchuk's design's outstanding
-characteristic: alternation and repetition of the exercise repertory in each mesocycle-block
-(every four weeks); the traditional period names, preparatory, competitive, and transitory,
-were kept, but Issurin notes "their essence is very different" in Bondarchuk's concept (PDF
-p. 32, printed p. 21). The claimed outcome: Bondarchuk coached the gold, silver, and bronze
-medalists in hammer throw at the 1988 and other Olympic Games, "the entire Olympic podium
-occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).
-**Why it works — the author gives no mechanism beyond the general BPC rationale** — Issurin
-does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
-(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
-as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
-reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
-logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
-retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.
-**When to apply — untested, use as a historical precedent, not as evidence** — Useful for
-explaining the lineage of block-periodization thinking. Issurin presents Bondarchuk's system
-as a parallel reform, not a source he built on: it appears in the text alongside "Issurin &
-Kaverin, 1985, Bondarchuk, 1986, 1988" as one of the era's several reforms away from
-traditional periodization (PDF p. 34, printed p. 23), and Issurin & Kaverin's own 1985
-publication predates Bondarchuk's cited 1986 and 1988 works. Useful as an alternative
-three-block naming scheme organized around competitive readiness
-(developmental/competitive/restorative) rather than ability type
-(accumulation/transmutation/realization); worth distinguishing the two schemes explicitly
-when citing "Bondarchuk's blocks" versus "Issurin's blocks."
-**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Population: elite (Olympic-level) Soviet male hammer
-throwers training under one coach; one Olympic final's podium (plus unspecified "other
-Olympic Games" results). This is a single coach's outcome with no comparison group, no
-report of what other finalists' training looked like, and total reliance on the coach's and
-Issurin's own secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
-is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
-talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
-evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
-illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
-should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy — see
-[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
-historically related, three-block system.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a coach citing "block periodization has a track record" should
-specify which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type
-blocks) and should not present the 1988 podium sweep as generalizable evidence beyond "one
-documented historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."
-**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
-[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]] — a comparable single-coach
-case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
-`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
-(vault) — the *same* coach (Bondarchuk), but a completely different, unrelated framework
-of his (an exercise-classification taxonomy by movement similarity, not a mesocycle-timing
-system). The two should never be conflated when either is cited.

+occupied by athletes of the same coach" (Bondarchuk, 1986 and 1988, as cited by Issurin).

+does not describe Bondarchuk's own stated reasoning for why these particular block lengths
+(4/4/2 weeks) were chosen. **Inference:** the entry's characterization of the three-way split
+as organized "by competitive readiness rather than by ability type" is this entry's own
+reading, not language Issurin uses; the mechanism Issurin offers is the same general BPC
+logic (concentrated, sequenced blocks beat simultaneous multi-ability training) applied
+retroactively to Bondarchuk's design.

+Issurin's own secondary account rather than an independent case audit. A three-medal sweep at one Olympics
+is a striking result but cannot isolate the training design's contribution from athlete
+talent, competitor variance on the day, or other coaching factors. Do not cite this as
+evidence that a 4/4/2-week block cadence "works" for hammer throw or any other event; it
+illustrates a design, not a validated dose-response finding. This is distinct from and
+should not be merged with Issurin's own accumulation/transmutation/realization taxonomy, see
+[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] for that separate, though
+historically related, three-block system.

+specify which system (Bondarchuk's competitive-readiness blocks or Issurin's ability-type

+documented historical instance this concept coincided with a strong outcome."

+[[case-study--issurin-kaverin-canoe-kayak-block-periodization]], a comparable single-coach
+case from the same era; consider also cross-referencing
+`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`

-# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay
-**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
-simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
-concentrated blocks.
-**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
-1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
-extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
-(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
-tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
-endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
-improve; explosive strength *decreased*, despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
-to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation has two separate
-parts: extensive endurance work captures the metabolic energy needed for post-exercise
-anabolism, which suppresses muscle hypertrophy; separately, coaches' and athletes'
-observations show that a strenuous, high-volume training program causes permanent fatigue,
-keeping central and peripheral neural factors far from the optimum needed for improving
-muscular contraction. Klausen (1990) is cited for a more general point about what conditions
-the neural mechanism (state of the CNS, sensitivity of the neuro-motor pool), not for the
-fatigue observation specifically.
-**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
-Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
-the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
-of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
-model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
-threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
-long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
-during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic workloads were
-replaced by more intense, event-specific exercises, and maximum-strength exercises were
-"reduced and even rejected as harmful for racing technique" (only maximum-strength work is
-called harmful in the source; the aerobic reduction is described as a substitution, not a
-harm judgment), and V-AT, peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive
-period. Distance velocity
-still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
-reduced force, i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
-aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
-was far from optimal."
-**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin gives two separate stated mechanisms (PDF
-p. 21, printed p. 10): extensive endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is
-necessary for anabolism during post-exercise recovery," which "suppresses muscle
-hypertrophy"; and, separately, "the observations of coaches and athletes show that a
-strenuous high volume training program causes permanent fatigue," so "the central and
-peripheral neural factors are far from optimum." Klausen (1990) is cited for a different,
-more general point in between the two, that enhancement of the neural mechanism "is
-conditioned by the state of the central nervous system and the sensitivity of the
-neuro-motor pool," not specifically for the fatigue observation. For the kayaker case, Issurin
-gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
-aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14); treat
-that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
-cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
-categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
-offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
-non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
-motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
-[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
-[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].
-**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the more detailed evidence of the two: it is an
-uncontrolled, single-group, uncited 8-week observation (no control group or reference given
-in this text, PDF p. 21, printed p. 10) with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
-useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
-programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
-many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
-mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
-letting it decay unaddressed."
-**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
-this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
-from this source alone; treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
-`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable: the swimmer
-study carries no citation at all in this text, not even an author or year, so there is no
-underlying source to check the numbers against. **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's
-own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
-observational across one season with no control group; it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
-not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
-athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
-competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
-the kayakers' single annual peak design.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
-strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
-failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
-load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
-programmed.
-**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
-which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
-[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

-# Case Study: The USSR Canoe-Kayak Team and the Original Accumulation/Transmutation/Realization Design
-**What it is** — Issurin's own account of where his accumulation-transmutation-realization
-taxonomy came from (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22): in the early 1980s, elite USSR canoe-kayak
-paddlers were training an "enormous exercise volume." "The prevailing opinion was that this
-load level was excessive and that the training design could be made more effective." The
-block-and-mesocycle-sequencing idea was "conceptualized, implemented and proved in
-practice" with the national team, then published (Issurin & Kaverin, 1985). The duration of
-the mesocycles was set "according to physiological and biochemical prerequisites that
-usually allowed four weeks for the accumulation and transformation mesocycles, and two weeks
-for realization." The modified design allowed "about a 10-15% reduction in the annual
-training volume." Follow-up testing during preparation reportedly showed "considerable
-improvement in the main fitness components in all subgroups." The claimed competitive
-outcomes: three gold and three silver medals at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and eight gold
-medals (1989) and nine gold medals (1990) at the World Championships.
-**Why it works — the author's own interpretation, not independently verified here** —
-Issurin attributes the improvement to reduced simultaneous multi-ability training and better
-volume management under the new block structure, consistent with the general BPC rationale
-in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]. No comparison data (e.g., what the
-same team's results looked like in prior Olympic/World Championship cycles under the old
-model, or what other nations' medal counts did over the same period) is presented in this
-chapter to isolate the training-design change from other factors (athlete development,
-equipment, competitor turnover).
-**When to apply — untested, treat as the concept's origin story, not as proof** — Useful
-as the direct provenance of Issurin's own taxonomy (see
-[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) and as a data point that a
-national federation with centralized, well-resourced athlete monitoring implemented this
-design at scale (not just with one athlete).
-**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The book gives the source publication as Issurin &
-Kaverin (1985) but does not itself state what Issurin's own role on the national team was.
-**Inference:** reading this as the concept's inventor reporting on his own uncontrolled
-intervention with his own national team is a reasonable inference from the shared authorship
-and the book's framing, not something the text says outright. Either way, the account here
-(2008 book) is a secondary retelling with no cited independent replication or outcome audit. As with the Bondarchuk case, do not treat the
-Olympic and World Championship medal counts as a controlled test of the training design;
-1980s Soviet sport had structural advantages (centralized athlete development, resourcing)
-that are not present in most other training contexts, including a US college football
-program. The "10-15% volume reduction" figure has no comparison baseline stated (reduction
-from what specific prior volume, over what specific prior period) beyond "the annual
-training volume."
-**Example** — Citing "block periodization produced Olympic medals" should specify this is
-one 1980s Soviet national-team case reported by the method's own originator, not a
-controlled trial, and should be paired with the caveat already logged in
-[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] about single-coach, single-program
-evidence.
-**Related** — [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
-[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]].

-# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power
-**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
-**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
-two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
-of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
-pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
-5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. The study
-authors attribute (Spreuwenberg et al., 2006, as cited by Issurin) the power difference to
-postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding whole-body power exercise.
-**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
-finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
-preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
-companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
-more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
-preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
-result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
-passage.
-**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
-session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
-hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
-while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
-resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
-strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
-stated goal of a given lift.
-**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
-Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
-whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull" — treat the direction of
-the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
-something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
-text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
-populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
-different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might
-sequence a moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting
-fewer total squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that
-follow; a hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.
-**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
-[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
-[[research-papers/hanson-2007-acute-effects-of-heavy-and-light-load-squat-exercise-on-the-kinetic-measures-of-vertical-j]] (vault),
-[[research-papers/hirayama-2014-acute-effects-of-an-ascending-intensity-squat-protocol-on-vertical-jump-performance]] (vault),
-[[research-papers/seitz-2017-a-sled-push-stimulus-potentiates-subsequent-20-m-sprint-performance]] (vault).

+**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
+session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
+hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
+while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
+resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
+strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
+stated goal of a given lift.
+**When NOT to apply: mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
+Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
+whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull", treat the direction of
+the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
+something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
+text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
+populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
+different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.
+**Example** — **Inference:** a power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might
+sequence a moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting
+fewer total squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that
+follow; a hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.
+**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
+[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]],
+[[research-papers/hanson-2007-acute-effects-of-heavy-and-light-load-squat-exercise-on-the-kinetic-measures-of-vertical-j]] (vault),
+[[research-papers/hirayama-2014-acute-effects-of-an-ascending-intensity-squat-protocol-on-vertical-jump-performance]] (vault),

514	The transfer ability of these exercises can be explained by the fact that they, to a good

523	exercises has been touched upon, it should be noted that there is a straight line 
524	relationship to the specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.  They have been

893	Methods Used to Determine the Effect of Training 
894	Transfer 
895	 
896	As a general rule, all the research touching on the study of training transfer determines 
897	the amount of interrelationship between separate results of the athletes’ motor activity.  
898	The number of factors studied depends upon the tests proposed, and the contingent and 
899	classification of the subjects.  The amount and direction of training transfer are 
900	determined with the help of statistical analyses.  To do this, correlations, regressions, 
901	dispersions, factor analyses and multiple correlations are used.  Their effectiveness at this 
902	time is generally acknowledged and the essence of each is written up in specialized 
903	papers.   
904	 
905	In studying the problems of training transfer, the amount of interrelation between 
906	achievements in specific training exercises is usually used.  It is usually expressed by the 
907	coefficient of correlation.   
908	 
909	It is absurd to criticize the generally used methods of statistical analysis when some 
910	researchers have started to use other methods in more recent studies without proposing 
911	some kind of exchange.  In considering the pertinent facts received in the process of 
912	experimental studies on the given problem, we will nonetheless take it upon ourselves to 
913	switch the reader’s attention to the fact that results in speed-strength disciplines, even in 
914	training elite athletes, do not always reflect the true essence of the interaction between 
915	different forms of activity and exercises.  This is explained by the fact that the direction 
916	and amount of training transfer is dependent first of all on the integration of activity in 
917	the brain, which characterizes the most complex interactions between the excitatory-
918	inhibitory processes.  Thus, we study the inter-tie-ins with a minimum of 5-6 indices in 
919	athletes having various sports qualifications. 
920	 
921	We will illustrate with one example, which according to our view, reflects the complexity 
922	of showing the positive inter-tie-ins between exercises.  We will address only one of the 
923	53

929	of what the athlete used the during the period of developing sports form, consisted of 
930	three exercises---A, B, and C.  This exercise consecutiveness was used for the duration of 
931	the entire experiment.  After its conclusion it was shown that sports results increased in 
932	the first (A) and in the third (C) exercise.  There was no increase in the second (B) 
933	exercise.   
934	 
935	The coefficient of correlation was sufficiently high between exercises A and B, which 
936	made it possible to think that both exercises had a positive action on one another.  
937	Naturally, the statistical analysis did not bring out the kind of influence exercise B had on 
938	exercise A or C.  Based on this, a conclusion was made that exercise B was not effective, 
939	or did now show a positive influence on exercise A or C.

941	The aim of the second experiment was to show the correctness of this conclusion.  The 
942	athletes used only two exercises--A and C for the duration of the study.  After ending the 
943	experiment it was shown that there was no increase in sports results in these exercises.  
944	Apparently in the first experiment there was some kind of stimulating action of exercise 
945	B on exercises A and C.  Thus it is possible to propose a “tie-in” effect of exercise B 
946	when exercises A and C show positive effects on one another only when together with 
947	exercise B.  We believe that in the future, additional studies will resolve this interaction 
948	and propose corresponding methods of analysis.

In the men, the indices in the above mentioned exercises were somewhat higher (see table

Correlational analyses in the specialized-preparatory, specialized-developmental and 
competitive exercises allowed us to show a general picture of transfer of physical abilities 
from one means of training to another.  It was seen that in all the jumpers, the greatest 
amount of interrelationship was observed between results in the jumps using a short and 
full (competitive) approach run.  The coefficient of correlation varied most frequently 
between 0.750-0.900.   
 
High amounts of transfer of the cumulative effect was seen in all the jump exercises in 
the long jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole-vaulters.  What is pertinent to the men and 
women athletes specializing in the high jump, is that in all cases, a weak interrelationship 
between the test results was observed on the 0.400 level.  
 
In we compare the amounts of correlational interrelationship between single and triple 
jumps (vertical jump, long jump, and triple jump from place) and multiple jumps (five-
and ten-fold) then it can be seen that the second form of exercises (multiple jumps) have 
a greater number of cases in which the correlation is higher than with the first exercises. 
 
The most transferable strength exercise is the half squat with the barbell on the shoulders.  
Here, both with the men and women, in the high jump and in the pole vault as well as 
with the women in the long jump and triple jump, the transfer of physical abilities is 
observed on all levels of sports mastery.  In the men’s long jump it appears on three 
levels and in the triple jump,--- on four.  In the second strength exercise (barbell snatch) 
the cumulative training effect had a place on several levels of sports mastery in most 
events except for the women’s high jump and men’s triple jump.

150m.

The transfer ability of these exercises can be explained by the fact that they, to a good 
extent, repeat the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement, have a similar 
appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones.  The duration 
of the effect can correspond to the entire distance or its main joint parts (as for example 
the starting acceleration), and if necessary, the effect can be made greater.  Besides this, 
all of these exercises can be executed in lighter as well as in more complex (with weights, 
jumps or skips for height and other) conditions.   
 
Since the problem of using of lighter and more complex conditions when executing jump 
exercises has been touched upon, it should be noted that there is a straight line 
relationship to the specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.  They have been 
and are used at the present time by athletes of various sports qualifications. 
 
Without expanding this problem we propose that with time, the volume of jump exercises 
with the use of lightened and more complex conditions will significantly increase in 
comparison to the amount of work which is presently being done.  Of course specialists 
will have to resolve several problems.  First will be to show the optimal correlation 
between training loads executed in the standard, lightened and more complex conditions.  
Second will be to determine the weight to be used.  Third will be to not use lighter and 
more complex conditions sporadically as is presently being done, but systematically for 
the duration of the entire cycle of developing sports form.  Only in this way will it be 
possible to resolve the problem of developing speed (lightened conditions) and strength 
(more complex conditions) abilities.   
 
Specialists should also devote  attention to the selection of the optimal angles of incline 
of the roads used for development of speed or strength capabilities.  Dependent upon this 
is not only the effectiveness of developing the necessary physical abilities, but also the 
number of technical errors that appear. These errors always play a role when doing the 
exercises.

For development of speed-strength abilities in the training of different level athletes, a 
large number of strength, jump, and throw exercises are used.  Their portion of the total 
amount of training time, in relation to the tasks being resolved, the qualifications of the 
athlete and their individual characteristics, can comprise from 10-30% of the total sports 
form development cycle time.  The strength exercises are executed with and without the 
barbell, in addition to using various training devices.  The strength exercises, in 
comparison to others, produce a wider range of effects in the process of developing 
speed-strength abilities.  With their use, it is possible to selectively develop the muscle 
strength abilities such as speed, strength and “explosiveness”.     
 
In experimental research, two strength exercises have been studied---the barbell snatch 
and the half squat with the barbell on the shoulders. These exercises are most frequently 
used in the training of athletes having various sports qualifications.  They make it 
possible to evaluate the total level of development of strength abilities of all the body 
links of the athlete (barbell snatch) and strength of the leg extensors (half squat with 
barbell on shoulders).  
 
Besides this, these two exercises, according to their biomechanical characteristics 
(direction of movement, consecutiveness of including muscle groups in the work, 
regimes of muscle work, and so on) duplicate many strength exercises that are 
systematically used in the training process.  Knowing the results in each of these 
exercises makes it possible to predict achievement in other exercises and consequently, 
have a more complete picture of the transfer of physical abilities when using similar 
exercises.   
 
The data received testify to the poor interrelationship between the competitive event and 
the snatch and the squat with the barbell on the shoulders.  We will begin with the 100m 
run (tables 51, 56).  With the men, the cumulative effect in these two exercises was seen 
up to the level of 11.10 - 11.40 seconds.  With the women, in the snatch, it showed up

shoulders, on two levels (11.80-12.0 and 12.70-12.90 seconds).

Methods Used to Determine the Effect of Training 
Transfer 
 
As a general rule, all the research touching on the study of training transfer determines 
the amount of interrelationship between separate results of the athletes’ motor activity.  
The number of factors studied depends upon the tests proposed, and the contingent and 
classification of the subjects.  The amount and direction of training transfer are 
determined with the help of statistical analyses.  To do this, correlations, regressions, 
dispersions, factor analyses and multiple correlations are used.  Their effectiveness at this 
time is generally acknowledged and the essence of each is written up in specialized 
papers.   
 
In studying the problems of training transfer, the amount of interrelation between 
achievements in specific training exercises is usually used.  It is usually expressed by the 
coefficient of correlation.   
 
It is absurd to criticize the generally used methods of statistical analysis when some 
researchers have started to use other methods in more recent studies without proposing 
some kind of exchange.  In considering the pertinent facts received in the process of 
experimental studies on the given problem, we will nonetheless take it upon ourselves to 
switch the reader’s attention to the fact that results in speed-strength disciplines, even in 
training elite athletes, do not always reflect the true essence of the interaction between 
different forms of activity and exercises.  This is explained by the fact that the direction 
and amount of training transfer is dependent first of all on the integration of activity in 
the brain, which characterizes the most complex interactions between the excitatory-
inhibitory processes.  Thus, we study the inter-tie-ins with a minimum of 5-6 indices in 
athletes having various sports qualifications. 
 
We will illustrate with one example, which according to our view, reflects the complexity 
of showing the positive inter-tie-ins between exercises.  We will address only one of the 
53 


===== PDF page 71 (viewer 72) =====
situations which frequently arise in the process of doing experimental studies on this 
problem.  The following schematic of individual training sessions that were characteristic 
of what the athlete used the during the period of developing sports form, consisted of 
three exercises---A, B, and C.  This exercise consecutiveness was used for the duration of 
the entire experiment.  After its conclusion it was shown that sports results increased in 
the first (A) and in the third (C) exercise.  There was no increase in the second (B) 
exercise.   
 
The coefficient of correlation was sufficiently high between exercises A and B, which 
made it possible to think that both exercises had a positive action on one another.  
Naturally, the statistical analysis did not bring out the kind of influence exercise B had on 
exercise A or C.  Based on this, a conclusion was made that exercise B was not effective, 
or did now show a positive influence on exercise A or C.   
 
The aim of the second experiment was to show the correctness of this conclusion.  The 
athletes used only two exercises--A and C for the duration of the study.  After ending the 
experiment it was shown that there was no increase in sports results in these exercises.  
Apparently in the first experiment there was some kind of stimulating action of exercise 
B on exercises A and C.  Thus it is possible to propose a “tie-in” effect of exercise B 
when exercises A and C show positive effects on one another only when together with 
exercise B.  We believe that in the future, additional studies will resolve this interaction 
and propose corresponding methods of analysis.  
 
Additional studies that looked at the problem of training transfer, revolved mainly around 
the problem of finding effective means of training and the interrelationships between 
them [25, 34, 49, 94, 128, 284, 288, 304].  In only some of the papers were the factors 
studied that made this process possible and which ensured it [34, 49, 153, 154].  Studies 
that examined means of training touched on the methodic for developing physical 
abilities (for example, determining the intensity zones, volume of training loads, muscle 
work regimes and others). Also studied was improvement of technique in one or another 
of these aspects (methods, zones of intensity and others).   
54

106	The Specifists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
107	Transfer 
108	 
109	One of those who established the base for specificity was E. L. Torndyke [223].  She 
110	called it the theory of identical elements.  In agreement with her, the transfer of training is 
111	seen when in two types of activities, there is some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of 
112	elements. Their absence does not make it possible to have transfer.  This appearance is 
113	completely specific according to its essence. 
114	 
115	The transfer of training takes place by using earlier acquired associated ties [284, 287, 
116	288, 294, 304].  Between them there must be identical elements in a definite order.  The 
117	theory of identical elements was criticized by many native specialists in the area of 
118	classical and sports physiology and psychology.  They quoted the learning’s of I. P. 
119	Pavlov and believed that naturally formed conditioned reflexes lie in the activity of the 
120	central nervous system.  They do not negate the significance of old associations in the 
121	systemic activity of the higher segments of the brain.   
122	 
123	The influence of the coinciding “working” elements in the process of forming functional 
124	systems was noted by P.K. Anokhin [7].  According to him, the functional systems are 
125	only as great as displayed in the existing exercise.  In execution of most exercises, similar 
126	muscle groups participate.  Besides this, any activity ensures the functioning of one or 
127	another body system in the process of adaptation that takes place in response to the 
128	external or internal effect.   
129	 
130	Similar muscular groups appear to work in the formation of simple as well as complex, 
131	physical exercises (according to their coordinational make-up) [25, 26, 79].  This allowed 
132	several authors to speak of the multi-sided structure of physical exercises [50, 128, 143].  
133	 
134	Physical exercises possess multi-functional and multi-system properties.  The multi-
135	functionality ensures activation of similar organs and body systems [94, 126, 140, 267].

140	The Generalists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
141	Transfer 
142	 
143	 The viewpoints of the generalists are distinguished from the specifists according to their 
144	formulation of training transfer.  Generalists recommend several general and specialized 
145	pedagogical principles which give special attention to harmonious, all-round 
146	development of the athletes in the process of sports improvement.  The essence of this 
147	viewpoint is in the principle of unity of general and specialized preparation. Separately, 
148	each cannot resolve the problems presented before it.  General preparation creates the 
149	prerequisites for increasing sports achievements in the specialized area.  Note that all-
150	round development of the athlete is determined by the laws of formation and 
151	improvement of motor skills.  The basic idea of general preparation somehow appears to 
152	be realized in the process of sports improvement with a transfer of training from the 
153	general to the specialized preparation [18, 153, 212].  
154	 
155	In the theory and methods of physical education, it is recommended that coaches use the 
156	unity of general and specialized preparation when constructing the multi-year process of 
157	sports improvement, as well as during separate cycles (periods) of sports form 
158	development.  Thus, on the base stage of preparation, which lasts from four to six years, 
159	it is believed that with the use of general preparation, it is possible to lay down a full 
160	value foundation for future movements, ensure all-round harmonious development of the 
161	body, increase the general level of the body’s functional capabilities, create a rich fund of 
162	differently formed movement skills and abilities, and form beginning basic sports 
163	mastery [154].  They believe that the achievement of sports results on a given stage does 
164	not influence the next stage or objective.  This is realized later on the stage of maximum 
165	realization of sports capabilities. 
166	 
167	Generalists recommend that cycles of sports form development be broken up into general 
168	and specialized preparatory stages, where naturally, a base is created at the beginning 
169	with the use of a large number of general preparation means and later, on the stage of 
170	5

176	two stages, but of three, four, or more. 
177	 
178	Of course, striving for harmonious and all-round development of the person as a valuable 
179	foundation for future sports results is very commendable and gratifying.  In this case, it is 
180	used when the task is physical normalization, not achievement of high sports results. 
181	 
182	The views of the generalists were formed during the years from 1940-1960.  Their views 
183	were a major contribution to the understanding of the process of sports improvement.  
184	However, with time, it has been shown that the general preparation means create a base, a 
185	foundation, only in the training of low level athletes [34, 57, 182].  What is pertinent to 
186	an increase in sports mastery of high level athletes is the transfer of training to the 
187	competitive event that can take place only with specialized preparation means [34, 57].   
188	 
189	With the advent of a greater number of research studies illuminating the specificity of 
190	training transfer, those on the side of unity of general and special preparation began to 
191	gradually “specialize” the means of general preparation.  In so doing, they brought out 
192	that the specialization of general preparation allows for fuller use of the positive training 
193	transfer effect.  The idea behind specializing the means of general preparation led to 
194	beginning training with the use of a certain number of specialized-preparatory exercises 
195	in the general preparatory stage cycles in the development of sports form.  If, at the 
196	beginning the correlation between the time spent on general and specialized preparation 
197	was expressed in a 3:1 ratio, it later changed in favor of an increased number of 
198	specialized preparation means.  
199	 
200	An impression is created that by ignoring the idea that it is necessary to specialize general 
201	preparation for the sake of more effective use of positive training transfer, many 
202	specialists do not want to admit the error of their views.  They cover it up with various 
203	word combinations or as best as possible, combine opposite meaning terms of 
204	“specialized” and “general” preparation to get away from the agony of the dreamed up

243	The Holistics Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
244	Transfer 
245	 
246	According to the holistics, the body appears as a single unit and any internal or external 
247	action affects all of it's systems to a certain degree.  From here it follows that 
248	development of single abilities cannot take place without the involvement of others.  In 
249	this, their inter-relationships and consequently their inter-effects always exist.  On the one 
250	hand, a certain exercise has an influence on the development of another or other physical 
251	abilities, and on the other hand, ensures the functioning of the entire body as a whole.  
252	Thus, it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics.  
253	 
254	However, we are interested in significant research on non-specific reactions by the body 
255	systems with which it is possible to influence the development of specific physical 
256	abilities of athletes, who specialize in different track and field events or other sports. The 
257	discussion here is about the multi-functional properties of specific or other exercises 
258	which bring about similar reactions of the blood vessels, heart-circulatory and respiratory 
259	systems and allow for an increase in sports results mainly in the cyclic disciplines,

366	Types of Training Transfer 
367	 
368	There are three types of training transfer: positive, negative, and neutral.  In the 
369	specialized literature it is also possible to find “indifferent” transfer. 
370	 
371	Positive transfer of training means that there is a positive effect of one exercise on 
372	another.  In other words, with an increase in the sports result in one exercise, a parallel 
373	increase takes place in another exercise. 
374	 
375	In negative transfer of training there is always a negative interaction between the 
376	exercises being used.  Here, with increased preparation in one exercise, there is a 
377	simultaneous decrease in other exercises. 
378	 
379	In neutral transfer of training there is no increase or decrease in sports achievement.  The 
380	training does not show any affect on another training. 
381	 
382	In addition to these three noted forms of training transfer we more rarely meet with 
383	indifferent transfer.  This is especially so when training high level athletes who use a 
384	whole complex of different exercises, and depends on their coordination structure and 
385	strength of their influence.  At the present time, the interrelationships between the 
386	exercises are complex and unpredictable, and they may have a double effect on one 
387	another. For example, there may be a positive affect on increasing the functional 
388	capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the technique an exercise [92].
