Indice 
 
Result 
Indice usually refers to the number of the recorded result of a 
particular exercise.  It may also refer to results in the exercise, results 
in the competition, etc. 
Level of 
Athlete  
 
Qualifications 
of Athlete 
These terms are used interchangeably.  They refer to an athlete’s level 
of ability, i.e., whether he or she is in the elite (world or professional 
level), high, average or low (novice) class. The categories are very 
distinct. 
Means and 
Methods 
Means refers to the type of training being done, as for example, 
strength, endurance, or specialized training.  Methods refer to the 
programs used in each of the means.  For example, strength training is 
the means and concentric, eccentric, interval, explosive, maximum 
strength training etc. are the methods. In the U.S., these terms are 
most often used interchangeably. 
Motor 
Analyzer 
This is a unique term that has no analogy in the English language.  
Typically, analyzer refers to the area of the brain that controls a 
particular function or functions. For example, the motor analyzer 
usually refers to the area of the brain (cortex) which is responsible for 
movement in the body.  It is in this area that the brain analyzes the 
incoming information and then responds by sending out the proper 
signals to guide the motor activity. 
Period 
 
Stage 
These terms are interchangeably. Stage of training is synonymous 
with period of training. At times, stage of training may also refer to 
level of training. 
Physical 
Education 
This term is used to denote the pure discipline.  The physical 
education discipline is more highly developed and scientific in the 
Russian literature than in the U.S. 
Qualifications   
of Athlete 
Level of              
Athlete 
These terms are used interchangeably.  They refer to an athlete’s level 
of ability, i.e. whether he or she is in the elite (world or professional 
level), high, average or low (novice) class. The categories are very 
distinct. 
xii 


===== PDF page 14 (viewer 15) =====
Result 
 
Indice  
Indice usually refers to the number of the recorded result of a 
particular exercise.  It may also refer to results in the exercise, results 
in the competition, etc.  
Specialized  
Exercises  
 
Specialized exercises have a direct correlation to the sports event.  
They have specific criteria and must duplicate various aspects of the 
competitive event, as for example, the biomechanical structure, energy 
source, range of motion in which strength is displayed, etc.  Also 
known as specialized physical preparation (SPP). 
Specialized-
developmental 
exercises 
These exercises repeat the competitive exercise in its separate parts.  
In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, 
together with activation of similar systems and organs.  They not only 
repeat the muscle work regime and other systems of the body which 
ensure further increases in the competitive exercise, but also supersede 
them.  The specialized-developmental exercises more or less recreate 
all the elements of the competitive activity, and in so doing, make it 
possible to more effectively and selectively have an effect on 
improving or developing the same or other physical abilities.  The 
levels achieved in these exercises are realized in further execution of 
the competitive exercises.  They serve for entry into the state of sports 
form.   
Specialized-
preparatory 
exercises 
These exercises as the general preparatory exercises, do not repeat the 
competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts.  However, 
they use similar muscle groups in their execution.  The training work 
serves to activate the functions and body systems from which an 
increase in sports results in the main movements depend.  Identical or 
close to identical regimes of muscle work and different functions of 
other systems are involved.   
Sports Form 
This term typically refers to when the athlete attains all that is possible 
from the specific training done over a specific period of time.  For 
example, entering sports form after working on a particular exercise 
and mastering it, means that the athlete has attained full mastery of the 
xiii 


===== PDF page 20 (viewer 21) =====
The Specifists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
Transfer 
 
One of those who established the base for specificity was E. L. Torndyke [223].  She 
called it the theory of identical elements.  In agreement with her, the transfer of training is 
seen when in two types of activities, there is some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of 
elements. Their absence does not make it possible to have transfer.  This appearance is 
completely specific according to its essence. 
 
The transfer of training takes place by using earlier acquired associated ties [284, 287, 
288, 294, 304].  Between them there must be identical elements in a definite order.  The 
theory of identical elements was criticized by many native specialists in the area of 
classical and sports physiology and psychology.  They quoted the learning’s of I. P. 
Pavlov and believed that naturally formed conditioned reflexes lie in the activity of the 
central nervous system.  They do not negate the significance of old associations in the 
systemic activity of the higher segments of the brain.   
 
The influence of the coinciding “working” elements in the process of forming functional 
systems was noted by P.K. Anokhin [7].  According to him, the functional systems are 
only as great as displayed in the existing exercise.  In execution of most exercises, similar 
muscle groups participate.  Besides this, any activity ensures the functioning of one or 
another body system in the process of adaptation that takes place in response to the 
external or internal effect.   
 
Similar muscular groups appear to work in the formation of simple as well as complex, 
physical exercises (according to their coordinational make-up) [25, 26, 79].  This allowed 
several authors to speak of the multi-sided structure of physical exercises [50, 128, 143].  
 
Physical exercises possess multi-functional and multi-system properties.  The multi-
functionality ensures activation of similar organs and body systems [94, 126, 140, 267]. 
3 


===== PDF page 22 (viewer 23) =====
The Generalists Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
Transfer 
 
 The viewpoints of the generalists are distinguished from the specifists according to their 
formulation of training transfer.  Generalists recommend several general and specialized 
pedagogical principles which give special attention to harmonious, all-round 
development of the athletes in the process of sports improvement.  The essence of this 
viewpoint is in the principle of unity of general and specialized preparation. Separately, 
each cannot resolve the problems presented before it.  General preparation creates the 
prerequisites for increasing sports achievements in the specialized area.  Note that all-
round development of the athlete is determined by the laws of formation and 
improvement of motor skills.  The basic idea of general preparation somehow appears to 
be realized in the process of sports improvement with a transfer of training from the 
general to the specialized preparation [18, 153, 212].  
 
In the theory and methods of physical education, it is recommended that coaches use the 
unity of general and specialized preparation when constructing the multi-year process of 
sports improvement, as well as during separate cycles (periods) of sports form 
development.  Thus, on the base stage of preparation, which lasts from four to six years, 
it is believed that with the use of general preparation, it is possible to lay down a full 
value foundation for future movements, ensure all-round harmonious development of the 
body, increase the general level of the body’s functional capabilities, create a rich fund of 
differently formed movement skills and abilities, and form beginning basic sports 
mastery [154].  They believe that the achievement of sports results on a given stage does 
not influence the next stage or objective.  This is realized later on the stage of maximum 
realization of sports capabilities. 
 
Generalists recommend that cycles of sports form development be broken up into general 
and specialized preparatory stages, where naturally, a base is created at the beginning 
with the use of a large number of general preparation means and later, on the stage of 
5 


===== PDF page 23 (viewer 24) =====
specialized preparation, realization of them.  This idea is maintained and used in different 
ways in constructing cycles of sports form development which can consist not only of 
two stages, but of three, four, or more. 
 
Of course, striving for harmonious and all-round development of the person as a valuable 
foundation for future sports results is very commendable and gratifying.  In this case, it is 
used when the task is physical normalization, not achievement of high sports results. 
 
The views of the generalists were formed during the years from 1940-1960.  Their views 
were a major contribution to the understanding of the process of sports improvement.  
However, with time, it has been shown that the general preparation means create a base, a 
foundation, only in the training of low level athletes [34, 57, 182].  What is pertinent to 
an increase in sports mastery of high level athletes is the transfer of training to the 
competitive event that can take place only with specialized preparation means [34, 57].   
 
With the advent of a greater number of research studies illuminating the specificity of 
training transfer, those on the side of unity of general and special preparation began to 
gradually “specialize” the means of general preparation.  In so doing, they brought out 
that the specialization of general preparation allows for fuller use of the positive training 
transfer effect.  The idea behind specializing the means of general preparation led to 
beginning training with the use of a certain number of specialized-preparatory exercises 
in the general preparatory stage cycles in the development of sports form.  If, at the 
beginning the correlation between the time spent on general and specialized preparation 
was expressed in a 3:1 ratio, it later changed in favor of an increased number of 
specialized preparation means.  
 
An impression is created that by ignoring the idea that it is necessary to specialize general 
preparation for the sake of more effective use of positive training transfer, many 
specialists do not want to admit the error of their views.  They cover it up with various 
word combinations or as best as possible, combine opposite meaning terms of 
“specialized” and “general” preparation to get away from the agony of the dreamed up 
6 


===== PDF page 24 (viewer 25) =====
principle of the “unity of general and specialized preparation”.  If we move away from 
multi-structure, multi-function and multi-system physical exercises, it becomes clear that 
even in the 1960-1970’s, general preparation means were practically not used in the 
training of athletes having different sports qualifications.  
 
In order to not make unsubstantiated statements we will present several examples.  In the 
training of jumpers and throwers, short distance runs were relegated to general 
preparation means.  But this is a specialized-preparatory exercise, in as much as their 
execution develops the speed-strength abilities of the leg flexor and extensor muscles that 
are actively involved in all throws and jumps.  Regardless of this, short distance runs are 
repeated in jumps as they are one of the structural components of the competitive event 
as for example, in the long jump.  Also, in the training of sprinters, jumpers and throwers 
how is it possible to execute a barbell clean or half squat with the barbell as a means of 
general preparation if these muscle groups participate in executing the competitive 
exercise?  The discussion here is related to the flexors and extensors of the legs. 
 
Even more surprising is the classification of middle and long distance running which has 
an aerobic effect, as a means of general preparation.  In execution of the workloads 
coordinated body systems (the nerve-muscle, respiratory, heart-circulatory, and other 
systems) participate even without taking into consideration running technique.   
 
No matter how we “specialize” the means of general preparation, no one and nowhere in 
sports practice is it possible to escape the negative effects when there is development of 
unnecessary muscle groups in one or another sports discipline, especially in speed-
strength events.  Specialists in the sprints, jumps and throws know that extreme 
development of speed-strength abilities of the leg flexor muscles shows up negatively on 
the physical ability of the leg extensors. 
 
This finding is related to the technique of executing the competitive exercise.  Also, 
extreme development of arm strength in the training of a hammer thrower leads to a 
7 


===== PDF page 26 (viewer 27) =====
The Holistics Viewpoint on the Theory of Training 
Transfer 
 
According to the holistics, the body appears as a single unit and any internal or external 
action affects all of it's systems to a certain degree.  From here it follows that 
development of single abilities cannot take place without the involvement of others.  In 
this, their inter-relationships and consequently their inter-effects always exist.  On the one 
hand, a certain exercise has an influence on the development of another or other physical 
abilities, and on the other hand, ensures the functioning of the entire body as a whole.  
Thus, it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics.  
 
However, we are interested in significant research on non-specific reactions by the body 
systems with which it is possible to influence the development of specific physical 
abilities of athletes, who specialize in different track and field events or other sports. The 
discussion here is about the multi-functional properties of specific or other exercises 
which bring about similar reactions of the blood vessels, heart-circulatory and respiratory 
systems and allow for an increase in sports results mainly in the cyclic disciplines, 
beginning with the sprints and ending with middle, long, and super-long distances. 
 
Many studies in the theory and methods of physical education substantiate that on the 
higher levels, the above named body systems do not function in the same manner in all 
types of sport.  This is especially true where an increase in achievement depends on a 
definite level of development of speed or specialized endurance.  For example, the 
functional capabilities of the blood vessels, heart-circulatory and respiratory systems can 
be increased equally well, as for example, in training middle distance runners, with the 
use of specialized means or by using exercises from other sports (rowing, cycling, 
swimming, sports games, and so on). 
 
At the present time the positive influence of cyclical sports on increasing the functional 
capabilities of the body systems is generally acknowledged.  However, using other 
9 


===== PDF page 28 (viewer 29) =====
with great changes in the understanding of the principles not only of training transfer, but 
the very method of training.  All of this is in the future.  
 
Now, we should take note of a major deficiency in the theory of the holistics in that they 
indirectly call for the use of one method of training for increasing the functional 
capabilities of the blood vessels, cardio-vascular and respiratory systems, in order to get 
corresponding adaptational changes in the neuro-muscular system.  This leads to 
disharmony, as the athlete enters the highest training state in non-specific exercises at the 
start and only after this, after several weeks, enters a state of sports form in the specific 
exercises.  It would be possible to ignore this if the functional levels achieved in non-
specific exercises were maintained while the athlete was still achieving corresponding 
increases in his physical preparation in the specific training means.  However, the level of 
trainedness decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized 
exercises. 
 
In the track and field jumps and throws and likewise in the hurdles, there is agreement 
with the holistics that is necessary to first develop the physical capabilities and only after 
this, perfect technical mastery.  Thus the “block” method of constructing cycles of sports 
form development oversees the separate preparatory periods in the blocks of physical and 
technical preparation [49].  Those in agreement with this concept do not believe that 
simultaneously introducing means of technical preparation into the training process 
develops the physical abilities together with improvement of technique. 
 
In these instances, there is a theoretical and practical error working at the base of the 
artificial division of form and content since they are united in all of their displays.  In the 
theory and methods of physical education this unity is expressed in the principle of 
conjugated training effects.  This was proposed in the 1960’s by head coach and scientist 
V.M. Dyachkov [81]. The essence of this method will be looked at further on since it 
provides answers to many questions that require a straight forward understanding of the 
training transfer process. 
 
11 


===== PDF page 29 (viewer 30) =====
The Principle of Conjugated Training Effects 
 
The use of training means for developing physical abilities and improving technical 
mastery is in accord with this principle.  These two factors should coincide and 
correspond to the competitive exercise according to their basic characteristics.  Later on, 
this principle was modified by other specialists who called it dynamic correspondence 
and the principle of resolving motor actions.  [157]. According to U.V. Menkhin [157] 
the conjugate principle should affect not only the competitive event, but all the 
specialized activity as a whole.   
 
Using the sport of gymnastics as an example, Menkhin showed that the best form of 
conjugation appears when the physical preparation ensures five main components of 
preparation for technical improvement or for learning technique:  
• Development of the motor qualities that are necessary for a specific activity that is 
sufficiently localized in the muscle groups;  
• A high level of motor qualities that define the demands of the biodynamic 
structure of gymnastic elements;  
• Suitability for realizing the motor potential in the most common forms of motor 
activity, that characterize the potential physical preparation needed for mastering 
technique; 
• Suitability for fulfilling long duration work in specific events in all-round 
competition that guarantees the gymnasts motor activity reliability [repeat 
ability]; 
• Suitability for realizing the motor potential in competitive combinations [routines] 
which is the main objective of the gymnast. 
 
We will not purposely end on the main components proposed by U.V. Menkhin in 
gymnastics as we believe that it can be used in the technical disciplines of track and field. 
 
12 


===== PDF page 30 (viewer 31) =====
The conjugate principle of training effects was used by us in working out the principle of 
all-round specialized preparation [265]. Over many years, it envisioned sports 
improvement through the use of primarily specialized preparation means.  General 
preparation means were used to a lesser extent and only for general warm ups and during 
the time of using restorative measures. Special-preparatory and special-developmental 
exercises create the “base”, “the foundation”, for improving sports results in a 
competitive event on each level in the cycle of developing sports form that produced the 
greatest sports improvement.   
 
The number of special-preparatory and special-developmental exercises used in each 
consecutive cycle (period) of developing sports form depends on the tasks to be 
accomplished.  They should be sufficient for resolution of the tasks.  Here, the transfer 
effect depends not only on the number of special-preparatory and special-developmental 
exercises used, but on their “newness” and the strength of their effect which should be 
greater in each consecutive cycle of sports form development.  This makes it possible to 
achieve a new level of adaptation, which serves to increase the sports result and naturally, 
the transfer of training. 
13 


===== PDF page 31 (viewer 32) =====
Types of Training Transfer 
 
There are three types of training transfer: positive, negative, and neutral.  In the 
specialized literature it is also possible to find “indifferent” transfer. 
 
Positive transfer of training means that there is a positive effect of one exercise on 
another.  In other words, with an increase in the sports result in one exercise, a parallel 
increase takes place in another exercise. 
 
In negative transfer of training there is always a negative interaction between the 
exercises being used.  Here, with increased preparation in one exercise, there is a 
simultaneous decrease in other exercises. 
 
In neutral transfer of training there is no increase or decrease in sports achievement.  The 
training does not show any affect on another training. 
 
In addition to these three noted forms of training transfer we more rarely meet with 
indifferent transfer.  This is especially so when training high level athletes who use a 
whole complex of different exercises, and depends on their coordination structure and 
strength of their influence.  At the present time, the interrelationships between the 
exercises are complex and unpredictable, and they may have a double effect on one 
another. For example, there may be a positive affect on increasing the functional 
capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the technique an exercise [92].  
In track and field, there is a noticeable worsening of technique in some throws with the 
use of heavier implements [18, 152]. In these cases, with an increase in strength, there is 
a negative change in the process of executing separate elements as well the entire 
movement as a whole [152]. 
 
The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent transfer) is most frequently 
explained by the use of exercises which, from the beginning, interfere with the unity 
between form and content.  Examples of indifferent transfer can be in the systems of 
14 


===== PDF page 32 (viewer 33) =====
training as for example, by athletes specializing in different walking events.  Included 
here is the use of a high volume of aerobic and anaerobic running for long periods of 
time, as in the general preparatory stage.  In this training there is a noted improvement in 
the functional abilities of the heart-circulatory, respiratory and blood vessel systems and a 
worsening of walking technique [94].  
 
There are similar inter-effects that come up in other sports.  In walking it is possible to 
get away from the negative influence by using mainly specialized-developmental and 
competitive exercises.  In certain running events, hurdles and throws, it is possible to 
maneuver between “good” and “poor” in selecting exercises, so that there would be more 
good ones rather than poor ones.  This makes it possible to eliminate the negative 
influence on technique in several weekly cycles. 
 
15 


===== PDF page 39 (viewer 40) =====
The Dependence of Training Transfer on the Duration 
of Different Stages, Blocks of Sports Form Development 
Cycles 
 
At the present time, after the regularities regarding development, maintenance and lose of 
sports form have been studied, it becomes clear that the duration of the stages, blocks, of 
sports form development cycles, as proposed by various authors, can serve to reveal the 
mechanisms of training transfer, or to create conditions that do not allow for transfer.  In 
the latter instance, we have in mind situations in which the idea of creating the “base”,  
“foundation”, remains only an idea.  The reason for this is that the work carried out in 
each of the previous stages, blocks, does not show an influence on increasing 
achievements in the training used over the duration of each successive stage.   
 
In life the idea is realized only when at the end of each previous stage, block, the athlete 
resolves the tasks put before him that allows him to enter the state of sports form in the 
training that is used for the duration of the work.  For this to happen it is necessary that 
the duration of the stages, blocks, correspond to the duration of the cycles of sports form 
development for each individual athlete.  From the literature it is known that most 
frequently, athletes, after the period of rest (transitional period), enter into the state of 
sports form over 2-3 months.  But there are also athletes whose individual cycles of 
sports form development take 4-7 and even 8 months. 
 
Practically, only when using the same yearly cycles of training with the duration of the 
general preparatory stage on the average, three months, athletes who enter the state of

yearly cycle, the athletes use a sufficiently large number of exercises repeating the basic 
movement in lighter and more difficult conditions --- i.e., using implements having 
different weights.  The deviation range when using lighter and heavier implements in 
comparison to the competitive implement weight, can vary from several percent to the 
tens and even hundreds of percent.

implement.  Heavier and lighter implements were used sporadically and in small volume.

# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the book credits
"About the Author" (Bondarchuk) and "About the Translator" (Michael Yessis) separately,
and the Glossary itself carries no byline. Definitions inside it cite the book's own
numbered bibliography (e.g. the "Block method" entry cites "Y.V. Verkhoshansky [49, 50]"
using the same reference numbers Bondarchuk's own chapters use), which is evidence the
Glossary is Bondarchuk's own material carried through translation rather than a
translator's separate addition — but the book gives no explicit statement either way, so
this entry treats the Glossary as **the book's** definitions rather than asserting they are
Bondarchuk's personal wording. Do not cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future
entry without that caveat:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises / GPP**: "do not repeat the competitive actions as a
  whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part in the work being done. The
  functional systems of the body are activated but do not ensure an increase in results in
  the competitive exercise." Function: all-round development, work capacity, and active
  rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises / SPP**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the
  competitive actions as a whole or in their separate parts. However, they use similar
  muscle groups in their execution," activating the functions and body systems the main
  movement depends on, with "identical or close to identical regimes of muscle work."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises / SDE**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its
  separate parts. In executing them, one and the same muscle groups participate, together
  with activation of similar systems and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work
  regime and other systems of the body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry
  into the state of sports form." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises / CE**: "the acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the
  athlete participates in competition," executed either in actual competition or in
  training as a model/repeat of competitive conditions, easier or harder (this definition
  spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The Glossary gives no stated mechanism for why these four classes
should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
does not frame its own tables that way.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is the book's own
classification scheme (see the voice note above on Glossary authorship). Two other sources
in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Soviet/Russian
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

**Related** — `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault) — the secondary, Moyer-course paraphrase of this same taxonomy; **reciprocal-link
suggestion**: add a note there pointing back to this primary-source entry once this book
clears the review gate. [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — the transfer
logic built on this classification. [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] —
the specifist theory this classification operationalizes.

# The Book's Four Exercise Classes, from Its Own Glossary: General Preparatory, Specialized-Preparatory, Specialized-Developmental, Competitive

**What it is** — This is the book's own definition of the classification Chapter 2's
correlational data depends on, drawn from its front-matter Glossary (PDF pp. 10-14,
printed pp. ix-xiii; Chapter 2's own prose, PDF p. 75, printed p. 58, assumes the reader
already knows these terms and does not redefine them). **Voice note:** the Glossary is
unsigned and contains lines in the translator's voice: "In the U.S., these terms are most
often used interchangeably" (Means and Methods entry) and "The physical education
discipline is more highly developed and scientific in the Russian literature than in the
U.S." (Physical Education entry), plus "This is a unique term that has no analogy in the
English language" (Motor Analyzer entry) — all PDF p. 13, printed p. xii. Per the task
brief's rule, a translator (Yessis) voice is not the author's. Treat the definitions below as
**the translated edition's**, possibly Yessis's own glosses; Bondarchuk's own usage of these
terms is visible in Chapter 1-2 prose instead (e.g. PDF p. 24, printed p. 7; PDF p. 62,
printed p. 45, "we did not take exercises from the general developmental group"). Do not
cite this entry as "Bondarchuk says" in a future entry without that caveat. The Glossary's
own abbreviation is "SPP" for **Specialized Exercises** ("Also known as specialized
physical preparation (SPP)," PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii) — a different label than
"specialized-preparatory," which the Glossary does not itself abbreviate. The Glossary
never abbreviates specialized-developmental exercises or competitive exercises as "SDE" or
"CE" either; those abbreviations below are this entry's own shorthand, not the book's:
- **General (Preparatory) Exercises ("GPP" — this entry's abbreviation)**: "do not repeat
  the competitive actions as a whole or their separate parts. Other muscle groups take part
  in the work being done. The functional systems of the body are activated but do not
  ensure an increase in results in the competitive exercise." Function: all-round
  development, work capacity, and active rest/restoration. (PDF p. 12, printed p. xi.)
- **Specialized-Preparatory Exercises ("SPE" — this entry's abbreviation; the Glossary's own
  "SPP" label attaches to a related but separately defined "Specialized Exercises" entry,
  see above)**: like general exercises, "do not repeat the competitive actions as a whole
  or in their separate parts. However, they use similar muscle groups in their execution,"
  activating the functions and body systems the main movement depends on, with "identical
  or close to identical regimes of muscle work." (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Specialized-Developmental Exercises ("SDE" — this entry's abbreviation, not the
  Glossary's)**: "repeat the competitive exercise in its separate parts. In executing them,
  one and the same muscle groups participate, together with activation of similar systems
  and organs. They not only repeat the muscle work regime and other systems of the
  body... but also supersede them," and "serve for entry into the state of sports form."
  (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii.)
- **Competitive Exercises ("CE" — this entry's abbreviation, not the Glossary's)**: "the
  acting definition... is 'sport event,' in which the athlete participates in competition,"
  executed either in actual competition or in training as a model/repeat of competitive
  conditions, easier or harder (this definition spans a page break). (PDF pp. 11-12, printed
  pp. x-xi.)
Chapter 2's own intro adds a cross-cutting distinction independent of the four classes: a
**local** exercise (uses separate parts/body links — squat, bench press, standing long
jump, vertical jump) versus a **global** exercise (uses all body links together — the
barbell clean). (PDF p. 75, printed p. 58.)

**Why it works** — The Glossary gives no stated mechanism for why these four classes
should differ in transfer value; it only defines them by how much of the competitive
movement each one reproduces. **Inference:** reading the four classes as an ordered
continuum, and connecting that continuum to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and the specifist "identical
elements" position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] (more shared
elements with the competitive movement predicting more reliable transfer), is this entry's
own synthesis across sections of the book, not a claim the Glossary or Chapter 2's intro
states in those words. Chapter 2's correlational data (see the claim entries below) can be
read as an empirical test of that inferred prediction, event by event, but the book itself
does not frame its own tables that way.

**When to apply** — Use as the primary-source definition when auditing any exercise
selection against this taxonomy, in place of or alongside secondary paraphrases of it.
**Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in HHPR 5355 is taught "on a spectrum from general
preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises
(Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific'"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`; `week1-lecture.md pp.32-36`) — this entry
gives that course material its primary-source citation and exact definitions. This
library already has a secondary-source treatment of the same taxonomy in
`fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/framework--sprint-exercise-classes-bondarchuk-four-categories.md`
(vault), built from Moyer's course paraphrase rather than Bondarchuk's own text; that
entry's table ("GPE/SPE/SDE/CE") matches this one closely but labels Moyer's own sprint
examples (bounding, banded pawback, etc.), not Bondarchuk's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, not proven: this is the book's own
classification scheme (see the voice note above on Glossary authorship). Two other sources
in this library already use it independently
(the `fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer` vault entry linked above, and Eric's HHPR 5355
course per `method-baseline.md`), which is evidence the taxonomy circulated beyond this
one book, but this ingest did not check how far it spread through the wider Soviet/Russian
sport-science literature, so that broader claim is not made here. It is a practitioner
taxonomy, not an independently tested causal model, and the boundary between
classes is fuzzy in application (the Moyer-derived entry below makes the same point about
sprint exercises specifically). The four-class definitions here are written for individual
track and field events; a football skill (e.g., a pass rush) is a much less discrete,
single "competitive exercise" than a 100m sprint or a hammer throw, so classifying a given
drill as SPP vs. SDE for football is Inference, not something Bondarchuk's glossary
addresses.

**Example** — For a shot putter: general preparatory = general conditioning running;
specialized-preparatory = barbell snatch, half squat (same leg-extensor muscle groups,
different movement); specialized-developmental = throwing a lighter or heavier shot
(repeats the throw's parts under altered load); competitive = throwing the 7.26kg
competition shot in a meet.

# "Current" vs. "Distant" Transfer: When in a Training Block the Earlier Work Actually Pays Off

**What it is** — Bondarchuk proposes that when a training cycle is built in successive
stages/blocks, the achieved level from a previous stage can transfer to the following
stage in one of three ways (PDF pp. 35-38, printed pp. 18-21):
1. **Transfer at the start** of the next stage/block — the previous stage's result can
   then be allowed to decrease, increase, or hold, because it already did its job of
   creating the "base."
2. **Transfer in the middle** of the next stage/block — the previous level must be
   actively maintained (not allowed to drop) while the next stage's exercises are
   developed, using reduced-volume maintenance work.
3. **Transfer at the end** of the next stage/block — the previous stage's level must be
   held all the way through.

He then names two broader modes across an entire multi-stage cycle: **"distant" transfer**
(entering sports form in one exercise class first, other classes only later — harder to
manage because you must simultaneously maintain the earlier gains and build the later
ones) versus **"current" (flowing) transfer** (all exercise classes reach sports form
together, because a consistent, unbroken mix of general/specialized-preparatory/
specialized-developmental/competitive exercises runs throughout every stage rather than
being introduced and dropped stage by stage). Current transfer is associated with
variational, combinational, and complex methods of cycle construction; distant transfer
with the stricter stage/block methods. (PDF pp. 41-42, 66-67, printed pp. 24-25, 49-50.)
He also states that excluding specialized-developmental and competitive exercises for more
than 3-4 weeks under the variational method causes a real loss of the previously achieved
level. (PDF p. 38, printed p. 21.)

**Why it works** — No physiological mechanism is offered; this is a purely descriptive,
practice-derived model the author says he arrived at by observing which cycle-construction
methods succeeded ("we came to the conclusion that..."), with no cited independent
verification or controlled comparison in the excerpted text. **Inference:** the "current
transfer" mode maps loosely onto what Western periodization literature calls concurrent or
conjugate training (train all qualities across the whole cycle, in varying proportions)
versus "distant transfer" mapping onto strict block/linear periodization (sequential
single-quality phases) — a connection this passage does not make itself.

===== PDF page 68 (viewer 69) =====
Characteristics of the Tests Used 
 
The study of training transfer mechanisms begins with the fixing of separately taken 
amounts of physical and technical preparation of athletes in the process of using specific 
(or other) exercises and then establishing the inter-relationships between them.  Foremost 
is to determine the influence the exercise has on the competitive exercise, which in all 
track and field events, is the most important test. 
 
As a result of studying multiple literary sources that examined this problem, it was 
concluded that in all speed-strength events and in the endurance group, general and 
specialized tests are used in the training process.  When talk is about general tests, we 
have in mind not those that determine preparation in general preparatory exercises, but of 
similar tests, used in mixed groups or between groups.   
 
For testing the functional state of the heart-circulatory, blood vessel and respiratory 
systems, almost all of the same tests are used in practice in all disciplines of track and 
field.  For example, maximum oxygen uptake is determined on a veloergometer and the 
limits possible while functioning at maximum O2 uptake, anaerobic threshold and others.   
 
In speed-strength sports, they more frequently use tests such as the 60 meter run from a 
low start (blocks), barbell snatch, half squat with the bar on the shoulders, standing long 
jump, vertical jump (according to V.M. Abalakov), triple jump from place, and throwing 
the shot forward, backward.  In specialized tests for each sport the exercises are very 
similar. 
 
In cyclical sports, the most frequently used general tests for endurance are those which 
characterize the level of functioning of the heart-circulatory, blood vessel, and respiratory 
systems (already touched on above).  Each event in this group has its own specific tests. 
 
The reliability of many tests has already been shown.  Foremost in most of these are 
those tests that show the level of preparation in specialized-developmental exercises.  
51 


===== PDF page 69 (viewer 70) =====
Included here are test results in the competitive exercises, executed in lighter and more 
complex conditions.  For example, in the throws, the tests measure results in throws with 
lighter and heavier implements.  In the jumps, the results are recorded in jumps with a 
short approach run.  In cyclical sports, the tests revolve around determining the number 
of segments executed at a given speed and by observing the planned intervals of rest 
between them. 
 
The reliability of tests that use general preparatory and specialized-preparatory exercises 
still have not been fully confirmed.  This will be tightened up in the near future. 
 
Previous studies in which we tried to determine the exercises that produce a positive 
transfer of training to the competitive exercise are detailed in Chapter 2.  We use those 
that are most frequently used in sports practice. 
 
52

# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each

**What it is** — Bondarchuk splits the tests used to study training transfer into two
families (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52):
- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
- **Specialized tests**: tests unique to each event's specific demands, most reliably
  results in **specialized-developmental exercises** — i.e., the competitive movement
  itself executed under lighter or more difficult conditions (lighter/heavier implements
  in throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
  events). He states specialized-developmental test reliability is the best-established
  of the test types; general-preparatory and specialized-preparatory test reliability is
  explicitly flagged as "not fully confirmed" and something to be "tightened up in the
  near future." (PDF p. 69, printed p. 52.)

**Why it works** — The text itself gives no mechanism connecting these two ideas; it simply
asserts that specialized-developmental test reliability "has already been shown" without
citing why. **Inference:** connecting this to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — specialized-developmental exercises
sit closest to the competitive event in that transfer chain, so tests built from those same
exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, prioritize tests that
are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the competitive skill under

# Two Test Families: "General" Tests Shared Across Events, "Specialized" Tests Unique to Each

**What it is** — Bondarchuk opens by naming the competitive exercise itself as the
benchmark: determining an exercise's influence on the competitive exercise, "which in all
track and field events, is the most important test" (PDF p. 68, printed p. 51). He then
splits the other tests used to study training transfer into two families (PDF pp. 68-69,
printed pp. 51-52):
- **General tests**: not tests of general-preparatory exercises specifically, but tests
  "used in mixed groups or between groups" — i.e., shared across many events. For
  heart-circulatory/respiratory function, nearly identical tests are used across all of
  track and field (max oxygen uptake on a veloergometer, time-to-exhaustion at max VO2,
  anaerobic threshold). For speed-strength sports, common general tests are the 60m run
  from blocks, barbell snatch, half squat with barbell, standing long jump, vertical jump
  (Abalakov method), triple jump from place, and forward/backward shot throws.
- **Specialized tests**: "In specialized tests for each sport the exercises are very
  similar" and "Each event in this group has its own specific tests" (PDF p. 68, printed
  p. 51) — tests unique to each event's specific demands (lighter/heavier implements in
  throws, shorter approach runs in jumps, varied segment/rest combinations in cyclical
  events).

Of tests generally, he singles out reliability separately from the general/specialized
split: the reliability of tests built from **specialized-developmental exercises** "has
already been shown," while the reliability of tests using general-preparatory and
specialized-preparatory exercises "still have not been fully confirmed. This will be
tightened up in the near future." (PDF pp. 68-69, printed pp. 51-52.)

**Why it works** — The text itself gives no mechanism connecting these two ideas; it simply
asserts that specialized-developmental test reliability "has already been shown" without
citing why. **Inference:** connecting this to
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] — specialized-developmental exercises
sit closest to the competitive event in that transfer chain, so tests built from those same
exercises should track competitive readiness more reliably than tests built
from more general exercises further from the competitive movement.

**When to apply** — When designing or auditing a testing battery, prioritize tests that
are themselves specialized-developmental-class movements (the competitive skill under
altered load/distance conditions) over generic strength/power tests when the goal is
tracking competitive readiness specifically; reserve the generic tests (snatch, squat,
vertical jump, etc.) for tracking general physical qualities, which the author himself
says have less-confirmed reliability as *transfer* indicators even though they are
common practice.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own
methodological framing for the correlational study that follows in Chapter 2, presented
without a formal reliability study of his own two test families in the excerpted pages
(he cites "already been shown" reliability for specialized-developmental tests, but gives
no reference number here). Population is Soviet track and field testing practice of the
1970s-80s; the specific listed general tests (barbell snatch, Abalakov jump, etc.) reflect
that era's tools, not necessarily current force-plate/GPS-based options. Applying the
general/specialized test distinction to Baylor's own battery design (`method-baseline.md`,

the underlying logic (prefer tests closest to the competitive movement for readiness
tracking) is directly portable.

be a competitive-adjacent movement under altered conditions (e.g., a route run against a

"general" test would be a standard vertical jump or broad jump shared across every
position group.

- **Specifists** (traced to E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements," cited as
  ref [223]): transfer between two activities happens only to the degree the activities
  share identical elements (muscle groups, coordination structure, biomechanics). No
  shared elements, no transfer. (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3.)
- **Generalists** (dominant 1940-1960, per the text): argue for the "unity of general and
  specialized preparation" — build a broad general base first (a multi-year "base stage"
  of 4-6 years), then specialize. Bondarchuk reports this view was later revised once
  research showed general-preparation means only build a base for **low-level** athletes;
  for high-level athletes, transfer to the competitive event comes only through
  specialized-preparation means (citing refs [34, 57, 182]). (PDF pp. 22-24, printed pp.
  5-7.)
- **Holistics**: the body acts as one system, so any exercise affects the whole body's
  systems to some degree (non-specific reactions of the heart-circulatory/respiratory
  systems from any cyclical exercise, e.g. rowing or cycling helping a middle-distance
  runner's aerobic base). Bondarchuk explicitly rejects the holistics' full conclusion
  ("it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics") but keeps their
  narrower point about non-specific systemic reactions, and credits the "block method"
  (physical-preparation block before a technical-preparation block) as the holistics'
  practical answer to sequencing. (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp. 9-11.)

# Three Competing Theories of Training Transfer: Specifist, Generalist, Holistic

**What it is** — Bondarchuk frames the entire theory of training transfer as a debate
between three schools (PDF pp. 20-28, printed pp. 3-11):
- **Specifists** (traced to E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements," cited as
  ref [223]): transfer between two activities happens only to the degree the activities
  share identical elements (muscle groups, coordination structure, biomechanics). No
  shared elements, no transfer. (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3.)
- **Generalists** (dominant 1940-1960, per the text): argue for the "unity of general and
  specialized preparation" — build a broad general base first (a multi-year "base stage"
  of 4-6 years), then specialize. Bondarchuk reports this view was later revised once
  research showed general-preparation means only build a base for **low-level** athletes;
  for high-level athletes, transfer to the competitive event comes only through
  specialized-preparation means (citing refs [34, 57, 182]). (PDF pp. 22-24, printed pp.
  5-7.)
- **Holistics**: the body acts as one system, so any exercise affects the whole body's
  systems to some degree (non-specific reactions of the heart-circulatory/respiratory
  systems from any cyclical exercise, e.g. rowing or cycling helping a middle-distance
  runner's aerobic base). Bondarchuk explicitly rejects the holistics' full conclusion
  ("it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics") but keeps their
  narrower point about non-specific systemic reactions, and credits the "block method"
  (physical-preparation block before a technical-preparation block) as the holistics'
  practical answer to sequencing. (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp. 9-11.)

**Why it works** — The author does not resolve these into a single mechanism in this
section; he uses the three-way split to set up why transfer is contested territory before
he presents his own correlational data in Chapter 2. **Inference:** the specifist view is
the closest ancestor of what this library already holds as
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining, Verkhoshansky/Siff)
and of Verkhoshansky's Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power"); the generalist/holistic debate maps onto
the general-preparation-vs-specialization sequencing question this library already tracks
via Bompa's multilateral development model (vault, not yet cross-checked in this batch).

**When to apply** — Use this three-way split as a diagnostic when reading any other
S&C source's claim about "general" vs "specific" training: ask which of the three
positions it is implicitly taking. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches exercise
selection on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation to
competitive exercises (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16`) — that is functionally a generalist-then-
specifist sequencing, not a pure specifist position, and this entry gives Eric's course
material a named theoretical lineage (Thorndike/specifist vs. the generalist sequencing
debate) that the transcript itself does not cite.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
literature synthesis of a decades-old Soviet-era academic debate among track and field
scientists, not an independently replicated finding, and the book gives no citation for
exactly how "generalist" views were falsified beyond two bracketed reference numbers
([34, 57, 182]) this ingest did not chase down. The population behind all three positions
is elite Soviet track and field athletes; extending any of the three views to football
programming (e.g., "GPP only helps low-level players") is Inference, not something this
passage states.

**Example** — A coach who says "just build a big general base before specializing" is
taking the classical generalist position Bondarchuk says was already revised by the
1970s-80s once high-level athlete data showed general work stops producing transfer past
a certain qualification level; see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] for the Chapter 2 data behind that
revision.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — the specifist position's closest modern-book relative in this library.
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the exercise taxonomy this book actually
uses to operationalize the specifist/generalist tension.

# Three Competing Theories of Training Transfer: Specifist, Generalist, Holistic

**What it is** — Bondarchuk frames the entire theory of training transfer as a debate
between three schools (PDF pp. 20-28, printed pp. 3-11):
- **Specifists** (traced to E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical elements," cited as
  ref [223]; the source text misgenders Thorndike as "She"): transfer between two
  activities happens only when there is "some kind of concurrence (identicalness) of
  elements" between them. No shared elements, no transfer. (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3.)
  **Inference:** this entry glosses "elements" as muscle groups, coordination structure,
  and biomechanics; the source itself only says "concurrence (identicalness) of elements"
  without spelling those out in this passage.
- **Generalists** (their views "were formed during the years from 1940-1960," per the
  text — not stated to have been dominant): argue for the "unity of general and
  specialized preparation" — build a broad general base first (a multi-year "base stage"
  of 4-6 years), then specialize. Bondarchuk reports this view was later revised once
  research showed general-preparation means only build a base for **low-level** athletes;
  for high-level athletes, transfer to the competitive event comes only through
  specialized-preparation means (citing three refs, [34, 57, 182]). (PDF pp. 22-24, printed
  pp. 5-7.) As that revision took hold, the ratio of training time given to general vs.
  specialized preparation shifted: "If, at the beginning the correlation between the time
  spent on general and specialized preparation was expressed in a 3:1 ratio, it later
  changed in favor of an increased number of specialized preparation means" (PDF p. 23,
  printed p. 6).
- **Holistics**: the body acts as one system, so any exercise affects the whole body's
  systems to some degree (non-specific reactions of the heart-circulatory/respiratory
  systems from any cyclical exercise, e.g. rowing or cycling helping a middle-distance
  runner's aerobic base). Bondarchuk explicitly rejects the holistics' full conclusion
  ("it is not possible to agree with the conclusions of the holistics") but keeps their
  narrower point about non-specific systemic reactions. He also names a deficiency in
  their theory: because holistics indirectly call for training the cardiovascular/
  respiratory systems first to drive neuromuscular adaptation, "the athlete enters the
  highest training state in non-specific exercises at the start and only after this...
  enters a state of sports form in the specific exercises," and "the level of trainedness
  decreases long before entering the state of sports form in the specialized exercises"

  theoretical and practical error... since they are united in all of their displays" (PDF
  p. 28, printed p. 11); his answer to that error is the principle of conjugated training
  effects (see [[principle--conjugated-training-effects]]). (PDF pp. 26-28, printed pp.
  9-11.)

17	chain of exercise classes rather than any exercise being able to transfer to any other:
18	"first is the influence of general developmental exercises on specialized-preparatory,
19	specialized-developmental, or competitive exercises. Second, is the effect of
20	specialized-preparatory exercises on specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.
21	Third are training questions on the effect of specialized-developmental exercises on the
22	competitive event." (PDF p. 33, printed p. 16.) He also notes transfer holds "within the
23	limits of one exercise" across joint angles or conditions (training leg extensors at one
24	joint angle transfers to other angles; throwing the full implement transfers to throwing
25	from a standing position; jumps with a full run-up transfer to short-run-up speed), and
26	"within the confines of whole motor actions" across related competitive events (an 800m
27	runner's training affects 400m and 1500m results). (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 16-17.)
28

30	to the competitive movement (in the classification given in

32	"identical elements" (see the specifist position in
33	[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]), so influence should flow
34	"downstream" toward more specific exercises more reliably than "upstream." **Inference:**

40	preparatory before specialized-preparatory before specialized-developmental before
41	competitive) rather than treating "sequence general to specific" as an arbitrary

43	competitive exercises are present at all — per this chain, they are the only exercise

45

47	model built from the same single Soviet track and field dataset referenced throughout the
48	book, not an independently tested causal chain. It describes track and field individual
49	events; a football position group's skill (e.g., pass protection) is a much more complex,
50	multi-factor competitive action than a single-event track result, so directly re-applying

asserted an ordered "chain" running only general to competitive, with specialized-
developmental and competitive exercises as "the only exercise classes with a direct claim
on transferring to the competitive result." The source does not support that direction-only,
SDE/CE-only reading. Bondarchuk names three factors under study, and the reverse-direction
question in the same breath:

"First is the influence of general developmental exercises on specialized-preparatory,
specialized-developmental, or competitive exercises. Second, is the effect of
specialized-preparatory exercises on specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.
Third are training questions on the effect of specialized-developmental exercises on the
competitive event." He immediately adds the reverse question: "it is necessary to know
how the general-preparatory, specialized-preparatory and specialized-developmental
exercises have an effect on the competitive exercise and **which form of the latter
exercises has an influence on the general-preparatory, specialized-preparatory and
specialized-developmental exercises**." (PDF p. 33, printed p. 16.) So general-preparatory
exercises acting directly on the competitive exercise, and the reverse (competitive-class
exercises influencing the more general classes), are both factors he names as under study,
not ruled out.

He also describes transfer "within the limits of one exercise": training the leg extensor
muscles at one joint angle has a positive effect on strength in other joint angles [95];
similar effects appear using the bench press and varying body angle; training throwers
with the entire throw simultaneously increases results throwing from a standing position;
and "in training long jumpers, when using jumps with a full or short run up, there is a
positive effect on the development of speed in the 30 or 60 meter run" — the run-up length
and the sprint segment, not one run-up length transferring to another. Separately, a
standard-weight implement throw "can have a positive or negative influence on results when
throwing a lighter or heavier weight (implement)" — i.e. this transfer within an exercise
family can run either direction, positive or negative. (PDF p. 33, printed p. 16.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism here. **Inference:** exercises sharing
more of the competitive event's biomechanics, muscle groups, or coordination structure
(see the specifist position in [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] and
the classification in [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]) would be expected
to influence each other more reliably, in either direction, than exercises sharing less —
this is this entry's own reading, not something the passage states.

**When to apply** — Use this as the reasoning behind checking both directions of an
exercise-selection audit: not just "does general-preparatory work feed the competitive
exercise" but "does the competitive-class exercise (or a specialized-developmental variant
of it) itself carry information back to how general or specialized-preparatory exercises
should be dosed." **Inference:** Chapter 2 gives two boundary conditions worth reading
alongside this factor list, though the author does not connect them to it in these terms
himself: specialized-preparatory exercises transfer to the competitive result only "up to
a specific level of sports mastery" (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158; see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]), and general-preparation means build a
"base, foundation" for the competitive event only in low-level athletes, refs [57, 266]
(PDF p. 64, printed p. 47; see also PDF p. 23, printed p. 6, refs [34, 57, 182]).

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is Bondarchuk's own descriptive
model built from the same single dataset referenced throughout the book, not an
independently tested causal chain. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and
field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic
cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed
p. 59); not football, not team sport. It describes track and field individual events; a
football position group's skill (e.g., pass protection) is a much more complex,
multi-factor competitive action than a single-event track result, so re-applying these
factors to a football skill is Inference, reasonable by analogy but untested here.

**Example** — **Inference:** in sprinting, general conditioning (GPE) may feed hill sprints
or resisted sprints. Resisted sprints repeat the actual sprinting action against added
load, so by the Glossary definition they are specialized-developmental (SDE), not
specialized-preparatory (PDF p. 14, printed p. xiii) — not the SPE example this entry
previously used. Flying-start segments or overspeed towing (also SDE) would then feed the
competitive 100m/40-yard result (CE). This chain of examples is this entry's own
construction, not the author's; the author's own within-exercise examples are the joint-
angle, throw-position, and jump-run-up cases given above.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
factors operate on. [[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] —
Chapter 2's empirical test of which specific exercises actually transfer most for
sprinters.

# Transfer Runs in a Chain: General to Specialized-Preparatory to Specialized-Developmental to Competitive

**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes training transfer as flowing through an ordered
chain of exercise classes rather than any exercise being able to transfer to any other:
"first is the influence of general developmental exercises on specialized-preparatory,
specialized-developmental, or competitive exercises. Second, is the effect of
specialized-preparatory exercises on specialized-developmental and competitive exercises.
Third are training questions on the effect of specialized-developmental exercises on the
competitive event." (PDF p. 33, printed p. 16.) He also notes transfer holds "within the
limits of one exercise" across joint angles or conditions (training leg extensors at one
joint angle transfers to other angles; throwing the full implement transfers to throwing
from a standing position; jumps with a full run-up transfer to short-run-up speed), and
"within the confines of whole motor actions" across related competitive events (an 800m
runner's training affects 400m and 1500m results). (PDF pp. 33-34, printed pp. 16-17.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond the chain's own logic: exercises closer
to the competitive movement (in the classification given in
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]]) share more of the competitive event's
"identical elements" (see the specifist position in
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]), so influence should flow
"downstream" toward more specific exercises more reliably than "upstream." **Inference:**
this is the theoretical basis for a common practical rule — sequence a training block from
general to specific — but the author does not explicitly rule out upstream transfer here,
only describes the direction he studied.

**When to apply** — Use this as the reasoning behind block sequencing (general
preparatory before specialized-preparatory before specialized-developmental before
competitive) rather than treating "sequence general to specific" as an arbitrary
convention. When auditing a program, check whether specialized-developmental and
competitive exercises are present at all — per this chain, they are the only exercise
classes with a direct claim on transferring to the competitive result.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is Bondarchuk's own descriptive
model built from the same single Soviet track and field dataset referenced throughout the
book, not an independently tested causal chain. It describes track and field individual
events; a football position group's skill (e.g., pass protection) is a much more complex,
multi-factor competitive action than a single-event track result, so directly re-applying
"general → specialized-preparatory → specialized-developmental → competitive" sequencing
to a football skill is Inference, reasonable by analogy but untested here.

**Example** — In sprinting, this chain implies: general conditioning (GPE) affects hill
sprints or resisted sprints (SPE) affects flying-start segments or overspeed towing
(SDE) affects the competitive 100m/40-yard result (CE) — each link transferring more
reliably than trying to jump straight from GPE to CE.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification this
chain is built on. [[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — Chapter
2's empirical test of which specific exercises actually sit closest to the competitive
end of this chain for sprinters.

# The Principle of Conjugated Training Effects: Physical Preparation and Technique Must Coincide

**What it is** — Physical-ability development and technical-mastery development should
be trained so they "coincide and correspond to the competitive exercise according to
their basic characteristics" rather than as separate tracks. Bondarchuk attributes the
principle to Soviet head coach/scientist V.M. Dyachkov in the 1960s (ref [81]), and notes
it was later "modified by other specialists who called it dynamic correspondence and the
principle of resolving motor actions," citing U.V. Menkhin (ref [157]) specifically —
**not Verkhoshansky** — for that renaming. (PDF p. 29, printed p. 12.) Using gymnastics as
Menkhin's example, the best conjugation requires five things at once: (1) motor qualities
localized to the right muscle groups, (2) motor qualities matching the biodynamic demands
of the skill, (3) transfer into the most common forms of motor activity used for learning
technique, (4) enough work capacity to repeat the skill reliably across a long
competition, and (5) transfer into the competitive combination itself. (PDF p. 29,
printed p. 12.) Bondarchuk says he used this same conjugate principle to build his own
"principle of all-round specialized preparation" (ref [265]): mostly specialized-
preparatory and specialized-developmental exercises, general preparation only for warm-up
and restoration, with each training cycle needing "new" and progressively stronger
special exercises to keep producing adaptation. (PDF p. 30, printed p. 13.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no explicit physiological mechanism here beyond the
form-and-content unity idea inherited from the holistics critique in the prior section
(see [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]): training physical qualities
and technique as artificially separate tracks is, in his view, a "theoretical and
practical error" because they are "united in all of their displays." **Inference:** this
reads as an early, narrower cousin of the ten-dimension specificity logic in
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining) — both argue that an
exercise's value depends on matching several specific parameters to the target skill, not
just training "strength" or "technique" in isolation.

**When to apply** — Use as a check when a program trains strength/power work and skill
work in completely separate blocks with no attempt to match them: ask whether the
strength work is being selected (per Menkhin's five criteria) to actually support the
target skill's muscle groups, biodynamics, and movement pattern, not just "get stronger in
general." **Eric's baseline:** the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
is credited there to Verkhoshansky, not Dyachkov/Menkhin (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`; `week1-lecture.md p.34`).
**This is a real lineage discrepancy worth flagging, not resolving here**: Bondarchuk's
own text credits the "dynamic correspondence" *name* to Menkhin's modification of
Dyachkov's conjugate principle, while Eric's course credits the *concept* to
Verkhoshansky. These may be the same idea moving through multiple Soviet-era authors who
each get cited differently in different secondary sources, or they may be distinct
formulations that later got merged under one name in Western coaching literature. Check
Supertraining's own Chapter 4.3 (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` in the Supertraining
staging folder) before treating "dynamic correspondence" as a single-author concept in any
future entry.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
reading of Dyachkov's and Menkhin's Soviet-era proposals, cited only by bracketed
reference number, not independently verified in this ingest. The five-component
gymnastics example is Menkhin's, imported by Bondarchuk into track and field without
restating it for that context; applying it to a specific football exercise-selection
decision is Inference. Population throughout is elite Soviet gymnasts (Menkhin's own
example) and track and field athletes (Bondarchuk's extension), not football or other
team-sport athletes.

**Example** — **Inference:** a football strength coach picking a trap-bar deadlift
variation for a linebacker should, per this principle, be asking not just "does this build
leg strength" but whether the pull's force direction, joint angles, and muscle-work regime
actually match the demands of a linebacker's competitive movement — the same "coincide and
correspond" test Bondarchuk describes for track and field exercise selection.

**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining,
staging) — cites Verkhoshansky's Dynamic Correspondence by name; flag the Dyachkov/Menkhin
vs. Verkhoshansky attribution question there too if that entry is revisited.
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]] — the holistics' form-and-content
unity critique this principle is offered to resolve.
