# The Principle of Conjugated Training Effects: Physical Preparation and Technique Must Coincide

**What it is** — Physical-ability development and technical-mastery development should
be trained so they "coincide and correspond to the competitive exercise according to
their basic characteristics" rather than as separate tracks. Bondarchuk attributes the
principle to Soviet head coach/scientist V.M. Dyachkov in the 1960s (ref [81]; PDF p. 28,
printed p. 11), and notes it was later "modified by **other specialists** who called it
dynamic correspondence and the principle of resolving motor actions. [157]." The text does
not name who coined the term "dynamic correspondence"; the bracketed ref [157] attaches to
the sentence as a whole, and the very next sentence separately credits U.V. Menkhin [157]
with a specific extension: "the conjugate principle should affect not only the competitive
event, but all the specialized activity as a whole." (PDF p. 29, printed p. 12.) Using gymnastics as
Menkhin's example, the best conjugation requires five things at once: (1) motor qualities
localized to the right muscle groups, (2) motor qualities matching the biodynamic demands
of the skill, (3) transfer into the most common forms of motor activity used for learning
technique, (4) enough work capacity to repeat the skill reliably across a long
competition, and (5) transfer into the competitive combination itself. (PDF p. 29,
printed p. 12.) Bondarchuk says he used this same conjugate principle to build his own
"principle of all-round specialized preparation" (ref [265]): mostly specialized-
preparatory and specialized-developmental exercises, general preparation only for warm-up
and restoration, with each training cycle needing "new" and progressively stronger
special exercises to keep producing adaptation. (PDF p. 30, printed p. 13.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no explicit physiological mechanism here beyond the
form-and-content unity idea inherited from the holistics critique in the prior section
(see [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]): training physical qualities
and technique as artificially separate tracks is, in his view, a "theoretical and
practical error" because they are "united in all of their displays." **Inference:** this
reads as an early, narrower cousin of the ten-dimension specificity logic in
[[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (Supertraining) — both argue that an
exercise's value depends on matching several specific parameters to the target skill, not
just training "strength" or "technique" in isolation.

**When to apply** — Use as a check when a program trains strength/power work and skill
work in completely separate blocks with no attempt to match them: ask whether the
strength work is being selected (per Menkhin's five criteria) to actually support the
target skill's muscle groups, biodynamics, and movement pattern, not just "get stronger in
general." **Eric's baseline:** the Principle of Dynamic Correspondence taught in HHPR 5355
is credited there to Verkhoshansky, not Dyachkov/Menkhin (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`; `week1-lecture.md p.34`).
**This is a real lineage discrepancy worth flagging, not resolving here**: Bondarchuk's
own text credits the "dynamic correspondence" *name* to Menkhin's modification of
Dyachkov's conjugate principle, while Eric's course credits the *concept* to
Verkhoshansky. These may be the same idea moving through multiple Soviet-era authors who
each get cited differently in different secondary sources, or they may be distinct
formulations that later got merged under one name in Western coaching literature. Check
Supertraining's own Chapter 4.3 (not yet ingested; see `_book.md` in the Supertraining
staging folder) before treating "dynamic correspondence" as a single-author concept in any
future entry.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported, not proven.** This is Bondarchuk's own
reading of Dyachkov's and Menkhin's Soviet-era proposals, cited only by bracketed
reference number, not independently verified in this ingest. The five-component
gymnastics example is Menkhin's, imported by Bondarchuk into track and field without
restating it for that context; applying it to a specific football exercise-selection
decision is Inference. Population throughout is elite Soviet gymnasts (Menkhin's own
example) and track and field athletes (Bondarchuk's extension), not football or other
team-sport athletes.

**Example** — **Inference:** a football strength coach picking a trap-bar deadlift
variation for a linebacker should, per this principle, be asking not just "does this build
leg strength" but whether the pull's force direction, joint angles, and muscle-work regime
actually match the demands of a linebacker's competitive movement — the same "coincide and
correspond" test Bondarchuk describes for track and field exercise selection.

**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives a
single illustrative case (his own words: "we will illustrate with one example"): a training
session using three exercises, A, B, and C in sequence. After an experiment, results
improved in A and C but not in B. A high correlation between A and B suggested (wrongly)
that B was ineffective or non-transferring. A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained
only A and C — and this time **neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation:
exercise B had a "tie-in effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even
though B itself showed no measurable within-exercise result and its own pairwise
correlation to A/C looked unremarkable. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is proposed beyond the observation itself; Bondarchuk
explicitly defers this to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." The
described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
between two *other* exercises.

**When to apply** — Use as a standing caution whenever a program change removes an
exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory
of other exercises in the same session/block before concluding it added nothing. This is
a genuinely underused idea in practical programming, where "cut what isn't working" is a
common simplification heuristic that this example directly complicates.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This entire finding rests on a single
worked example ("we will address only one of the situations") with no stated sample size,
no statistical test, and no independent replication in the excerpted text — it is
presented by the author himself as an open question for future research, not a settled
result. Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise combination has a tie-in
effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what pairwise correlation studies
(including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect. Population and exercises A/B/C
are unspecified in the text (not named events or lifts), so there is nothing concrete to
generalize from besides the logical structure of the example.

**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives one
illustrative case, which he frames as typical rather than isolated ("we will address only
one of the situations which frequently arise in the process of doing experimental studies
on this problem," PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54): a training session using three
exercises, A, B, and C in sequence. After an experiment, results improved in A and C but
not in B. "The coefficient of correlation was sufficiently high between exercises A and B,
which made it possible to think that both exercises had a positive action on one another.
Naturally, the statistical analysis did not bring out the kind of influence exercise B had
on exercise A or C. Based on this, a conclusion was made that exercise B was not
effective." A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained only A and C — and this time
**neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation: exercise B had a "tie-in
effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even though B itself showed no
measurable within-exercise result. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)

**Why it works** — The author's own explanation for why a single pairwise correlation can
mislead: "the direction and amount of training transfer is dependent first of all on the
integration of activity in the brain, which characterizes the most complex interactions
between the excitatory-inhibitory processes" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53) — this is also his
stated reason for insisting on a minimum of 5-6 indices per athlete group rather than
single pairwise comparisons. Beyond that stated reason, he defers the tie-in mechanism
itself to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." **Inference:** the
described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
between two *other* exercises — this structural-blindness framing is this entry's own
reading, not the author's stated point.

**When to apply** — Use as a standing caution whenever a program change removes an
exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory
of other exercises in the same session/block before concluding it added nothing.
**Inference:** this is a genuinely underused idea in practical programming, where "cut
what isn't working" is a common simplification heuristic that this example directly
complicates — that practical framing is this entry's own, not the author's.

**Method (applies to every Chapter 2 correlation entry in this book folder):**
questionnaires from native (USSR) and foreign athletes of mixed qualification, carried out
over four Olympic cycles, plus published individual results (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp.
vii-viii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); "a positive interrelationship between exercises begins
at 0.349" (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59; 0.423 for women's pole vault, PDF p. 111, printed
p. 94); and the data is restricted to training systems **without** steroid use, because
steroid use raises results across all exercises used and not used, masking which exercise
actually drove the transfer (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. vii-viii).

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This finding rests on one worked
example, with no stated sample size, no statistical test, and no independent replication
in the excerpted text — it is presented by the author himself as an open question for
future research ("we believe that in the future, additional studies will resolve this
interaction"), not a settled result, even though he frames the underlying situation as one
that "frequently arise[s]." Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise
combination has a tie-in effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what
pairwise correlation studies (including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect.
Exercises A/B/C are unspecified in the text (not named events or lifts), so there is
nothing concrete to generalize from besides the logical structure of the example and the
Method note above.

**What it is** — Bondarchuk describes his standard method for the whole book: statistical
analysis (correlation, regression, dispersion, factor analysis, multiple correlation) of
interrelationships between results in different training exercises, using a minimum of
5-6 indices per athlete group because a single pairwise correlation "does not always
reflect the true essence of the interaction." (PDF p. 70, printed p. 53.) He then gives a
single illustrative case (his own words: "we will illustrate with one example"): a training

that B was ineffective or non-transferring. A follow-up experiment dropped B and trained
only A and C — and this time **neither A nor C improved**. Bondarchuk's interpretation:
exercise B had a "tie-in effect," stimulating the positive transfer between A and C even
though B itself showed no measurable within-exercise result and its own pairwise
correlation to A/C looked unremarkable. (PDF pp. 70-71, printed pp. 53-54.)

explicitly defers this to "additional studies" that "will resolve this interaction." The
described method (pairwise correlation across a sequence of exercises) is structurally
blind to exactly this kind of three-way interaction, since it only measures direct
pairwise relationships, not an exercise's indirect enabling effect on the relationship
between two *other* exercises.

exercise because it looks "ineffective" by direct correlation or by the athlete's own
result in that exercise not improving: check whether removing it changes the trajectory

result. Do not cite this as evidence that any specific exercise combination has a tie-in
effect; treat it only as a methodological caution about what pairwise correlation studies
(including Bondarchuk's own Chapter 2 tables) cannot detect. Population and exercises A/B/C

**Example** — **Inference:** a strength coach who drops an unweighted plyometric drill

improving might, per this heuristic, want to check whether removing it also flattens the
sprint-speed gains the program was otherwise seeing — the drill could be a tie-in exercise
even though its own metric looks stagnant.

# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle

**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
though some individuals take 4-8 months. A general-preparation stage/block can only
function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the following specialized stage if it lasts
at least as long as that individual's own sports-form development timeline. He gives a
worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
23-25.)

**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
developmental phase in itself.

**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month (up to 4-8 month)
sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
specific citation in the excerpted pages, and is drawn from elite Soviet track and field
athletes on year-round training cycles. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
is more portable than the specific duration numbers.

**Example** — A 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very unlikely to
produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the Bondarchuk sense; it
functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training stress, and should
be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building a real strength or
conditioning "base."

**Related** — [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]] — the transfer-timing
model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
duration question applies to.

# A General-Preparation Stage Only "Counts" If It Lasts as Long as the Athlete's Own Sports-Form Cycle

**What it is** — Bondarchuk states that most athletes, after a rest/transition period,
take 2-3 months to enter a state of "sports form" in whatever exercises they are doing,
though some individuals take "4-7 and even 8 months" (PDF p. 39, printed p. 22). A
general-preparation stage/block can only function as a real "base" or "foundation" for the
following specialized stage if it lasts at least as long as that individual's own
sports-form development timeline. He gives his own worked numbers for how this plays out:
in a single-cycle training year, the general-preparation stage runs "on the average, three
months," long enough to let most athletes actually enter sports form in it; in a two-cycle
year, the second general-preparation stage shrinks to "4-6 weeks," and in a three-cycle
year to "2-3 weeks" — both too short for athletes to "have time to enter into full sports
form in the exercises used." (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) He gives a
worked counter-example: a sprint/hurdle program with a 10-day general-endurance stage, a
15-day general-strength stage, a 6-8 week speed/speed-endurance stage, and a 2-3 week
entry-into-form stage. Because the first two stages are far shorter than the 2-3+ months
needed to reach sports form, he argues it is "impossible to resolve" real development of
general endurance or general strength in that time — those stages become mere "followers"
(tag-alongs) that prep the body for the next stage, not genuine developmental blocks in
their own right, and sports form only actually begins developing once the speed/speed-
endurance stage starts. (PDF pp. 39-40, printed pp. 22-23.) Only stage, block,
stage-variant, and block-variant methods (which run long enough) can create a real
transferable base; very short 1-3 week rotating stages cannot produce "distant" transfer
of a created base — only "current" transfer is possible under those short-cycle designs
(see [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]]). (PDF pp. 40-42, printed pp.
23-25.)

**Why it works** — The claim rests on Bondarchuk's premise (stated, not derived here) that
entering "sports form" for a given exercise complex takes a fairly fixed, athlete-specific
duration (2-3 months typical, up to 8 months for some individuals); a stage shorter than
that duration cannot complete the adaptation cycle it is nominally targeting, so whatever
training happens in it is incidental preparation for the next stage rather than a genuine
developmental phase in itself.

**When to apply** — Use as a sanity check on any periodization plan with short (1-3 week)
"phases" labeled by quality (a "strength phase," a "conditioning phase"): ask whether that
phase is actually long enough, for this athlete population, to produce a real adaptation
in that quality, or whether it is functioning only as a short lead-in to the phase after
it. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 teaches training residual effects that set a
retraining cadence — aerobic capacity and max strength need re-exposure roughly every 30
days, speed roughly every 5 days (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27`) — that is a maintenance-cadence claim,
distinct from but complementary to Bondarchuk's claim here about how long an *initial*
developmental stage must run to create a base in the first place.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** The 2-3 month (up to 4-8 month)
sports-form timeline is stated by the author as known "from the literature," without a
specific citation in the excerpted pages, and is drawn from elite Soviet track and field
athletes on year-round training cycles. A college football off-season/summer/fall-camp
calendar is structured very differently (fixed NCAA calendar windows, not free-running
sports-form cycles), so directly importing "your GPP phase must be 2-3 months to count" as
a hard rule for football is Inference — the underlying logic (a phase shorter than the
adaptation timeline for the targeted quality risks being incidental, not developmental)
is more portable than the specific duration numbers.

**Example** — A 2-week "GPP block" before fall camp, by this logic, is very unlikely to
produce genuine general strength or conditioning adaptations in the Bondarchuk sense; it
functions instead as preparation for the next block's actual training stress, and should
be programmed and evaluated as such rather than credited with building a real strength or
conditioning "base."

**Related** — [[framework--current-vs-distant-training-transfer]] — the transfer-timing
model this duration rule directly feeds. [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]]
(Supertraining, staging) — the general-preparation/work-capacity concept this stage
duration question applies to.

# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration

**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
well as for carrying out restorative measures." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He goes
further, speculating that specialized-preparatory exercises may function as
"'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the transfer to
the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves — a direct
echo of the "tie-in effect" idea from Chapter 1 (see
[[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]). (PDF p. 175, printed
p. 158.)

**Why it works** — No new mechanism beyond the tie-in-effect hypothesis already flagged as
untested in Chapter 1; this is the author's own explicit hedge against a naive
misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data shows no further correlation,
therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns against).

**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance (residual strength
retention, consistent with the roughly-30-day residual training effect windows this
library already tracks — see `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power") and for its
restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
separately tested finding in its own right — he flags his "stimulational factor" idea as
speculative ("it is very possible that... other methods... will be proposed"). Population
context is the same elite Soviet track and field throwers/sprinters/jumpers as the ceiling-
effect claims it responds to. Applying "keep it for maintenance, not for further gains" to
a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
different reasoning.

**Example** — A discus thrower whose squat numbers have plateaued relative to further
distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
than dropping squats from the program entirely.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]] and
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the data findings this heuristic is
a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —
the Chapter 1 idea (tie-in effect) this heuristic's "stimulational factor" speculation
echoes.

# Don't Cut a Strength Exercise Just Because It Stopped Predicting Further Competitive Improvement — Keep It at Lower Volume for Maintenance and Restoration

**What it is** — Having shown across sprints, jumps, and throws that specialized-
preparatory exercises (snatch, clean, squat, bench: see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]) stop predicting further competitive
improvement past a certain level of mastery, Bondarchuk draws an explicit practical
conclusion rather than leaving it as a pure data finding: "it does not mean that
specialized-preparatory exercises should be excluded from the training. In our view, it is
necessary to use them but to a somewhat lesser volume to maintain the achieved level, as
well as for carrying out restorative measures." He adds two further, separately unhedged
and untested claims (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158): first, that future methods may "widen
the range of transfer with the specialized-preparatory exercises to the competitive and
specialized-developmental exercises"; second, that specialized-preparatory exercises "can
appear as 'stimulational factors' which on the brain level, create conditions for the
transfer to the main movement" even without producing measurable further gains themselves.
Neither claim is tested in the excerpted text.

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond the "stimulational factors... on the brain
level" phrase itself, which the author does not unpack further. This is the author's own
explicit hedge against a naive misreading of his own ceiling-effect data (i.e., "the data
shows no further correlation, therefore cut the exercise" — which he directly warns
against). **Inference:** the "stimulational factor" idea reads as an echo of the "tie-in
effect" from Chapter 1 (see [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]),
where an exercise with no measurable direct effect nonetheless enabled other exercises'
gains — but the author does not himself connect these two passages.

**When to apply** — Whenever a program uses Bondarchuk's own ceiling-effect findings (or
any similar correlation-based finding) to justify dropping a strength exercise once an
athlete's numbers plateau relative to competitive results, apply this counter-heuristic:
keep the exercise in the program at reduced volume for maintenance (residual strength
retention, consistent with the roughly-30-day residual training effect windows this
library already tracks — see `method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power") and for its
restorative/active-recovery role, rather than removing it outright.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** This is the author's own explicit
practical recommendation, offered as reasoned judgment built on his data rather than as a
separately tested finding in its own right — he flags his "stimulational factor" idea as
speculative ("it is very possible that... other methods... will be proposed"). Population
context is the same elite Soviet track and field throwers/sprinters/jumpers as the ceiling-
effect claims it responds to. Applying "keep it for maintenance, not for further gains" to
a football strength program's in-season lifting philosophy is Inference, though it is
directly consistent with Baylor's own stated in-season rule of "maintain intensity, reduce
volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21`) and its roughly-30-day strength residual
training effect window (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25`) — two independent sources converging on
the same practical conclusion (reduce, don't eliminate) even though they arrive at it from
different reasoning.

distance gains should keep squatting at a lower volume/frequency for strength maintenance
and recovery purposes, while shifting the primary developmental emphasis to implement-
weight variation (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), rather
than dropping squats from the program entirely.

a direct response to. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] —

echoes.

# Energy-System Loads Share Many Cardiorespiratory Indices but Not Time-to-Form: Anaerobic-Lactate Work Shortens Entry to Form in Other Loads — the Book States the Alactate/Aerobic Direction Both Ways

**What it is — corrected from a NO-GO review finding.** The prior version of this entry
claimed "a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate capacity" and titled itself around broad, one-directional aerobic-to-
alactate transfer. The source states close to the opposite for the specific question of
whether aerobic loads help alactate **sports form**, and it also contradicts itself
internally on a related point. Both corrections below.

**1. Aerobic training does not build alactate sports form, and hurts speed.** Right after
counting how many cardiovascular/respiratory **indices** transfer between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate loads (see the counts below), Bondarchuk states plainly: "The first form
of loads (aerobic) does not show an influence on the development of sports form in the
second form of loads. In other words, in the state of sports form development the aerobic
and anaerobic-alactate abilities of the athlete that come into play are not-dependent on
one another (our data)... aerobic work shows negatively on the development of speed
capabilities." (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146, opened as an image to confirm the text layer.)
So the index-transfer counts below describe shared cardiorespiratory adaptation, not
transfer of competitive sports form, which the author explicitly denies for this pair.

**2. Internal contradiction on which load shortens time-to-form between aerobic and
anaerobic-alactate — kept visible per the brief, not harmonized, `confidence: contested`.**
Three passages give different answers:
- PDF p. 164, printed p. 147 (discussing Table 106, anaerobic-alactate → anaerobic-lactate):
  "The anaerobic-alactate training loads do not influence the time of entering the state of
  sports form in anaerobic-lactate. At the same time the latter (anaerobic-lactate) shorten
  the amount of time for entering into the given state in the first form of loads
  (anaerobic-alactate)." This passage is about alactate/lactate, not aerobic/alactate.
- PDF p. 165, printed p. 148 (closing the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate discussion, table 109):
  "Anaerobic-alactate training loads shorten the amount of time of entering into a state of
  sports form in the aerobic exercises. At this time the latter appear to be inert in
  comparison to the first."
- PDF p. 173, printed p. 156: "It was found that anaerobic-lactate loads shorten the time
  for entering into the sports form state in aerobic and anaerobic-alactate. At this time,
  the latter do not influence (do not shorten) the amount of time taken to enter the given
  state in the anaerobic-lactate training loads."
PDF p. 165 says **anaerobic-alactate** shortens aerobic's time-to-form; PDF p. 173 says it
is **anaerobic-lactate** that shortens both aerobic's and anaerobic-alactate's time-to-form.
These cannot both be the full picture. Do not resolve this silently; treat both statements
as the book's own record and cite both locators whenever citing either.

**Index-transfer counts (cardiorespiratory and related indices, not sports-form transfer):**
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: "6 of 7" cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices
  are "fully transferable" (Table 104, PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable:
  blood-lactate level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with
  different fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers
  in anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: "of the 16 tests looked at, only four were
  non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: "non-transferable factors here are all the remaining
  factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147), attributed to the
  oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus the oxygen-dependent
  structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: Table 107's data show the anaerobic-lactate
  loads "bring about much greater functional shifts in the corresponding body systems than
  the anaerobic-alactate, even though the same (white) muscle fibers participate," and "the
  first form of work [anaerobic-lactate] shortens the time period for entering into the
  state of sports form in the second form of loads [anaerobic-alactate]" — the author adds
  "It is not known why." (Table 107, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147.) This is a one-way
  shortening effect (lactate → alactate), not a "also limited" finding.
- Table 106's own printed title reads "Aerobic-Alactate... to the Aerobic-Lactate" (PDF
  p. 168, printed p. 151) — a source typo to note, not a transcription error in this entry.

Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of well-combined aerobic/anaerobic training:
"S. Auita" (**Inference:** almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held world records
simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within tenths of a
second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional career bests:
200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11. (PDF p. 172,
printed p. 155.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation for the index-transfer pattern is
fiber-type recruitment: aerobic training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers,
while anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch)
fibers. He states plainly for the alactate→alactate asymmetry that "it is not known why"
one direction shortens time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed
p. 147) — the author himself flags this as an open question. No mechanism is given for the
aerobic/anaerobic-alactate sports-form independence in point 1 above, or for the internal
contradiction in point 2. Do not read a fuller physiological explanation into this than the
fiber-type note the text actually gives.

**When to apply** — Use this entry as a caution against assuming energy-system training
transfers to competitive sports form the way shared physiological indices might suggest.

second form of loads. In other words, in the state of sports form development the aerobic

one another (our data)... aerobic work shows negatively on the development of speed
capabilities." (PDF p. 163, printed p. 146, opened as an image to confirm the text layer.)

transfer of competitive sports form, which the author explicitly denies for this pair.

  comparison to the first."

# Aerobic-to-Anaerobic-Alactate Transfer Is Broad and One-Directional; Anaerobic-Alactate-to-Aerobic Transfer Is Almost Absent

**What it is** — Tables 104-109 (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 149-154) report, for pairs
of energy-system training loads (aerobic, anaerobic-alactate, anaerobic-lactate), how many
of a set of physiological indices (heart rate, respiratory rate, lung ventilation, oxygen
reserve/debt, VO2max, blood lactate, energy expenditure/source, muscle fiber type, and
effect on time-to-sports-form) are "fully transferred," "frequently transferred," or
"non-transferred" from one training-load type to the other. The pattern is asymmetric, not
mutual, between each pair:
- **Aerobic → anaerobic-alactate**: mostly transferable — Bondarchuk states "6 of 7" of
  the cardiovascular/respiratory functional indices are "fully transferable" (Table 104,
  PDF p. 162, printed p. 145). Non-transferable factors are specifically blood-lactate
  level and most energy-formation/energy-source factors, consistent with different
  fiber-type recruitment (red/slow fibers in aerobic work vs. white/fast fibers in
  anaerobic-alactate work, per the table's own row).
- **Aerobic ↔ anaerobic-lactate**: broadly transferable both ways — "of the 16 tests
  looked at, only four were non-transferable" (Table 105, PDF p. 163, printed p. 146); the
  anaerobic-lactate load actually *shortens* the time to enter sports form in aerobic
  training, while aerobic training does not shorten anaerobic-lactate's timeline (PDF pp.
  163-165, 171, printed pp. 146-148, 154).
- **Anaerobic-alactate → aerobic**: almost no transfer — "non-transferable factors here
  are all the remaining factors — 13 out of 15" (Table 108, PDF p. 164, printed p. 147),
  attributed to the oxygen-deficient conditions anaerobic-alactate work requires versus
  the oxygen-dependent structure of aerobic work.
- **Anaerobic-lactate → anaerobic-alactate**: also limited, though the reverse direction
  (anaerobic-lactate loads shorten anaerobic-alactate's time to sports form, but not vice
  versa) shows a similar one-way asymmetry to the aerobic/anaerobic-lactate pair (Tables
  106-107, PDF pp. 164, 169, printed pp. 147, 152).
Bondarchuk names a single-athlete example of the practical upshot of well-combined
aerobic/anaerobic training: "S. Auita" (almost certainly Saïd Aouita, transliterated) held
world records simultaneously across the 1500m, 5000m, and 2-mile distances, was within
tenths of a second of record pace at 2000m/3000m/1 mile, and is listed with additional
career bests: 200m-22.8, 400m-46.9, 1000m-2:15.16, steeplechase-8:21.92, 10,000m-27:26.11.
(PDF p. 172, printed p. 155.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own stated explanation is fiber-type recruitment: aerobic
training loads primarily adapt red (slow-twitch) fibers, while anaerobic-alactate and
anaerobic-lactate loads primarily adapt white (fast-twitch) fibers, and he states plainly
for at least one asymmetry that "it is not known why" one direction shortens
time-to-sports-form and the other does not (PDF p. 164, printed p. 147) — the author
himself flags this as an open question, not a resolved mechanism. Do not read a fuller
physiological explanation into this than the fiber-type note the text actually gives.

**When to apply** — Use this asymmetry as a caution against assuming energy-system
training transfers symmetrically: a block of aerobic work may build a genuine base for
anaerobic-alactate and anaerobic-lactate capacity (per the "fully transferred" majority in
Tables 104-105), but a block of anaerobic-alactate (pure sprint/power) work should **not**
be expected to build aerobic capacity — per this data it does not, on all but 2 of 15
tracked physiological indices. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches that all
three energy systems are always active simultaneously and that programming should target
the intended adaptation rather than the drill label (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning
and energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.19`; `class-4-2026.md p.15`) — this
entry's asymmetry finding sharpens that general principle into a specific, one-directional
claim about which energy-system work can substitute for which.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported** for the aggregate Tables 104-109
findings (described as "collective data" in each table's own title, i.e. pooled across
Bondarchuk's tested athletes, sample size not stated in the excerpted pages).
**Confidence is untested for the S. Auita/Aouita example**, a single named-athlete case
offered as illustration, not independent evidence. The tested population is elite Soviet
and international middle/long-distance track athletes; the specific physiological index
values (e.g. lactic acid concentrations, VO2 figures) are dataset-specific and should not
be treated as current normative standards. Applying this energy-system transfer asymmetry
directly to football conditioning (a repeated-sprint, intermittent-effort sport rather than
a continuous single-energy-system event) is Inference — no football or team-sport
population appears anywhere in this book.

**Example** — A program that substitutes heavy sprint/power ("anaerobic-alactate")
conditioning for aerobic base work, expecting it to also build aerobic capacity, is not
supported by this data: per Table 108, 13 of 15 tracked indices showed no transfer in that
direction. The reverse substitution (using aerobic work to partially support
anaerobic-alactate capacity) has much more support in this data (Table 104).

**Related** — No existing library entry addresses this specific aerobic/anaerobic transfer
asymmetry; cross-reference with `method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems,"
for Eric's own energy-system programming framework, and with
[[claim--endurance-event-transfer-range-widens-with-distance]] for the companion finding
on how far training segment distances (rather than energy-system type) transfer within a
single distance-running event.

**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase in
the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments" — 800m and
1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
steeplechase starts from 600m and women's 3000m from 400m; 5000m runners' range starts
around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women) — i.e., the
*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
longer (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144). Separately, and stated as a distinct
finding, he adds the book's main correlation-strength regularity for this section: "with a
decrease in the difference between the competitive distances and the test exercises used,
the coefficient of correlation increases" (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144) — the
closer a training segment sits to the race distance, the higher its correlation with the
competitive result tends to run. Elsewhere the same data is described as "with an increase
in the competitive distance, the range of transfer of physical abilities increases" (PDF
p. 145, printed p. 128, discussing 800m vs. 1500m runners) and, in the chapter's own
closing summary, "the range of transfer in the short distances in most endurance events is
significantly wider than in the long distances" (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144) — both
statements are the author's own, given with their own locators; this entry keeps them side
by side rather than picking one.

Representative correlation values: men's 800m showed its strongest correlations with the
400m, 600m, and 1000m segments (0.700-0.912, biggest at 1000m: 0.912, 0.876, 0.905, 0.856;
PDF p. 144, printed p. 127, Table 89), with a sharp drop by the 1500m and further by
3000-5000m; women's 3000m showed positive transfer "on all levels of the segments tested"
except that "transfer to the competitive event from the 100 and 200m runs were
non-existent," strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m (0.725-0.906, Table 99, PDF p. 146, printed
p. 129). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners (and 10km-walk
women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer* than the
competitive distance. The author gives this as two separate sentences, not one
"because"-clause: "In these cases, it is not possible to observe the presence of the
cumulative effect with distances that are longer than the competitive event. In sports
practice similar tests do not exist." (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)

# The Longer the Competitive Distance, the Wider the Range of Segment Distances That Transfer to It — Except at the Ultra-Endurance Extreme

**What it is** — Tables 89-103 (PDF pp. 149-160, printed pp. 132-143) correlate training
segment distances (60m to marathon/50km) against competitive results in the 800m through
marathon and 10/20/50km race walks. Bondarchuk's own summary pattern: "with an increase
in the distance, transfer of physical abilities begins with the longer segments" — 800m
and 1500m runners show a cumulative effect starting as short as the 60m segment; men's
steeplechase and women's 3000m start from 600m and 400m respectively; 5000m runners' range
starts around 600m; marathoners' range starts at 5000m (men) or 3000m (women) — i.e., the
*shortest* segment that still transfers gets longer as the competitive event itself gets
longer. (PDF pp. 160-161, printed pp. 143-144.) Representative correlation values: men's
800m showed its strongest correlations with the 400m, 600m, and 1000m segments (0.700-0.912,
Table 89), with a sharp drop by the 1500m and further by 3000-5000m; women's 3000m showed
positive transfer across every tested segment, strongest with 1000m/1500m/5000m
(0.725-0.906, Table 99). At the ultra-endurance extreme, the pattern breaks: marathoners
(and 10km-walk women / 50km-walk men) show **no** cumulative effect from segments *longer*
than the competitive distance, "because in sports practice similar tests do not exist" —
there is nothing longer to test against. (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) Race-walkers'
running-distance correlations (5000m/10000m run vs. walk results) were uniformly weak
(0.354-0.400), far below their same-discipline walk-distance correlations (up to 0.800+).
(PDF pp. 148-149, printed pp. 131-132.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk attributes the general pattern to "the specifics of the
interaction of systems involved in the training effect" — different aerobic/anaerobic-
alactate/anaerobic-lactate energy-system demands at different distances (general systemic
reactions) plus the individual athlete's short- and long-term adaptational responses
(specific reactions). (PDF p. 161, printed p. 144.) He does not fully resolve *why* the
transfer range widens with distance beyond this general systems-interaction language.
**Inference:** one possible reading is that longer events draw on a broader mix of energy
systems and pacing demands, so a wider band of training distances can stress a
physiologically relevant system for that event; this interpretation is this entry's own
reading, not stated by the author, and no outside exercise-physiology source was checked
in this ingest to confirm it.

**When to apply** — Use as historical support for distance-specific training range
selection: shorter competitive events (800m-1500m) can be trained effectively with a
narrower, shorter set of segment distances; longer events (5000m-marathon) benefit from
(and require) a wider spread of training distances, from well below race distance up to
race distance itself, to cover the full transfer range this data shows. **Eric's
baseline:** HHPR 5355 already treats aerobic-system training for speed-power athletes as
mainly serving inter-effort recovery rather than distance capacity, kept below anaerobic
threshold at roughly a 1:1-1:2 work:rest ratio (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and
energy systems," citing `week3-lecture.md p.51`) — this book's population is exclusively
dedicated distance-event specialists, a very different training context from a
speed-power athlete's incidental aerobic work, so this entry's distance-range findings
should not be imported into football conditioning design without that distinction in mind.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
middle/long/ultra-distance runners and race walkers, both sexes; the specific segment
distances and correlation values are dataset-specific. This entry covers **running/walking
segment distances only** — it says nothing about strength, jump, or throw-exercise
transfer to endurance events (not tested in this chapter). Applying "wider transfer range
for longer events" to a team-sport repeated-sprint or intermittent-endurance context
(football's actual endurance demand, per `method-baseline.md`'s energy-systems framing) is
Inference: football conditioning is not a single continuous-distance competitive event in
the way every sport in this dataset is.

**Example** — A 10,000m runner's program using training distances from 600m intervals up
to marathon-length long runs is well-supported by this data's transfer-range findings; a
marathoner's program should not expect any additional transfer benefit from segments
longer than the marathon itself, since no such segment exists to test or train.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — general classification
these segment distances fall under (specialized-developmental to competitive, depending on
how close the segment is to full race distance).

# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). **High
jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
0.400 level" for running exercises specifically. Instead, per his prose (PDF p. 105,
printed p. 88), "the most informative and transferable exercise appears to be the vertical
jump with a short run-up," at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women) — **note an
unresolved source discrepancy**: those exact figures match the "10-fold jump from place"
row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965), not the row literally labeled
"Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women 0.680-0.808, which
the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may be a
translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's row
label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian or
a second translation. Barbell snatch showed almost no
transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested, but this
connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation. High
jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
long jumpers, high jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole vaulters, both sexes. The "high jump
breaks the pattern" finding is specific to Bondarchuk's Soviet-era high jump technique
population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
data exists in this source.

**Example** — A long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique jumps (at
reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
transfers the same way.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

# Jump-from-a-Short-Run-Up Is the Single Most Transferable Assistance Exercise for Every Jump Event; High Jump Is the Outlier

**What it is** — Tables 61-68 (PDF pp. 104-112, printed pp. 87-95) correlate running,
jumping, and strength/throw exercises against long jump, high jump, triple jump, and pole
vault results, men and women. Across long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, **all**
running and jumping exercises showed a cumulative positive effect; the two throwing
exercises (shot forward/backward) showed essentially none. The single strongest, most
consistent exercise across event types was the **jump/vault with a short run-up**: long
jumpers' correlation to a short-approach jump ran 0.721-0.890 for men, 0.830-0.967 for
women (Tables 61-62); triple jumpers' short-run-up triple jump ran 0.890-0.954 for men,
0.700-0.906 for women (Tables 65-66); pole vaulters' short-run-up vault ran 0.706-0.845
for men, 0.788-0.865 for women (Tables 67-68). **High
jump was the outlier**: the author states plainly that in men's and women's high jump,
"in all cases, a weak interrelationship between the test results was observed on the
0.400 level" for running exercises specifically. Instead, per his prose (PDF p. 105,
printed p. 88), "the most informative and transferable exercise appears to be the vertical
jump with a short run-up," at 0.876-0.945 (men) / 0.865-0.965 (women) — **note an
unresolved source discrepancy**: those exact figures match the "10-fold jump from place"
row in Tables 63-64 (men 0.876-0.945, women 0.886-0.965), not the row literally labeled
"Jump from a short run-up" in the same tables (men 0.706-0.805, women 0.680-0.808, which
the prose separately describes as merely "sufficiently high"). This may be a
translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's row
label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian or
a second translation. Barbell snatch showed almost no
transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects; the half squat
with barbell transferred more consistently, especially for high jump and pole vault (all
levels for both sexes in those two events). (PDF pp. 104-113, printed pp. 87-96.)

**Why it works** — The tables report these correlations without explaining them.
**Inference:** reading this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] and
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]], the short-run-up version of each
event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it
closest to the competitive event in the transfer chain — consistent with it outperforming
general-preparatory sprint and strength exercises across every jump event tested, but this
connection is this entry's own reading, not the author's stated explanation. High
jump's break from the sprint-correlated pattern of the other three jump events is not
explained mechanistically by the author; **Inference:** the high jump's approach and
takeoff (curved run, back-to-the-bar rotation) differs enough biomechanically from a
straight-line sprint that raw straight-ahead sprint speed may simply share fewer
"identical elements" with it than with long jump, triple jump, or pole vault approaches.

**When to apply** — When selecting assistance work for a jump-event athlete, this data
supports prioritizing a short-approach version of the competitive jump itself as the
highest-value transfer exercise, over generic sprint times or barbell strength numbers,
with the explicit exception of high jump, where multi-jump (10-fold) and short-approach
vertical jump work outperformed straight sprint speed as a predictor.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
long jumpers, high jumpers, triple jumpers, and pole vaulters, both sexes. The "high jump
breaks the pattern" finding is specific to Bondarchuk's Soviet-era high jump technique
population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
data exists in this source.

**Example** — A long jump program prioritizing short-approach full-technique jumps (at
reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
transfers the same way.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining why the short-run-up version outperforms more general exercises.
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] — the parallel finding for
sprinters using jump exercises as assistance work (the reverse direction of transfer).

be a translation/editing inconsistency between the prose's exercise name and the table's
row label; do not assume which one is authoritative without checking the original Russian
or a second translation.

almost no transfer anywhere in this section except isolated single-level effects." The
source states more transfer than that: for men's pole vault, "a positive transfer was
observed on all levels of sports results in the barbell snatch and in the half squat with
the barbell on the shoulders" (PDF p. 111, printed p. 94); more broadly, "in the second
strength exercise (barbell snatch) the cumulative training effect had a place on several
levels of sports mastery in most events except for the women's high jump and men's triple
jump" (PDF p. 112, printed p. 95). Men's long jump snatch correlations ran 6.5-7.3m level
(PDF p. 103, printed p. 86). The half squat with barbell transferred even more
consistently — all levels, both sexes, in high jump and pole vault (PDF p. 112, printed
p. 95).

was not the short-run-up vault: it was the 60m run from blocks (0.856, 0.886), above the

event's own competitive movement is itself a specialized-developmental exercise (repeats
the competitive action's parts under an altered, easier condition), which would place it

population (likely predominantly the Fosbury Flop or straddle technique of that era) and
should not be over-generalized without checking which technique his athletes used (not
stated in the excerpted pages). Applying any of these specific exercise priorities to a
football skill (e.g., a receiver's high-point jump) is Inference — no football population
data exists in this source.

reduced run-up length) as the top assistance tool, alongside sprint work, is
well-supported by this data; the same prioritization for a high jumper should shift toward
short-approach vertical jumps and multi-jump work rather than assuming sprint speed
transfers the same way.

===== PDF page 65 (viewer 66) =====
It also became clear that achieving a definite level of test results, even in the specialized-
developmental exercises, does not guarantee an increase in sports achievement in the 
main event.  All of this once again is evidence of the complexity of the process of 
training transfer in situations relating to the training of high level athletes.  For 
understanding this, it is necessary to have a new quality level of understanding. 
 
*********************************************************************** 
 
The theoretical and experimental material that has been put together makes it possible to 
explain many factors involved in the process of training transfer.  This is related 
primarily to the different methods of constructing cycles of sports form development.  
Each one of them is distinguished from the other in the system of using general-
preparatory, special-preparatory, special-developmental and competitive exercises.  The 
systems of exercises looked at appear as some kind of expediently organized aggregate 
that is always directed to achievement of the end purpose.  This purpose is primarily 
directed to entry into the state of sports form in the competitive exercise at the end of the 
sports form development cycle and achievement of a definite level of sports results.   
 
Depending upon the schematic of the means used for constructing the above mentioned 
cycles of sports training, transfer of training from one form of exercise to another can 
take place in sequence or at the same time.  In the first case, are ways of constructing 
sports form development that consist of a certain number of stages, blocks.  For each 
stage, block, the previous one creates the “base”, “foundation” for the one following.  In 
the second case, the discussion is primarily of the complex method.  Here, the exercises 
used over the entire cycle of sports form development have a mutual effect on one 
another which then serves to produce simultaneous entry into the state of sports form as 
well as showing improvement in the competitive exercise.   
 
The training process is constructed so that the general-preparatory, special-preparatory 
and special-developmental exercises promote an increase in results in the main event.  
Here, the “base”, “foundation”, is created along the lines of entry into the state of sports 
48

# Bondarchuk Publishes 34 Normative Tables Linking Assistance-Exercise Results to Competitive-Result Bands, by Age and Qualification

**What it is** — Tables 1-34 (PDF pp. 44-67, printed pp. 27-50; this ingest sampled
representative tables rather than transcribing all 34) give normative "model
characteristics": for a given competitive-result band (e.g., 100m in 10.00-10.20s vs.
10.80-11.00s), a matching range of expected results in assistance exercises. Examples
pulled directly: **Table 1** ties 100m sprint splits (10m through 100m segments) to
five 100m-time bands. **Table 2** ties speed-strength markers (standing long jump,
triple/5-fold/10-fold jump from place, single-leg and alternate-leg jumps for time) to
those same five 100m bands — e.g., a 10.00-10.20s sprinter should stand-long-jump
3.10-3.30m, a 10.80-11.00s sprinter 2.70-2.90m. Similar tables exist for 200m, 400m,
women's 100m hurdles, and age-banded (15-16 / 17-18 / 19+) versions for 400m men and
women across successive preparatory/competitive periods (Tables 10-14). Table 8 also
gives named-athlete individual data (L. Evans, T. Smith, V. Markin, and others) with
columns for 100m result, 200m result, a "repeated results in the 200m" value, the 400m
result, the difference between the repeated-200m value and the 400m result, and a
"Speed Reserve" column (e.g. L. Evans: 100m 10.2s, 200m 20.3s, repeated-200m 40.6s, 400m
43.86s, difference 3.26s, Speed Reserve 0.765). **The table does not state how "Speed
Reserve" is calculated**, and this ingest could not reverse-engineer a formula that
reproduces 0.765 from the other listed columns — do not assume a derivation for this
metric without finding the author's own definition elsewhere in the book (possibly in a
section not read in this batch). (PDF pp. 44-49, printed pp. 27-32.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given; these are purely descriptive normative
benchmarks compiled from the author's dataset, presented as targets an athlete "should"
hit at a given competitive level, not as evidence of a causal relationship. **Inference:**
this functions the same way modern S&C "standards tables" (e.g., a vertical-jump-by-40-
time chart) function — useful as a rough talent-identification or gap-analysis tool, not
as proof that improving the assistance-exercise number will improve the competitive time.

3.10-3.30m, a 10.80-11.00s sprinter 2.70-2.90m. Similar tables exist for 200m, 400m,
women's 100m hurdles, and age-banded (15-16 / 17-18 / 19+) versions for 400m men and

columns for 100m result, 200m result, a "repeated results in the 200m" value, the 400m
result, the difference between the repeated-200m value and the 400m result, and a "Speed
Reserve" column (e.g. L. Evans: 100m 10.2s, 200m 20.3s, repeated-200m 40.6s, 400m 43.86s,
difference 3.26s, Speed Reserve 0.765). The table does not state how "Speed Reserve" is
calculated. **Inference:** it reproduces cleanly as (400m time / 4) minus 100m time —
L. Evans: 43.86/4 - 10.2 = 0.765; T. Smith: 44.1/4 - 10.2 = 0.825; D. Carr: 46.2/4 - 10.4 =
1.150 — every row this ingest checked against that formula matched Table 8's printed
value. The book itself does not give this derivation. (PDF pp. 44-49, printed pp. 27-32.)

**Tables 35-40** give expected distance differences between the competitive implement and
lighter/heavier implements in the throws, by sex — e.g. men's hammer, 7.260kg vs. 5kg:
+13m (±3.4); 7.260kg vs. 10kg: -16m (±1.3) (Table 35, PDF p. 62, printed p. 45); similar
tables exist for shot, discus, and javelin (men and women). (PDF pp. 62-64, printed
pp. 45-47.)

**Norms were built two ways.** "Individually-selected": each exercise's best mark is drawn
from whichever of the ten strongest athletes in the world/country produced it (so
different exercises in the same row can come from different athletes). "Collective-
average": the ten best athletes' marks in each exercise are summed and averaged, and that
average serves as the target; this is the method "used most frequently." (PDF p. 61,
printed p. 44.)

**The author's own not-causal caveat.** Bondarchuk states this limitation himself, not
only as this entry's inference: test levels in these exercises let a coach "judge the
speed-strength abilities of each individual separately. However, this does not to any
degree determine the amount of increase in the competitive exercises (events)" (PDF p. 61,
printed p. 44). Later in the chapter he restates it for the specialized-developmental
exercises specifically: "achieving a definite level of test results, even in the
specialized-developmental exercises, does not guarantee an increase in sports achievement
in the main event" (PDF p. 65, printed p. 48).

hit at a given competitive level, not as evidence of a causal relationship (the author's
own caveat above makes this explicit, not just an inference). **Inference:** this
functions the same way modern S&C "standards tables" (e.g., a vertical-jump-by-40-
time chart) function — useful as a rough talent-identification or gap-analysis tool, not
as proof that improving the assistance-exercise number will improve the competitive time.

10.80-11.00s), a matching range of expected results in assistance exercises. Examples
pulled directly: **Table 1** ties 100m sprint splits (10m through 100m segments) to
five 100m-time bands. **Table 2** ties speed-strength markers (standing long jump,
triple/5-fold/10-fold jump from place, single-leg and alternate-leg jumps for time) to
those same five 100m bands — e.g., a 10.00-10.20s sprinter should stand-long-jump
3.10-3.30m, a 10.80-11.00s sprinter 2.70-2.90m. Similar tables exist for 200m, 400m,
women's 100m hurdles, and age-banded (15-16 / 17-18 / 19+) versions for 400m men and
women across successive preparatory/competitive periods (Tables 10-14). Table 8 also
gives named-athlete individual data (L. Evans, T. Smith, V. Markin, and others) with
columns for 100m result, 200m result, a "repeated results in the 200m" value, the 400m
result, the difference between the repeated-200m value and the 400m result, and a
"Speed Reserve" column (e.g. L. Evans: 100m 10.2s, 200m 20.3s, repeated-200m 40.6s, 400m
43.86s, difference 3.26s, Speed Reserve 0.765). **The table does not state how "Speed
Reserve" is calculated**, and this ingest could not reverse-engineer a formula that
reproduces 0.765 from the other listed columns — do not assume a derivation for this
metric without finding the author's own definition elsewhere in the book (possibly in a
section not read in this batch). (PDF pp. 44-49, printed pp. 27-32.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given; these are purely descriptive normative
benchmarks compiled from the author's dataset, presented as targets an athlete "should"
hit at a given competitive level, not as evidence of a causal relationship. **Inference:**
this functions the same way modern S&C "standards tables" (e.g., a vertical-jump-by-40-
time chart) function — useful as a rough talent-identification or gap-analysis tool, not
as proof that improving the assistance-exercise number will improve the competitive time.

Baylor's own sport-specific normative tables (a named gap in `method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment," citing `performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase
2`): Bondarchuk's tables show what a rigorous, qualification-banded normative table looks
like (multiple assistance exercises per competitive-result band, banded by age where
relevant), even though the specific numbers are 1970s-80s Soviet track and field data and
not directly usable for a 2026 football roster.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported**, and only as a description that these
tables exist and roughly what they show — this entry does not treat any individual number
as validated for use as a current standard. The population is elite/sub-elite Soviet-era
male and female track and field athletes (refs [52], [74], [75] per the tables), not
football players; the specific split times, jump distances, and the Table 8 "speed
reserve" formula are Inference if applied to any other sport or era without
re-derivation. This ingest did not transcribe all 34 tables (only Tables 1-14 were pulled
in full); a future batch revisiting this chapter should note that gap before citing a
table number 15-34 that was not directly checked here.

**Example** — A recruiting or testing-standards project comparing "where does our sprinter
sit" could borrow the *format* (competitive-result band -> matching assistance-exercise
range, split by age where useful) from Table 2/10-14 without adopting the actual Soviet-
era numbers.

Eric's own gap analysis in `method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment," for the live
Baylor need this table format could inform.
