# Specialized-Developmental Runs (Flying 30m, Blocks 30-200m) Correlate Strongly with Sprint/Hurdle Competitive Results

**What it is** — Tables 41-50 (PDF pp. 78-87, printed pp. 61-70) report correlation
coefficients between competitive results and other specialized-developmental/competitive
run distances, for men's and women's 100m, 200m, 400m, 110m/400m hurdles (men) and
100m/400m hurdles (women), each split by "high level" vs. "low level" athlete
qualification (the table note: high-level in the numerator, low-level in the denominator
for these specific tables — Tables 41-50 only; see the reversed convention noted in
`_book.md` for the throws tables). Bondarchuk's own summary: "the coefficients of
correlation in most cases are in the range of 0.700-0.800" (PDF p. 87, printed p. 70).
Representative individual values pulled directly (high-qualification/low-qualification):
100m runners' 30m-flying-start correlated 0.678/0.778 with the 30m-from-blocks segment and
0.756/0.876 with the 100m-from-blocks segment (Table 41); 110m hurdlers' 110m-hurdles
result correlated only 0.562/0.420 with the 200m-from-blocks segment, the weakest pairing
in that table (Table 44); 400m hurdlers' 400m-hurdles result correlated as high as
0.890/0.806 with the 600m-from-a-high-start segment (Table 45).

**Why it works** — The tables report the correlations without explaining them. **Inference:**
reading this through
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] and
[[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — these are all specialized-developmental
or competitive-class exercises (shorter/longer runs at or near race intensity), sharing
most of the sprint or hurdle event's biomechanics and energy-system demands, which would
predict the high correlation observed — but this connection is this entry's own reading,
not a claim the author makes for this specific table set.

**When to apply** — Use as historical evidence that assistance runs at varied distances
(flying starts, sub-maximal and supra-maximal segment lengths) are a reliably transferable
training tool for sprint/hurdle athletes, supporting programs that use varied-distance
sprint work rather than only full-distance reps. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355's
linear-sprint testing already uses split-time interpretation by physical quality (0-10m
acceleration, 30-40m speed) rather than total time alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed
and sprint," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`) — this book's high
segment-to-total correlations support treating those splits as meaningfully diagnostic,
not just a total-time proxy.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite and sub-elite
Soviet-era male and female sprinters and hurdlers (refs implicit in the tables' athlete
qualification split; exact sample sizes are not given in the excerpted pages). The
correlations described are all between running-based specialized-developmental/
competitive exercises — this entry does NOT cover strength or jump-exercise transfer,
which is markedly weaker (see
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] and
[[claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]]). Applying these specific
coefficients to football skill-position speed training is Inference: football speed
development sits inside a team-sport context with far less training-time devoted purely
to sprinting than a specialized Soviet track program, so the magnitude of these
correlations should not be assumed to hold as-is.

**Example** — A 200m runner's training program built heavily around 150m and 300m
repeats at race-adjacent intensity is well-supported by this data (150m-to-200m and
300m-to-200m correlations were among the higher entries in Table 42), more so than a
program relying mainly on much shorter (30m) segments for that specific event.

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification these
correlated exercises fall into. [[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] —
the much weaker transfer picture for non-running assistance exercises in the same event
group.

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts

**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and triple
jump from place each showed positive transfer only on two-to-three of five levels for most
events, and high jump/pole vault-style single jumps were even more level-restricted for
sprint events specifically (not their own competitive event). He generalizes: "with an
increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises, there
is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
exercises over long ground-contact segments (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.)

**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) **Inference:** reading
this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real
sprint-relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing
jump does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict
exactly
the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.

**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
diagnostic/training value.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
sprinters and hurdlers, both sexes; "leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from
place" are specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding
or plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference; no outside
plyometrics source was checked in this ingest to confirm the pattern holds beyond
Bondarchuk's own track and field dataset.

**Example** — A sprint-development block choosing between a session of standing long
jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m would, per this
data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider range of athlete
ability levels.

running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.
[[claim--jump-event-exercise-transfer-patterns]] — the parallel (and partly consistent)
finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.

# Among Assistance Exercises, Multi-Jump Work (Ten-Fold Jump, Leg-to-Leg Bounds) Transfers to Sprinting Most Consistently — More Than Single Jumps, Throws, or Barbell Lifts

**What it is** — Comparing all the specialized-preparatory assistance exercises tested
against sprint/hurdle competitive results (barbell snatch, half squat, standing long jump,
vertical jump, triple jump from place, 10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m,
forward/backward shot throws), Bondarchuk identifies the **10-fold jump from place** and
**leg-to-leg (bounding) jumps for 50m** as "more transferable than other specialized-
preparatory exercises," measured not by having the single highest correlation coefficient
but by the number of qualification-level bands across which a positive cumulative effect
appears (PDF p. 99, printed p. 82). Concretely: leg-to-leg jumps for 50m showed a
cumulative effect on **all levels** for both men's and women's 100m, and across the full
range for women's 100m hurdles (12.80-15.80s) and men's 400m hurdles (49.50-55.50s) (PDF
p. 100, printed p. 83). **Exceptions to that consistency**, cutting against reading it as
uniform: leg-to-leg 50m appeared on only one qualification level in men's 200m (20.50-
21.00sec), men's 110m hurdles (15.50-16.00sec), and women's 400m hurdles (58.00-59.00sec)
(PDF p. 100, printed p. 83). By contrast, the standing long jump, vertical jump, and
triple jump from place did not show a uniform two-to-three-of-five-levels pattern: the
vertical jump appeared on five of five levels in men's 110m hurdles and four of five in
women's 100m hurdles, while the triple jump from place appeared on four of five levels in
women's 100m (PDF pp. 90-91, printed pp. 73-74) — stronger than "two-to-three for most
events" in those specific cases, even while the overall claim (multi-jump work is more
consistent than single jumps) still holds directionally. There is no high-jump or
pole-vault exercise tested against sprint results anywhere in this table set (Table 51's
rows are snatch, half squat, standing long jump, vertical jump, triple jump from place,
10-fold jump from place, leg-to-leg jumps for 50m, and forward/backward shot throws, PDF
p. 91, printed p. 74) — an earlier draft of this entry invented a high jump/pole vault
comparison that does not exist in the source; it has been removed. He generalizes: "with
an increase in a number of take-offs when executing the above mentioned jump exercises,
there is an increase in the number of cases of positive transfer" — proposing multi-jump
exercises "executed over long segments of time" (20-150m) as the most broadly transferable
jump category for track and field generally. (PDF pp. 100-101, printed pp. 83-84.) He adds
a practical recommendation this entry had not previously captured: specialists should
systematically use lightened and more complex (weighted) jump conditions for the full
duration of the sports-form cycle rather than sporadically as was then common, and should
attend to the optimal angle of incline used for speed vs. strength development, since
incline affects both effectiveness and the number of technical errors (PDF p. 101, printed
p. 84).

**Why it works** — His own stated mechanism: multi-jump exercises over distance "repeat
the biomechanical parameters of the competitive movement" more closely than single jumps,
"have a similar appearance to the muscle work regimes, and use the same intensity zones,"
and can duplicate the sprint's actual duration/segment structure (e.g. matching a starting-
acceleration segment specifically). (PDF p. 101, printed p. 84.) **Inference:** reading
this through [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], repeated bounding over a real
sprint-relevant distance sits closer to specialized-developmental than a single standing
jump does, which under [[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict
exactly
the stronger, more level-consistent transfer observed here.

**When to apply** — When choosing between plyometric/jump exercise variants for a
sprint-focused program, this data favors prioritizing repeated multi-jump/bounding work
over set distances (matched to the target phase of the sprint — acceleration vs. max
velocity) over single-effort jumps (standing long jump, vertical jump) as the more
consistently transferable choice, while still using single jumps for their own
diagnostic/training value.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
sprinters and hurdlers, both sexes; "leg-to-leg jumps for 50m" and "10-fold jump from
place" are specific, defined tests in this text, not a stand-in for every modern bounding
or plyometric variation. The claim is about *transfer consistency across qualification
levels*, not about which exercise has the single highest correlation value — do not
conflate the two when citing this entry. Applying this preference (multi-jump over
single-jump assistance work) to football speed/power training is Inference; no outside
plyometrics source was checked in this ingest to confirm the pattern holds beyond
Bondarchuk's own track and field dataset.

**Example** — A sprint-development block choosing between a session of standing long
jumps and a session of 10-15 continuous alternate-leg bounds over 30-50m would, per this
data, expect the bounding session to transfer more reliably across a wider range of athlete
ability levels.

**Related** — [[claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations]] — the
running-based exercises that transfer even more strongly than jumps in this event group.

finding for jump-event athletes' own competitive results.

representative, not narrow.

shoulders to the competitive event in the men's and women's 400m hurdles, as well as the

own text at PDF p. 89, printed p. 72). Throws of the shot forward/backward
were even weaker transfer exercises, positive only for 110m hurdlers at two narrow bands
(13.50-14.00s and 14.00-14.50s) and absent elsewhere. (PDF pp. 88-90, printed pp. 71-73.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: "the cumulative effect from strength
exercises will appear only when they are close to the competitive event according to the

lifts (see [[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for

variation without its own data. This is track and field data; extending "barbell strength
work plateaus in its transfer to top-end speed past a certain level" to football speed
training is Inference. No outside source was checked in this ingest to confirm whether
this pattern holds beyond Bondarchuk's own dataset; treat it as this book's finding only
until cross-checked.

squat or snatch PRs to reliably predict further 100m improvement, per this data; a
developing sprinter in the 11.0-11.5s range is more likely to still be inside the band
where this book's data shows a measurable (if still modest) positive relationship.

stronger transfer picture for running-based assistance work in the same event group.

# Three Types of Training Transfer, Plus "Indifferent" (Double-Effect) Transfer

**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three types of training transfer (PDF p. 31, printed

- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in

addition: "In the specialized literature it is also possible to find 'indifferent'
transfer." He returns to it separately: "In addition to these three noted forms of
training transfer we more rarely meet with indifferent transfer" — **indifferent transfer
is the double-effect case**, not a synonym for neutral. It shows up "especially... when
training high level athletes who use a whole complex of different exercises," and can have
"a double effect on one another": a positive effect on one dimension and a negative effect
on another at the same time. Example: heavier-implement throws can be "positive... on
increasing the functional capabilities of the body systems and a negative effect on the
technique," and "there is a noticeable worsening of technique in some throws with the use
of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]) — with increased strength, "a negative change in
the process of executing separate elements as well as the entire movement as a whole"
[152]. (PDF p. 31, printed p. 14.)

anaerobic running in general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory
function but worsened walking technique [94] — a positive-physiological/negative-technical
double effect. He also gives a remedy: walkers can avoid the negative influence "by using
mainly specialized-developmental and competitive exercises"; in other running events,
hurdles, and throws, coaches can select among exercises so "there would be more good ones
rather than poor ones," which "makes it possible to eliminate the negative influence on
technique in several weekly cycles." (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)

give an explanation: "The double effect of certain exercises on others (indifferent
transfer) is most frequently explained by the use of exercises which, from the beginning,
interfere with the unity between form and content" (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15) — the

technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
illustration. **Inference:** flagging any high-volume general-conditioning block for a
technical, timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect
risk is this entry's own extension of the walking case, not something the passage states

exercises, or bias exercise selection toward "good" over "poor" options) applies whichever
sport is in question.

technique) are drawn from Soviet-era track and field research cited only by bracketed

data mainly from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results

# Training Transfer Comes in Four Flavors: Positive, Negative, Neutral, and Indifferent

**What it is** — Bondarchuk names three standard types of training transfer plus a fourth
he flags as rarer and specific to high-level athletes (PDF pp. 31-32, printed pp. 14-15):
- **Positive**: an increase in one exercise's result parallels an increase in another.
- **Negative**: an increase in preparation for one exercise coincides with a decrease in
  another.
- **Neutral** (also "indifferent" in some literature he cites): no measurable effect
  either way.
- **Indifferent/double effect** (his own added category, "met more rarely," specifically
  in high-level athletes using a complex of different exercises): one exercise can help
  and hurt at the same time along different dimensions, e.g. heavier-implement throws
  positive for strength but negative for technique — "there is a noticeable worsening of
  technique in some throws with the use of heavier implements" (refs [18, 152]). Bondarchuk
  gives a specific example: race walkers doing high volumes of aerobic/anaerobic running in
  general preparation showed improved heart-circulatory/respiratory function but worsened
  walking technique (ref [94]), a case of positive-physiological/negative-technical
  double effect. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 15.)

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk gives no mechanism for why transfer takes these particular
forms; he presents the three-way split as received terminology ("in the specialized
literature it is also possible to find 'indifferent' transfer," without naming a specific
source for that term) and adds the fourth (double-effect) category as his own observation.
**Note on scope:** Chapter 1's earlier discussion of E.L. Thorndike's "theory of identical
elements" (PDF p. 20, printed p. 3; see
[[framework--three-viewpoints-on-training-transfer]]) is presented by Bondarchuk as the
basis for the *specifist* position on transfer generally, not explicitly linked by him to
this positive/negative/neutral/indifferent typology — this entry does not claim that link
was Bondarchuk's own. **Inference:** the double-effect category is a plausible, useful name
for a pattern coaches encounter often (an exercise that builds one quality while degrading
another), but this is this entry's own framing, not a claim from the text about how common
or well-recognized that pattern is elsewhere.

**When to apply** — Use the four-way split as a checklist when introducing a new
exercise: is the expected effect positive, negative, neutral, or a **double effect**
where it will help one quality while hurting another (most often physical capacity up,
technique down, from overloaded implements/loads)? The walking example is the clean
illustration — flag any high-volume general-conditioning block for a technical,
timing-sensitive sport skill (sprinting, throwing, agility) as a double-effect risk, not
just a "general conditioning is fine" default.

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary: "there is
almost always a place for mutually correlated interrelationships... the amounts of these
interrelationships are sufficiently great," with only two exceptions found in the entire
dataset (javelin: no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and the 3-4kg standing
throw; no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements). (PDF p. 132, printed p.
115.) He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (Tables 85-86, PDF pp. 130-131,
printed pp. 113-114). Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his
implement-weight throws increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances
(Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.

**When to apply** — This is the strongest, most consistent transfer finding in the entire
book: for throwing events specifically, varying implement weight while keeping the
competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training method across nearly the
full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any strength, jump, or sprint
assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter. He does flag a real caveat: heavier
implements can degrade technique (release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect
he says clears up "in several weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the
double-effect pattern named in [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa/Shulta individual case data (Tables
85-88) is **untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not
as independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. Population throughout is elite Soviet-bloc throwers (Olympic and world
champions/record holders for the case studies). This finding is specific to implements
that can be made lighter or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact
(shot, discus, javelin, hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight
manipulation in most football skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement
identical" as a general training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a
quarterback) is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — A hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of 5-6 different
implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight) targeting both speed and
strength qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as
a transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat.

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary: "there is
almost always a place for mutually correlated interrelationships... the amounts of these
interrelationships are sufficiently great," with only two exceptions found in the entire
dataset (javelin: no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and the 3-4kg standing
throw; no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements). (PDF p. 132, printed p.
115.) He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (Tables 85-86, PDF pp. 130-131,
printed pp. 113-114). Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his
implement-weight throws increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances
(Table 88, PDF p. 141, printed p. 124).

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.

**When to apply** — This is the strongest, most consistent transfer finding in the entire
book: for throwing events specifically, varying implement weight while keeping the
competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training method across nearly the
full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any strength, jump, or sprint
assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter. He does flag a real caveat: heavier
implements can degrade technique (release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect
he says clears up "in several weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the
double-effect pattern named in [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa/Shulta individual case data (Tables
85-88) is **untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not
as independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. Population throughout is elite Soviet-bloc throwers (Olympic and world
champions/record holders for the case studies). This finding is specific to implements
that can be made lighter or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact
(shot, discus, javelin, hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight
manipulation in most football skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement
identical" as a general training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a
quarterback) is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — A hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of 5-6 different
implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight) targeting both speed and
strength qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as
a transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat.

champions specifically). This finding is specific to implements that can be made lighter

training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a quarterback) is

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary quote is broader
in scope than "lighter/heavier vs. competitive": "there is almost always a place for
mutually correlated interrelationships between special-developmental exercises (throws and
'shot putting' various implements having different weights from place) and exercises with
lighter, heavier and competitive implements" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115) — i.e. it covers
standing throws of various weights against full lighter/heavier/competitive throws, not
only the lighter/heavier-vs.-competitive pairing this entry's title highlights. He gives
**three** exceptions, not two: javelin, no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and
the 3-4kg standing throw; javelin, no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements;
and, in women, "no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the competitive
implement and in standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115).

**The dose that produces the strongest correlations.** "The greatest amounts of
correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations
[from competition weight] was insignificant in relation to the competitive — from 10-20%."
The weakest values in the whole dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the
16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at
the 20-21m level — notably, that 0.365 weak value sits at the *top* competitive level, not
a low one, so "near-universal transfer" should carry that qualifier. (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98.) **A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the
0.365 value above only barely clears it.

He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125, not PDF
pp. 130-131 as an earlier draft of this entry cited). The same passage contrasts this with
his *specialized-preparatory* exercise results, which tracked the competitive result in
only 8 of 35 cases and were "autonomous" (untracking) in the other 27 — a sharp difference
from the implement-weight throws' near-lockstep pattern (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125).
Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his implement-weight throws
increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances (Table 88, PDF p. 141,
printed p. 124), against his specialized-preparatory exercises tracking in only 32 of 49
instances (32 with, 17 without) (PDF p. 141, printed p. 124) — the same implement-weight-
vs.-specialized-preparatory contrast Sedikh's data shows.

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as the strongest, most consistent transfer
finding in the excerpted chapters — for throwing events specifically, varying implement
weight while keeping the competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training
method across nearly the full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any
strength, jump, or sprint assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter — but that
cross-chapter comparison is this entry's own judgment, not a claim the author makes; his
own claim is narrower: "throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to be the most
transferable to the competitive exercise" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98), without comparing
across chapters. He does flag a real caveat: heavier implements can degrade technique
(release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect he says clears up "in several
weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the double-effect pattern named in
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported for the aggregate correlational
finding (Tables 69-84)**, but the Sedikh/Ubartasa/Shulta individual case data (Tables
85-88) is **untested**: single elite-athlete case studies, presented as illustration, not
as independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. Population throughout is elite Soviet-bloc throwers (Olympic and world
champions/record holders for the case studies). This finding is specific to implements
that can be made lighter or heavier while keeping the throwing motion otherwise intact
(shot, discus, javelin, hammer); there is no directly equivalent implement-weight
manipulation in most football skills, so applying "vary the resistance, keep the movement
identical" as a general training principle to football (e.g., weighted-ball throwing for a
quarterback) is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — A hammer thrower's training plan built around a rotation of 5-6 different
implement weights (lighter and heavier than competition weight) targeting both speed and
strength qualities within the same movement pattern is strongly supported by this data as
a transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for
that same purpose (see [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]).

**Related** — [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]] — the classification
explaining this exercise's near-maximal transfer. [[claim--throws-strength-exercise-ceiling-effect]]
— the much more limited transfer picture for barbell strength exercises in the same event
group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat.

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw, but **only up to a specific result level for each
exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive improvement
disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m
(men) / 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended
furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three.
In shot put, snatch ended at 17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m
(men)/14-25m (women, likely an OCR artifact for a narrower band), squat at 19-20m
(men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). In javelin, snatch and power
clean both ended at 65-70m (men); at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for
either the squat or the bench press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat "showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135,
printed pp. 116-118.) Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the
close of this chapter: "specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an
increase in the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports
mastery. Further on, they do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.

**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
strength work maintained rather than chased.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — what to do with
strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the parallel (and even more limited)
ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw, but **only up to a specific result level for each
exercise and event**, after which the correlation with further competitive improvement
disappears. Worked examples with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m
(men) / 55-60m (women); power clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended
furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m (women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three.
In shot put, snatch ended at 17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m
(men)/14-25m (women, likely an OCR artifact for a narrower band), squat at 19-20m
(men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). In javelin, snatch and power
clean both ended at 65-70m (men); at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for
either the squat or the bench press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean
50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat "showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135,
printed pp. 116-118.) Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the
close of this chapter: "specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an
increase in the sports result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports
mastery. Further on, they do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.

**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
strength work maintained rather than chased.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] — what to do with
strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.
[[claim--sprint-strength-exercise-transfer-ceiling]] — the parallel (and even more limited)
ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.

# Barbell Snatch, Power Clean, Squat, and Bench Press All Transfer to Throwing — But Only Up to a Specific Result Level, Then Plateau

**What it is** — Across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer, Bondarchuk finds that all
four major strength exercises (snatch, power clean, squat with barbell on shoulders,
bench press — bench excluded for hammer throwers, who "do not use it") show a positive
transfer to the competitive throw **in most event/sex groups** (exception: javelin, see
below), but **only up to a specific result level for each exercise and event**, after
which the correlation with further competitive improvement disappears. Worked examples
with locators: in discus, snatch transfer ended at 45-50m (men) / 55-60m (women); power
clean and squat ended at 50-55m; bench press extended furthest, to 55-60m (men) / 65-70m
(women). In hammer, snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean 65-70m, squat 60-65m; women's
cumulative effect ran further, to 45-60m across all three. In shot put, snatch ended at
17-18m (men)/15-16m (women), power clean at 14-15m (men)/14-25m (women — a probable typo
in the printed text, not an OCR artifact: the source PDF has a real text layer, not a
scanned/OCR'd page, so this is either a source misprint or an unusually wide band), squat
at 19-20m (men)/17-18m (women), bench at 18-19m (men)/19-20m (women). **In javelin, the
"all four transfer" pattern breaks**: snatch and power clean both ended at 65-70m (men);
at the 50-55m level "there was no correlation seen" for either the squat or the bench
press (men); women's snatch ended at 60-65m, power clean 50-55m, bench 45-50m, and squat
"showed no cumulative transfer effect" at all. (PDF pp. 133-135, printed pp. 116-118.)
Bondarchuk's own aggregate summary across the whole book, at the close of this chapter:
"specialized-preparatory exercises have a positive influence on an increase in the sports
result in the basic event but up to a specific level of sports mastery. Further on, they
do not show a positive effect." (PDF p. 175, printed p. 158.) He also notes, from the same
chapter's closing material, that "the leading throwers (world and Olympic champions and
world record holders) do not always have the best absolute results in the specialized-
preparatory exercises" (PDF p. 139, printed p. 122) — a further data point supporting the
ceiling: being the best thrower does not require the best strength numbers.

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why the ceiling occurs at these specific
levels; **Inference:** this is consistent with a training-age/diminishing-returns pattern
common across strength and power sports — general strength qualities predict performance
strongly at lower levels of mastery, but as an athlete's absolute strength approaches the
level "required" for the skill, further strength gains stop being the limiting factor and
technical/specialized qualities (captured better by the specialized-developmental
exercises in [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]) take over as the
binding constraint. Bondarchuk does not state this diminishing-returns interpretation
himself in the excerpted text; it is this entry's own reading.

**When to apply** — Use as a rationale for shifting a throwing (or other power-sport)
athlete's programming emphasis away from general barbell strength work and toward
specialized-developmental work (implement-weight variation, technical throws) once the
athlete's absolute strength numbers cross into the "cumulative effect ends here" range for
their event, rather than continuing to chase strength PRs as the primary lever for
competitive improvement.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** Population is elite/sub-elite Soviet
throwers of both sexes, using a specific set of four lifts (Olympic-style snatch and power
clean, not necessarily modern variations; a barbell squat and bench press without stated
depth/technique standards). The exact result-level thresholds are specific to this
1970s-80s dataset and should not be treated as current standards. This entry does NOT mean
"stop lifting" once the ceiling is reached — see
[[heuristic--maintain-specialized-preparatory-exercises-past-ceiling]] for the author's own
explicit statement that these exercises should still be used at reduced volume for
maintenance and restoration. Applying this ceiling-effect logic to a football strength
athlete (e.g., an offensive lineman) is Inference: no football population data exists
here, and a lineman's "competitive exercise" is far less discrete than a single measured
throw.

**Example** — A discus thrower already squatting well past the 50-55m-equivalent strength
level, per this data, should not expect further squat PRs alone to keep driving discus
distance; continued improvement is better targeted through implement-weight variation and
technical work (see [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]]), with
strength work maintained rather than chased.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
specialized-developmental alternative that keeps transferring past this ceiling.

strength work once this ceiling is reached, in the author's own words.

ceiling pattern for strength exercises in sprinting.

significance tests, or population age/sex breakdowns beyond "high qualification" vs "low
qualification"** groups (the tables' own note: "the coefficient of correlation of high
level athletes is in the numerator and for low level athletes, in the denominator," with

(41-50, high/low) and the throws tables (70, 72, 74, 76, 78: "low qualifications... in the
numerator and high level athletes in the denominator" — the reverse). This flip is real,
not a transcription slip; see `claim--sprint-hurdle-specialized-developmental-correlations.md`
and `claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal.md` for the locators. Treat
any single number pulled from these tables with that reversal risk in mind.

# Implement-Weight Variation Works Best Close to Competition Weight, and History Shows an Overdose Is Possible: The "Throwing Boom"

**What it is — new entry, review's Missing Item 4.** This entry gathers three related
facts about how throwers historically dosed lighter/heavier-implement work, none of which
were captured by the correlational-transfer entry
[[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] even after that entry's own
review fixes.

**1. The dosing law: correlations peak close to competition weight, not far from it.**
"The greatest amounts of correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in
cases where the deviations [from the competitive implement weight] was insignificant in
relation to the competitive — from 10-20%." The weakest values in the whole implement-weight
dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the 16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m
level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at the 20-21m level. (PDF p. 115,
printed p. 98.)

**2. Historical practice and how much training time this now takes.** "It is generally
known that for developing strength abilities, heavier implements are used and for speed,
lighter." For most of the 20th century, throwers used mainly the competitive-weight
implement, with lighter/heavier implements used "sporadically and in small volume" —
heavier implements in the fall-winter season, lighter implements immediately before
competition, typically in 4-6 week cycles. "In the last two decades" (relative to this
book's writing) that changed: lighter, heavier, and competitive-weight implement work
together now comprises **30-50% of the total training time** across the yearly cycle. (PDF
p. 114, printed p. 97.) Distance-difference norms for specific implement/weight pairs by
event and sex are given in Tables 35-40 (PDF pp. 62-64, printed pp. 45-47; see
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] for the values).

**3. The "throwing boom" overdose warning.** Bondarchuk names a real historical error, not
a hypothetical one: "the 'throwing' boom which lasted for several Olympic cycles, in which
the athletes in one training session executed from 200-300 or more throws from place using
lighter or heavier implements. My record holders were included in this group. For example,
some hammer throwers executed up to 500 [1] throws of a weight in one training session."
He dates it: "The 'throwing' boom began after the 19th Olympic games in Mexico and ended
before the 22nd Olympic games in Moscow" (i.e., roughly 1968-1980). He states the boom
"produced negative after-effects" and recommends specialists "increase the volume of
training loads of specialized-developmental exercises up to reasonable amounts in order to
avoid the errors made by throwers in past years." Separately, he notes that in sports
practice "many specialists are already convinced that the use of imitational exercises
without resistance[s], do not have a positive influence on the development of physical
abilities of low as well as high level athletes" — i.e. dropping the implement's weight
entirely (miming the throw) is not a safe substitute either; the dosing problem runs in
both directions. (PDF p. 133, printed p. 116.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given for why 200-300+ throws per session produced
negative after-effects, or for why the 10-20% weight-deviation band produces the strongest
correlations. **Inference:** both points are consistent with a dose-response reading —
enough load variation to stress the target quality (strength via heavier, speed via
lighter) without drifting so far from the competitive movement's loading that technique or
recovery capacity breaks down — but the author does not state this interpretation himself
in the excerpted text.

**When to apply** — When programming implement-weight variation for a thrower (or
building an analogous variable-resistance protocol for another sport), use this entry as a
historical caution on both dosing axes: (a) keep the weight deviation from competition
implement modest (per the 10-20% band above) rather than assuming "more extreme is
better," and (b) do not assume "more volume of variable-weight throws is always more
transferable" — the throwing-boom history shows a real, named historical case where
volume (200-500 throws/session) produced negative after-effects, not better transfer.
**Inference:** mapped loosely onto a non-throws context, this reads as a general caution
against unbounded volume escalation of any specialized-developmental variant, not just
implement-weight throws — that generalization is this entry's own, not the author's.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is supported.** **A positive interrelationship begins
at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); this entry's dosing law describes which correlations
run highest within that already-positive range, not a pass/fail threshold. **Population:**
native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of mixed qualification, data mainly
from questionnaires over four Olympic cycles plus published individual results (PDF p. 8,
printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not football, not team sport. The "throwing
boom" is a specific, dated historical episode (roughly 1968-1980) in Soviet-bloc throws
training, not a controlled study; Bondarchuk gives no session count, athlete count, or
comparison-condition data for the "negative after-effects" claim, and he includes his own
record-holding athletes among those who did it, without saying whether or how it affected
their specific results. Applying the 200-300-throw figure as a hard ceiling for a different
sport's variable-resistance work is Inference by analogy, not something this data tests.

**Example** — **Inference:** a hammer throwing program that rotates through implements
7.26kg (competition), 6kg, and 8kg (roughly 10-17% off competition weight) is better
supported by the dosing law above than one that jumps straight to 16kg or a bare-bar
imitation throw; and a coach programming 200+ standing throws in a single session, echoing
the historical "throwing boom," should treat that volume as a documented historical
cautionary case, not a target.

**Related** — [[claim--throws-implement-weight-transfer-near-universal]] — the
correlational finding this entry's dosing law and overdose warning were missing from.
[[claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]] — Tables 35-40's specific
distance-difference norms by implement/weight pair. [[heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]]
— this book folder's Method paragraph (questionnaires, four Olympic cycles, 0.349
threshold, steroid exclusion), which this entry's dosing-law correlations also fall under.

# Throwing Lighter and Heavier Versions of the Same Implement Transfers to the Competitive Throw Almost Universally, Across Nearly Every Level of Mastery

**What it is** — Tables 69-84 (PDF pp. 116-130, printed pp. 99-113) correlate results
throwing lighter/heavier implement weights (e.g., a 5-10kg shot, a 1.5-2.5kg discus, a
0.5-1kg javelin, a 3-16kg hammer/weight) against the competitive-weight throw, for men and
women across shot put, discus, javelin, and hammer. Bondarchuk's summary quote is broader
in scope than "lighter/heavier vs. competitive": "there is almost always a place for
mutually correlated interrelationships between special-developmental exercises (throws and
'shot putting' various implements having different weights from place) and exercises with
lighter, heavier and competitive implements" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115) — i.e. it covers
standing throws of various weights against full lighter/heavier/competitive throws, not
only the lighter/heavier-vs.-competitive pairing this entry's title highlights. He gives
**three** exceptions, not two: javelin, no relationship between the 0.6kg implement and
the 3-4kg standing throw; javelin, no relationship between the 0.7kg and 4kg implements;
and, in women, "no cumulative effect at the 40-45m level in throws with the competitive
implement and in standing throws with the shot weighing 3kg" (PDF p. 132, printed p. 115).

**The dose that produces the strongest correlations.** "The greatest amounts of
correlational interrelationships were most frequently found in cases where the deviations
[from competition weight] was insignificant in relation to the competitive — from 10-20%."
The weakest values in the whole dataset came from the largest deviations: 0.425 for the
16kg hammer weight at the 60-65m level, and 0.365 between the 5.0kg and 7.260kg shot at
the 20-21m level — notably, that 0.365 weak value sits at the *top* competitive level, not
a low one, so "near-universal transfer" should carry that qualifier. (PDF p. 115, printed
p. 98.) **A positive interrelationship begins at 0.349** (PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); the
0.365 value above only barely clears it.

He illustrates the practical power of this with individual elite-athlete case data
(**single-case, untested**, not aggregate correlation): two-time Olympic hammer champion
Yu. Sedikh held unofficial world-best-adjacent marks in the 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10kg
implements and the 16kg weight alongside his 86.74m competitive record, with year-by-year
dynamics (1980-86) showing his lighter/heavier implement results moving in lockstep with
his competitive result in 35 of 38 tracked instances (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125, not PDF
pp. 130-131 as an earlier draft of this entry cited). The same passage contrasts this with
his *specialized-preparatory* exercise results, which tracked the competitive result in
only 8 of 35 cases and were "autonomous" (untracking) in the other 27 — a sharp difference
from the implement-weight throws' near-lockstep pattern (PDF p. 142, printed p. 125).
Discus thrower R. Ubartasa's five-year log similarly shows his implement-weight throws
increasing alongside his competitive result in 29 of 34 instances (Table 88, PDF p. 141,
printed p. 124), against his specialized-preparatory exercises tracking in only 32 of 49
instances (32 with, 17 without) (PDF p. 141, printed p. 124) — the same implement-weight-
vs.-specialized-preparatory contrast Sedikh's data shows.

**Why it works** — Bondarchuk's own explanation: lighter/heavier-implement throws are
"identical to themselves according to the basic parameters beginning with the technical
and rhythmical composition and ending with the consecutiveness of inclusion of the
muscular groups... the muscle work regimes and so on" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98).
**Inference:** in the terms of [[framework--bondarchuk-four-exercise-classes]], this is as
close to a pure specialized-developmental exercise as exists in this book (the same
movement, only the resistance changes), which under
[[framework--transfer-chain-general-to-competitive]] would predict the near-universal
positive transfer observed — this classification-based reading is this entry's own, not
stated by the author in these terms.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this reads as the strongest, most consistent transfer
finding in the excerpted chapters — for throwing events specifically, varying implement
weight while keeping the competitive movement intact is a reliably transferable training
method across nearly the full range of athlete qualification, more consistent than any
strength, jump, or sprint assistance exercise tested elsewhere in this chapter — but that
cross-chapter comparison is this entry's own judgment, not a claim the author makes; his
own claim is narrower: "throws with lighter and heavier implements appear to be the most
transferable to the competitive exercise" (PDF p. 115, printed p. 98), without comparing
across chapters. He does flag a real caveat: heavier implements can degrade technique
(release angle, trunk lean, reduced amplitude), an effect he says clears up "in several
weekly cycles" once the heavier implement is dropped — the double-effect pattern named in
[[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]].

independent evidence of the mechanism, and Bondarchuk himself frames them as examples
rather than proof. **Population:** native (USSR) and foreign track and field athletes of

published individual results (PDF p. 8, printed p. vii; PDF p. 76, printed p. 59); not

transfer-reliable method, more so than substituting generic barbell strength work for

group. [[claim--three-types-of-training-transfer]] — the double-effect pattern behind the
heavier-implement technique caveat.
